2.title: Pre-treatment module at a glance
2.gist: This divider lists the three optional readiness sessions that come before the core curriculum: barriers, personal reasons, and a pros-and-cons weighing. The order is deliberate, moving from what stops people to what might pull them forward.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The sequence mirrors decisional balance from the transtheoretical model (Prochaska & DiClemente): before asking for action, help people see both sides of the ledger. Starting with barriers signals that their hesitation is taken seriously.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Tell the group up front that these three sessions are about deciding, not proving anything. Framing the module as a choice point lowers the guard of members who expect to be lectured.

ask: Why might opening with obstacles build more motivation than opening with benefits?
Which of the three sessions would your current group most need, and why?

3.title: Why a readiness module exists
3.gist: The page explains that these optional sessions target members who show little motivation, using motivational interviewing skills to soften resistance. It sets the goals: normalize resistance, name barriers, explore costs and benefits, and begin building trust.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Motivational interviewing (Miller & Rollnick) treats ambivalence as normal rather than as a character flaw. Resistance is read as a signal about the relationship and the timing, which the facilitator can change, not a fixed trait of the client.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: MI-based pre-treatment work tends to improve engagement and retention, especially for people who start out angry or reluctant. Effects on long-term substance use are more modest and vary across studies, so it works best as a doorway, not the whole house.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: In a mandated setting, 'readiness' can be ambiguous: attendance is required, so members may perform motivation. Watch for compliance that looks like change but is really self-protection.

ask: How do you tell genuine ambivalence from strategic compliance in a custody setting?
If motivation should be addressed throughout the program, what does that look like in Module 4 or 5?

terms.d: Core MI skills: open questions, affirmations, reflective listening, and summaries.
How prepared and willing a person is to engage in change work right now.

4.title: Pre-treatment worksheet lineup
4.gist: A list of the worksheets tied to each pre-treatment session, from spotting roadblocks to setting change goals. Use it to prep copies and see how each tool builds on the last.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The worksheets climb a ladder: name obstacles, connect use to life costs, rate readiness, weigh pros and cons, then commit to goals. Each step asks slightly more of the member than the one before.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Keep completed sheets in a folder per member. Returning to an early roadblock list in a later session lets people see their own movement, which is persuasive in a way your words are not.

ask: Which worksheet here asks the biggest emotional leap, and how would you prepare for it?
What would be lost if you skipped the practice work between sessions?

5.title: Barriers, responsivity, and withholding judgment
5.gist: The background frames session 1: people differ in what blocks their engagement, and naming internal and external barriers tells the facilitator about responsivity. It warns that a judgmental reply to a barrier will undo the session.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is the responsivity principle from risk-need-responsivity (Andrews & Bonta): delivery must fit the learner's culture, age, gender, history, and trust in the system. A barrier list is also a responsivity assessment in disguise.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The sarcastic retort about paying for drugs is tempting because it feels logical. Instead, reflect the cost honestly, something like: treatment asks a lot of you, and money is one more weight. Agreement disarms; argument recruits defense.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Procedural justice research suggests people cooperate more with systems they see as fair and respectful. Group-written rules are a small dose of that: authority shared rather than imposed.

ask: Which responsivity factors in your groups do you notice least often?
Why might group-made expectations be followed more than posted program rules?

terms.d: Matching how treatment is delivered to a person's learning style, culture, and circumstances.

6.title: Session 1 materials and flow
6.gist: The outline lists supplies and the six steps of the first session: greet, introduce, set expectations, brainstorm barriers, do Worksheet 1, and assign practice work. It is the session's skeleton for planning.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Greeting each person at the door is not small talk; it is the first data point on mood and the first signal that they are seen. In custody, a name said warmly can matter more than any handout.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Before the session, write one sentence you want every member to leave with. Check at the end whether anyone could say it back in their own words.

ask: Which step is most likely to run long, and what would you trim?
How does the first five minutes of a group shape the next twelve weeks?

7.title: Opening the first group, setting rules
7.gist: The script welcomes members, frames the sessions as a chance to weigh treatment's downsides and upsides, and guides the group to generate its own expectations by consensus. It reminds facilitators to disclose mandatory reporting limits.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Eliciting rules instead of announcing them uses self-determination theory: autonomy fuels internalized motivation. The question about who will do most of the talking quietly hands ownership to members.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Confidentiality in a correctional group is never complete; peers can repeat things and staff have reporting duties. Promising more privacy than exists erodes trust later, so name the limits plainly.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When asking if anyone strongly disagrees, pause long enough to be uncomfortable. A rushed consensus is just silence; a real one leaves room for a dissent you can negotiate.

ask: What does confidentiality honestly mean in your facility, and how would you say it to a skeptic?
How might an icebreaker backfire with men who distrust disclosure?

8.title: Brainstorming roadblocks: inside and outside
8.gist: Members list what makes treatment hard, then sort each barrier as internal (thoughts, feelings) or external (money, transport, childcare). Sorting sets up different strategies for each kind.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The split echoes the Stoic dichotomy of control from Epictetus: some things are up to us, others are not. CBI keeps the practical part of that idea while still teaching problem solving for what lies outside.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect someone to call every barrier external, such as the judge, the program, or the officer. Do not argue; ask what thought shows up when that happens. The internal piece usually surfaces on its own.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members vote with a hand signal on whether each item is internal or external. Split votes are gold: barriers like feeling overwhelmed are often both.

ask: Are attitudes like 'these programs don't work' purely internal, or shaped by real past experience?
How does sorting barriers change a person's sense of agency?

terms.d: A thought, belief, or feeling that gets in the way of engaging.
A practical circumstance outside the person, like cost or transportation.

9.title: Two kinds of barriers, two kinds of fixes
9.gist: External barriers call for problem solving, while internal ones are changed by catching and replacing unhelpful thoughts. Members then pick and rank their own barriers on Worksheet 1 and share a few.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is a preview of the whole CBI model: problem solving for situations, cognitive restructuring for thinking. Members are being introduced to the program's two main tools before they know they are learning them.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The point that internal barriers are more controllable but harder to change fits clinical experience: beliefs are rehearsed for years and resist quick fixes. That is why CBT relies on repeated practice rather than insight alone.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Reinforce sharing specifically: name what the person did, such as being honest about doubt. Vague praise sounds like staff talk; specific praise teaches the group what you value.

ask: Why might ranking barriers matter more than listing them?
When is an internal barrier actually an accurate reading of an unfair situation?

10.title: Practice work and closing session 1
10.gist: Members take home a worksheet to brainstorm options for one internal and one external barrier and name people who could help. The facilitator thanks members for honesty and previews next session's focus on reasons to push past barriers.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Naming supportive people plants the seed of prosocial support, one of the central eight risk/need areas in the RNR literature. Even early on, the program is pointing members toward allies.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In custody, 'people who could help' may be thin. Accept staff, a cellmate in recovery, a chaplain, or a family member by phone. A blank line is information, not failure.

ask: What would you do if a member writes that no one can help them?
How can closing a session on gratitude shape whether people return?

11.title: Reasons to change, without pushing
11.gist: Session 2 explores how substance use has affected life areas and links personal goals to treatment. It introduces importance and confidence ratings and warns against forcing members to admit change would help.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Importance and confidence come straight from MI's readiness rulers. Low importance calls for awareness and reframing; low confidence calls for skill practice to build self-efficacy, Bandura's term for belief in one's capacity to act.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If a member rates importance a 3, ask why not a 1. It invites them to voice their own reasons for change, which they believe more than yours. This is a classic MI move for drawing out change talk.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Two ratings simplify a messy reality: someone may value change but doubt the program specifically. Clarify what the number refers to before planning around it.

ask: Why does forcing an admission tend to harden resistance?
How would you work differently with a member who is high importance but low confidence?

terms.d: A person's belief that they can successfully carry out a specific behavior (Bandura).
A person's own statements favoring change, which MI tries to draw out and strengthen.

12.title: Session 2 materials and flow
12.gist: The outline lists three worksheets and the steps: check-in, review rules and last practice work, introduce reasons to engage, complete the impact and why-change sheets, and assign the readiness rating.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Review practice work even if few completed it. Ask those who did not what got in the way; that is a live barrier and fits the theme perfectly. Shaming non-completion teaches people to hide.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Open with a one-word check-in about how members arrived today. It takes a minute and gives you a mood map before the heavier impact worksheet.

ask: How do you keep practice-work review from feeling like a test?
What sequencing logic puts the impact worksheet before the why-change worksheet?

13.title: Thumb check-in and quick review
13.gist: Session 2 opens with a thumbs up, down, or sideways mood check, a brief review of rules and last week's concepts drawn out by open questions, and a quick round on the roadblocks practice work. It establishes the ritual every later session repeats.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A predictable opening ritual lowers anxiety and builds group norms. Rating a feeling also starts emotional awareness, a skill later modules build on when members learn to notice feelings as signals.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The pointer warns against problem solving a disclosure on the spot. Holding that line is hard for helpers; instead offer brief group support and a one-on-one after. It keeps the session on track and protects the person from a public fix.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A three-point thumb scale is fast but coarse, and in a prison group many will show sideways to stay invisible. Notice the pattern over weeks rather than trusting any single rating.

ask: What does a consistently neutral thumb tell you, if anything?
Why elicit last week's concepts instead of summarizing them yourself?

14.title: Looking honestly at what use gave and took
14.gist: Members complete the Impact of Substance Use worksheet, look for patterns in their ratings, then star the three life areas that matter most and discuss how use touched them. The page openly allows that use helped in some ways.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking how use has been good to people is a deliberate MI move: acknowledging benefits makes the conversation credible. Starring valued areas then sets up developing discrepancy between what people care about and what they do.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Acceptance and commitment therapy (Hayes) also builds change around chosen values. Starring three areas is a mini values clarification, and values pull harder than fear of punishment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect bravado: use was all good. Accept it and ask what it gave them, such as relief, belonging, or energy. Those answers map the needs a recovery plan will have to meet some other way.

ask: Why might admitting the benefits of use make change more, not less, likely?
What needs did substances meet that your members will still have after release?

terms.d: An MI process of highlighting the gap between a person's values or goals and their current behavior.

15.title: From reasons to personal goals
15.gist: Members write three ways lifestyle change might help them, then pair each reason with a personal goal that makes life better without harming anyone. Unfinished sheets can come back next time.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Tying a reason to a goal converts avoidance motivation (stay out of jail) into approach motivation (more time with my kids). Approach goals tend to be more sustaining, a theme also central to the Good Lives Model (Ward).

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by reading a few goals aloud and asking what the first small step would be. Keep it light; the aim today is a direction, not a plan.

ask: How does an approach goal feel different from an avoidance goal for someone in custody?
What would you do with a member whose only goal is to get out?

16.title: Readiness rating as homework
16.gist: Members take home a rating of how important treatment feels and how confident they are of finishing it, and are thanked for their honesty. The next session will weigh treatment's pros and cons.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Importance and confidence are separate levers. Someone can see change as crucial yet doubt they can pull it off, and that combination often looks like resistance when it is really fear of failing.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Rate yourself on a change you have been putting off: importance and confidence, 0 to 10. Notice which number is lower and what would raise it by one point.

ask: Why might honest low ratings be more useful to you than high ones?
How could a member's confidence rating be shaped by past program failures?

17.title: Ambivalence as a doorway, not a defect
17.gist: Session 3 combines barriers and reasons into a cost-benefit analysis of participating in the program. The facilitator stays neutral, uses reflections, and links choices to goals to nudge members toward the preparation stage.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Decisional balance is a core process in the stages of change (Prochaska & DiClemente): as people move toward preparation, perceived pros of change rise relative to cons. The CBA makes that internal tally visible on paper.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Real decisions are not tidy spreadsheets; emotion, identity, and peer status weigh more than listed items. A CBA can be intellectualized. Its power lies in the conversation it sparks, not the arithmetic.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Withholding your opinion is the hardest skill here. If you catch yourself about to persuade, turn it into a reflection: part of you wants this, and part of you thinks it is a waste.

ask: Why does neutrality from a staff member carry special weight in a correctional setting?
Is moving someone toward preparation a neutral goal? How do you square that with staying neutral?

terms.d: Feeling two ways about change at once; MI sees it as a normal step, not resistance.
Stage of change where a person intends to act soon and starts planning.

18.title: Session 3 materials and flow
18.gist: The outline covers check-in, review, a public readiness rating exercise, a group-built example CBA, a personal CBA on joining treatment, and CBA practice work. Two sets of worksheets per person are needed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Pre-draw the two readiness scales and the CBA grid before members arrive. Setup during group burns attention and invites side talk.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Do your own CBA on running this group well versus coasting. It makes you a more credible model when you walk members through theirs.

ask: Why practice the CBA on a neutral example before a personal one?
What could go wrong putting readiness ratings on a public board?

19.title: Initials on the readiness scale
19.gist: After the usual check-in and review, members walk to the board and put their initials by their importance and confidence ratings. The facilitator then summarizes where the group clusters.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Making ratings public turns private doubt into shared data. Seeing that others also rated low normalizes ambivalence; seeing peers rate high can create gentle social influence, a form of observational learning (Bandura).

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Public rating can pressure people to inflate numbers to look good to staff or to deflate them to look tough to peers. Allow passes and treat numbers as conversation starters rather than truth.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Summarize without praising high scorers over low ones. Something like: we have a spread, which is exactly what honest groups look like.

ask: How would peer status in your unit shape where people place their initials?
What would you lose by making these ratings anonymous?

20.title: Why short-term wins mislead
20.gist: Members explain their low and high ratings while the facilitator records reasons and highlights those favoring change. Discussion then shifts to big decisions and how short-term payoffs often hide long-term costs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Emphasizing pro-change reasons is MI's selective reflection: you acknowledge everything but strengthen change talk. Short-term thinking connects to delay discounting, where distant outcomes feel less valuable, a pattern well documented in people with addictions.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Behavioral economics names this temporal discounting; philosophers since Aristotle discussed akrasia, acting against one's better judgment. The CBA is a practical tool for an ancient human weakness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask for a decision members are proud of, not only regrets. A good past decision proves they can already weigh long-term costs.

ask: Is short-term thinking always irrational for someone who grew up in an unpredictable environment?
How could you reflect a low-rating reason without endorsing it?

terms.d: Valuing rewards less the further away in time they are.

21.title: Building the four-box CBA
21.gist: The facilitator draws the CBA on the board and defines benefits, costs, and short- versus long-term consequences. Part 1 covers staying the same, filled in with a neutral example before anyone does their own.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Starting with the benefits of staying the same is deliberate. Honoring the payoff of the status quo lowers defensiveness, so members can look at the costs without feeling cornered.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Pick a neutral example the group actually cares about, such as quitting soda, getting up for count, or calling home more. Neutral means low stakes, not boring.

ask: Why use a neutral example rather than drug use for the demo?
Which box do you think members will find hardest to fill, and why?

22.title: Worked example: starting exercise
22.gist: The page models a two-part CBA on starting an exercise program, listing benefits and costs of staying the same and of changing. It shows how the grid captures both quick and slow consequences.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The example shows an asymmetry: costs of change land early (soreness, early mornings) while benefits arrive late (health, energy). Most worthwhile changes share that shape, which is why they are hard.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Swap in an example that fits custody, like starting a workout routine in the yard or finishing a GED. Ask the group to fill boxes before you read the sample answers.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members which single box would most move them. Their answer tells you whether they respond to near or far consequences.

ask: Why do costs of change tend to be short-term and benefits long-term?
How might seeing that pattern help a member tolerate early discomfort in recovery?

23.title: Personal CBA: staying out of treatment
23.gist: Members now complete their own CBA on actively participating, starting with what is good and costly about not engaging. Facilitators circulate but must not supply pros or cons, only open questions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-generated reasons persuade more than given ones, a finding related to self-perception theory (Bem) and central to MI. If you hand out answers, members become passive and the exercise turns into compliance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking what surprised them in their own boxes. Defining active participation first matters: showing up silent is not the same as engaging.

ask: What does active participation look like for a quiet, guarded member?
Why might illegal behavior show more short-term benefits than prosocial choices?

24.title: Personal CBA: choosing to engage
24.gist: Members fill in Part 2, the costs and benefits of actively joining the group, and share discoveries. The facilitator records common themes and frames the right-side items as motivators and the left-side as barriers.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The pointer forbids helping members find more reasons to keep antisocial behavior. Reflections are selective: you accept what they say but do not amplify sustain talk, the MI term for arguments against change.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Check marks next to shared items are powerful: they show that a reason is collective, not just one person's. Close by stressing that the decision belongs to them, which protects autonomy.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to circle the one item on their whole CBA that weighs the most. One heavy reason often beats ten light ones.

ask: How do you stay neutral while still choosing which reasons to reinforce?
Why might framing control as theirs increase actual engagement?

terms.d: A person's statements favoring keeping things as they are.

25.title: Linking choices to goals, then homework
25.gist: The facilitator ties the CBA back to personal goals, asking how joining treatment helps or hurts them, then reviews and assigns a second CBA on another behavior. Practice work is framed as the start of watching one's thoughts.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking how a choice moves you toward or away from a goal develops discrepancy without lecturing. The closing note on attending to thoughts quietly introduces the cognitive model that the rest of the curriculum teaches.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A quiet place to write is rare in a housing unit. Problem solve it with the group: library time, after count, early morning. Turning that logistics barrier into a mini problem-solving exercise reinforces session 1.

ask: What behavior would you expect most members to choose for this homework, and what does that reveal?
Why is noticing thoughts presented as the first step before changing actions?

26.title: Recognizing Roadblocks worksheet
26.gist: Members list up to five internal and five external barriers to engaging, guided by examples like resentment at being sent and losing a kitchen job, then rank them by difficulty.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing barriers down externalizes them, making a vague dread into a concrete list that can be worked. Ranking forces prioritization, which is the first step of problem solving.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The examples are well chosen for custody, since losing a paid job assignment is a real cost. Debrief by asking which barrier ranked first and whether it is mostly a thought or a circumstance.

ask: What does it signal when a member lists only external barriers?
How would you use the number-one barrier in later sessions?

27.title: Running Over Roadblocks practice work
27.gist: For the top internal barrier, members rate how risky it is; for the top external one, they brainstorm options, pick the best, and list people who could support them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rating risk on an internal barrier builds metacognition, thinking about one's own thinking. Brainstorming options before choosing is a compressed version of the problem-solving model taught later in the program.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief the supports section carefully. If someone names people who are part of their using network, do not dismiss them; ask whether that person would support this specific goal.

ask: Why rate the internal barrier rather than brainstorm solutions for it here?
What makes a support person genuinely helpful for treatment success?

28.title: Impact of Substance Use, items 1-7
28.gist: Members rate on a -3 to +3 scale how use has affected relationships, basic needs, family, education, work, career, and hobbies. The scale allows positive as well as negative impact.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A bipolar scale invites honesty: members can mark real benefits, which makes the negatives they mark more believable to themselves. It is a structured form of decisional balance by life domain.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some will rate basic needs as positive because selling drugs paid the rent. Take it seriously; it points to employment and money as real needs to address before release.

ask: What does a positive score on basic needs tell you about a person's risk factors?
How might a member's ratings differ if done again after six months sober?

29.title: Impact of Substance Use, items 8-16
29.gist: The scale continues with happiness, freedom, caring for dependents, spirituality, money, financial duties, security, friendships, and self-regard.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Items like feeling secure and feeling good about myself capture what substances often do in the short run: soothe fear and shame. That is the negative-reinforcement engine of addiction.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Freedom is a pointed item for incarcerated members. Ask what freedom meant while using versus now; many discover that use felt like freedom but functioned as a cage.

ask: How would you explain negative reinforcement to a group without jargon?
Why might making money and meeting financial responsibilities score very differently?

terms.d: A behavior grows stronger because it removes something unpleasant, like using to escape anxiety.

30.title: Impact of Substance Use, items 17-20
30.gist: The final items cover independence, living by one's values, relationships with children, and physical health, completing a twenty-area life map.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Living up to my values is the hinge item: when it scores negative, the gap between identity and behavior is in plain view. That gap, felt rather than told, is what MI aims to surface.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draw a quick bar for each starred area to see their life profile at a glance. Visual patterns often hit harder than numbers.

ask: Which of the twenty areas would your members most often star, and why?
How can a negative score on children be used without triggering shame?

31.title: Why Should I Change? worksheet
31.gist: Members write three ways lifestyle change could help them and pair each with a personal goal, following an example about rebuilding family trust.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pairing reasons with goals turns abstract motivation into something to aim at. Writing it in one's own handwriting is a small act of commitment, which tends to increase follow-through.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking how they would know the goal is starting to happen. Concrete signs, like a returned phone call, make goals feel reachable.

ask: What separates a reason for change from a goal?
How would you help someone whose three reasons all center on avoiding punishment?

32.title: Readiness Rating Form
32.gist: Members rate how important finishing treatment is and how confident they are, list reasons for each score, and explain why they did not score lower.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The why-not-lower question is classic MI: defending a higher number makes the person argue for change in their own words. It pulls out change talk even from someone who scored a 2.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note that the confidence scale on this page appears to begin at 3 in the printed text; check your copy, as the scale may be cut off or misprinted.

ask: Why does asking why not lower work better than asking why not higher?
What would you do with a member who rates importance 10 and confidence 1?

33.title: CBA Part 1: staying the same
33.gist: Members name a target behavior and fill a grid with short- and long-term benefits and costs of continuing it unchanged.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Listing benefits of staying the same first honors what the behavior provides. In debrief, the short-term benefit column usually reveals the function of the behavior, which a replacement must also serve.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to read across one row at a time. The contrast between short-term benefits and long-term costs is the lesson; let them say it.

ask: What does the function of a behavior mean, and why does it matter for replacing it?
Which column do members typically fill fastest?

34.title: CBA Part 2: making the change
34.gist: Members name the new behavior they would do instead and list short- and long-term benefits and costs of changing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Requiring a replacement behavior matters: stopping something leaves a vacuum. Behavioral research consistently finds that changes stick better when a new action fills the same need.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If the cost-of-change boxes are empty, the plan is probably unrealistic. Gently ask what will be hard in week one; honest costs make the plan sturdier.

ask: Why might a CBA without listed costs of change be a warning sign?
How does naming a replacement behavior change the conversation?

35.title: Changes and Goals worksheet
35.gist: Members write a personal goal with at least three steps toward it, then start another CBA on a behavior they are considering changing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Breaking a goal into steps builds what Gollwitzer called implementation intentions: concrete plans for when and how to act. Specific plans tend to raise follow-through over vague intentions.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for steps small enough to do this week inside the facility. A first step that waits for release is a wish, not a step.

ask: What makes a step small enough to actually happen?
How does this worksheet bridge the pre-treatment module into Module 1?

terms.d: An if-then plan specifying when, where, and how one will act toward a goal.

36.title: Module 1: Motivational Engagement overview
36.gist: The divider lists Module 1's six sessions: curriculum intro, an emergency plan, values, cost-benefit analysis, goal setting, and an introduction to cognitive-behavioral work. It moves from engagement to the core CBT model.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Module 1 repeats some pre-treatment tools on purpose. Motivation is not a one-time hurdle; in stages-of-change terms people cycle back, so the program keeps feeding it while skills are introduced.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Members who did the pre-treatment sessions may feel the CBA and goals are repetitive. Frame repetition as deepening: the same tool aimed at a bigger target.

ask: Why might an emergency plan come so early, before values?
What changes when the CBA moves from treatment participation to substance use itself?

37.title: What Module 1 is built to do
37.gist: The overview explains Module 1's arc: cohesion, a crisis plan for urges, values, costs and benefits, goals, and the iceberg model linking thought to behavior. It says resistance in a non-voluntary group is a treatment target, not grounds for removal.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Treating dissonance as a target reflects a shift in correctional practice: from screening out the unmotivated to building motivation. RNR research suggests higher-risk people benefit most from treatment, so excluding resisters can mean excluding those with the most to gain.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Cognitive dissonance (Festinger) is the discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs or acting against values. The module uses it on purpose: values work makes the gap felt so people want to close it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Teaching urge strategies in session 2, before members trust the group, assumes they will disclose cravings early. Some will not; keep the emergency plan practical and private enough to use anyway.

ask: Why might the most resistant members be the ones the program most needs to keep?
How does dissonance help change, and when might it backfire into defensiveness?

terms.d: Mental discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs or acting against one's values.

38.title: Module 1 objectives, continued
38.gist: The list finishes the module goals: basic goal setting, discrepancy between goals and antisocial behavior, normalizing resistance, introducing CBI, and raising motivation. A few bullets repeat, likely a print duplication.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Discrepancy appears twice as a goal, against values and against goals. Values answer who do I want to be; goals answer what do I want to get. Hitting both widens the motivational base.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Write one sentence per objective describing what you would see a member do if it were met. Observable signs keep objectives from staying abstract.

ask: What is the difference between a value and a goal, and why target both?
How would you measure whether resistance was addressed in a normalizing way?

39.title: Module 1 worksheet map
39.gist: The list pairs each Module 1 session with its worksheets, from the participant agreement through the emergency plan, values, CBA, preparing for change, a feelings chart, and the iceberg.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Note the feelings chart sits just before the iceberg: members need words for emotions before they can map how thoughts drive them. Emotional vocabulary is a quiet prerequisite for CBT.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Flag which sheets feed the Success Plan from day one. Members who know their work will be reused treat it more seriously.

ask: Why might emotional vocabulary come before the cognitive model?
Which worksheet here would you most want members to keep after release?

40.title: How to read the manual's symbols
40.gist: The legend explains the cues used throughout: responsivity tips, pointers, scripted SAY text, board WRITE notes, options, prompts, discussions, Success Plan stairs, model content, and worksheet codes. It is the map for reading every later page.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Scripted manuals support treatment fidelity: delivering the program as designed. Fidelity matters because evaluations of correctional programs often find weaker results when core elements drift.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A script can make facilitators sound robotic. The best practice is to learn the intent of each SAY and deliver it in your own voice, keeping content while adapting words, which the responsivity tips encourage.

ask: Where is the line between adapting a script and drifting from fidelity?
Which responsivity factors in your groups would most need a tip?

terms.d: How closely a program is delivered as its designers intended.

41.title: Binders and behavior management
41.gist: The page advises giving members binders, sometimes kept in the treatment area for privacy, and setting a clear system of reinforcers and consequences for compliance before the group begins.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Predictable consequences come from operant learning: behavior follows its outcomes. Correctional research generally favors a higher ratio of rewards to sanctions; a commonly cited target is about four positives per negative, though that ratio is a guideline rather than a law.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Announce consequences before anyone breaks a rule. A rule invented after the violation feels personal; one announced in advance feels fair.

ask: What reinforcers actually matter to people in your facility?
Why might keeping binders in the treatment area protect members?

42.title: Cohesion first, and resistance as data
42.gist: Session 1 aims to build group cohesion, where members can rehearse social skills before using them outside. It explains that resistance shifts with importance and confidence and should be explored, not fought.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Irvin Yalom described cohesion as a key therapeutic factor in groups, alongside universality and interpersonal learning. A cohesive group becomes a safe practice arena, which is the logic behind role play throughout CBI.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Group research generally links cohesion to better engagement and outcomes, though the direction of cause can run both ways: people who improve may also feel closer to the group.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In prison, cohesion competes with code: snitching fears and status. Build it with low-risk shared tasks first, like naming a group norm, before asking for personal stories.

ask: How does inmate culture work for or against group cohesion?
If resistance is dynamic, what could make it rise in the middle of the program?

terms.d: The sense of belonging and mutual trust that binds group members together.

43.title: Matching help to low importance or confidence
43.gist: A short note: low importance calls for raising awareness and restructuring thinking, while low confidence calls for practicing new behaviors to build self-efficacy.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Bandura identified mastery experiences as the strongest source of self-efficacy. Rehearsal in group gives people small wins that make the next step feel possible.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: For each member, jot whether importance or confidence seems lower. Revisit in a month; the answer guides whether to talk more or practice more with that person.

ask: Why is doing more powerful than hearing for building confidence?
How might cognitive restructuring raise importance?

44.title: Session 1 materials and flow
44.gist: The outline covers greeting, introductions, group expectations, a program overview, the participant agreement, the introductions worksheet, and confidence-rating practice work. Binders are suggested.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: With seven steps in a first session, pacing is the risk. Decide in advance which step you will shorten if introductions run long, so you do not cut the program overview.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Time yourself reading the scripted SAY sections aloud. Knowing how long they take tells you how much room is left for discussion.

ask: Which part of a first session is most important not to rush?
How does a signed agreement change a member's relationship to the group?

45.title: Welcome, the CBT promise, and the agreement
45.gist: The facilitator welcomes members, explains the cognitive-behavioral approach of learning how thoughts drive feelings and actions, and guides the group to agree on expectations. Members then sign an agreement naming why the group matters to them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Promising members they will become experts on their own thinking is a strong framing. It positions them as active scientists of their own minds, close to Beck's collaborative empiricism, rather than patients being fixed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If someone refuses to sign, the pointer says to meet privately afterward. A refusal in front of peers is often about face; in private the real fear, such as what is done with the form, usually comes out.

ask: What would make a signature meaningful rather than a formality?
How would you explain the CBT model in one sentence to a skeptical member?

terms.d: Beck's idea that therapist and client test thoughts together like co-investigators.

46.title: Introductions worksheet and public ratings
46.gist: Volunteers read the introduction questions aloud, members answer and share briefly, then rate importance and confidence and post initials on the board. Facilitators note limited insight but do not challenge it yet.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking for volunteer readers protects members with low literacy, a common responsivity factor in prisons. Withholding confrontation early follows MI: rapport first, challenge later and gently.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The floor-numbers option gets bodies moving and is harder to fake than initials. For returning pre-treatment members, ask how their numbers have shifted; movement in either direction is useful data.

ask: Why delay challenging low-insight comments rather than correcting them now?
How might literacy issues hide behind apparent resistance?

47.title: Motivation needs skills: the Success Plan
47.gist: After discussing reasons behind ratings, the facilitator notes that motivation alone fails without skills, and introduces the Success Plan, a personal relapse-prevention roadmap built from worksheets marked with the stairs symbol.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The Success Plan draws on relapse prevention (Marlatt & Gordon 1985): identify high-risk situations and rehearse coping responses. Here relapse means returning to any trouble behavior, not only drug use.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The skydiving example captures a point from skill-learning research: confidence follows competence. Willpower without practiced skills tends to collapse under stress.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Show a sample finished Success Plan page so members see the end product. A visible destination makes the weekly worksheets feel like building blocks, not busywork.

ask: Why broaden relapse to mean any return to trouble behavior?
What happens to a Success Plan if members lose their worksheets, and how can you prevent that?

terms.d: CBI-SUA's personal relapse-prevention plan, assembled from key worksheets in the final module.

48.title: Session 1 review and practice work
48.gist: The session closes by asking why expectations matter and assigning a confidence rating on following each group expectation, to spot trouble areas early.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rating confidence per rule is a micro version of high-risk situation mapping: where am I likely to slip? It trains the forecasting habit the Success Plan relies on.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When reviewing, thank people for low ratings. Admitting a rule will be hard is exactly the honesty you want to reinforce.

ask: What would a member's lowest-rated expectation tell you about their risk?
Why ask about trouble spots before any rule is broken?

49.title: Why an emergency plan comes early
49.gist: Session 2 gives members a small, rehearsed toolkit for crisis moments that could lead to use, such as home passes or approaching release. It previews the full Success Plan and urges facilitators to practice the skills before demonstrating them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: In relapse prevention (Marlatt & Gordon), a lapse often happens in a high-risk moment when no coping response is ready. Giving coping tools before deeper work is triage: the full plan takes weeks, but risk does not wait.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Practice the relaxation scripts on yourself first, out loud. A facilitator who rushes or feels awkward signals that the skill is silly, and the group will follow that cue.

ask: What high-risk moments exist for your members while still in custody?
Why teach coping tools before the cognitive model rather than after?

50.title: Check-in and reviewing confidence ratings
50.gist: After the usual check-in and review, members share which group expectations they felt least confident about, and the group looks for common trouble spots.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Publicly naming a weak spot and getting peer strategies is a group form of problem solving and social support. It also reframes rules from impositions into shared challenges.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If many rate punctuality low, the cause may be the institution, such as late escorts or count delays. Acknowledge real system barriers; pretending they are personal failings costs credibility.

ask: How do you separate personal from institutional causes of rule-breaking?
What does the most common low-confidence rule tell you about your group?

51.title: Stop, drop, and roll for cravings
51.gist: The facilitator compares a craving plan to stop, drop, and roll: rehearsed until automatic. Craving management is laid out in four parts, and this session focuses on staying calm and using strategies.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Under stress, people fall back on well-practiced habits; deliberate reasoning narrows. Overlearning a response, as with fire drills, makes it available when the thinking brain is flooded.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Neuroscience broadly supports this: acute stress shifts control toward habit systems and away from flexible prefrontal planning. That is why insight alone fails in a crisis and rehearsal matters.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members what they did automatically in their last emergency, like a fight or an accident. Their answer shows that rehearsed responses already run their lives.

ask: Why might a well-understood plan still fail if never rehearsed?
What would make a craving plan truly automatic for someone?

52.title: What cravings are, and distraction
52.gist: The group discusses four features of cravings: normal, common, time-limited, and a sign of progress, noting that each unanswered craving weakens the trigger. Members then brainstorm distractions and pick two or three.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Each unanswered craving weakening the trigger is extinction learning: a cue repeatedly not followed by the drug loses pull. Marlatt's urge surfing adds that cravings rise, peak, and fall like waves if you ride them out.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Cravings are a meaningful predictor of relapse in many studies, but the link is not absolute; plenty of people crave and do not use. That gap is exactly where coping skills operate.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Adapt the distraction list to the unit: a bath is not an option, but push-ups, a letter, a chess game, or reciting a poem are. Ask which work at 2 a.m. in a cell.

ask: Why might calling cravings a sign of change reduce shame?
Which distractions work in custody but not at home, and vice versa?

terms.d: A learned response weakens when the cue is repeatedly not followed by its usual reward.
Observing a craving rise and fall without acting on it (Marlatt).

53.title: Progressive muscle relaxation practice
53.gist: The group learns that strategies must fit daily routines, then practices progressive muscle relaxation together: tensing each muscle group for about ten seconds and releasing it, head to toes.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Edmund Jacobson developed progressive relaxation in the early twentieth century. The tension-release contrast teaches people to notice tension they normally miss, which is itself an early warning signal.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: For members with trauma, closing eyes or dimming lights in a room of strangers can feel unsafe. Offer eyes open, gaze down, and let anyone opt out without comment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect laughter at first; it is nerves. Keep your voice slow and steady and do not stop the exercise. The second round is usually quieter.

ask: How would you adapt relaxation for someone with a trauma history?
Why might noticing body tension help someone catch a craving earlier?

54.title: Deep breathing and pleasant imagery
54.gist: The facilitator links breathing to body signs of rising emotion, demonstrates four simple steps, and practices with a longer exhale than inhale. Pleasant imagery is introduced as a mental trip to a calm, substance-free scene using all five senses.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Slow breathing with a longer exhale is widely thought to engage the parasympathetic system, the body's calming branch, lowering heart rate. It works on the body directly, so it helps even when thoughts are racing.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Contemplative traditions from yoga to Zen used breath long before psychology studied it. Modern research on slow breathing is promising but still developing, so present it as a useful tool, not a cure.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking about body signs of anger first matters: members often notice the body before they can name the feeling. That builds the cue-detection skill needed later.

ask: Why might body signals be easier to catch than thoughts in a crisis?
How would you sell breathing to a member who thinks it is soft?

55.title: Imagery demo and positive self-talk
55.gist: The facilitator models a sensory beach scene, members picture their own place, then small groups write at least ten self-talk statements to post on the wall, such as reminders of strength or past coping.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-talk statements are a seed of Meichenbaum's self-instructional training and stress inoculation: rehearsed coping sentences ready for the hard moment. They also preview cognitive restructuring later in CBI.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Generic affirmations can ring hollow, and some research suggests they may backfire for people with low self-esteem. Statements tied to real evidence, like having survived worse, tend to be more credible.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to turn one posted statement into a personal one, naming a specific time they did resist. Specific beats slogans.

ask: What makes a self-talk statement believable rather than empty?
How could imagery be risky for someone whose memories of peace involve using?

terms.d: Meichenbaum's method of preparing for stress by rehearsing coping thoughts and skills in advance.

56.title: Daily emergency plan logs
56.gist: Members take home a log to complete each day until the next session, practicing their strategies on any behavior they want to curb, or at least reading their plan nightly.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Daily repetition matters more than intensity for habit formation. Applying the plan to small urges like overeating or procrastinating gives low-stakes practice reps for the big moments.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Make it concrete: count the days aloud and write the number of logs on the board. Ambiguous homework tends not to get done.

ask: Why practice craving skills on non-drug urges?
What would a realistic daily log look like for a busy unit schedule?

57.title: Values, conflict, and dissonance
57.gist: Session 3 helps members name their values and see where use supports or undermines them, creating cognitive dissonance. It notes the same value, like family, can drive opposite behaviors, and asks facilitators to stay neutral.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Shalom Schwartz's theory of basic values arranges values in a circle where neighbors fit together and opposites clash, such as stimulation and pleasure versus conformity and security. Antisocial acts often serve one value at another's expense.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Philosophers call this the problem of conflicting goods: Sophocles' Antigone is torn between family duty and the law of the city. Members selling drugs for their family face a version of the same tragedy.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When a member says they did crime for family, do not argue. Reflect the value, then ask what their family actually lost and gained. Let the conflict surface from their own account.

ask: Can a value itself be antisocial, or only the way it is pursued?
How will you keep these values alive in later modules, as the page suggests?

terms.d: Identifying and ranking what matters most to a person to guide choices.

58.title: Session 3 materials and flow
58.gist: The outline lists 11 index cards per member, the values worksheet, and the Living Your Values practice work, with steps from check-in through the card-sort exercise.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Check facility rules on index cards and pens ahead of time. Some units restrict materials, and a missing supply can kill a hands-on exercise.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Do the card sort yourself before the group. Knowing how it feels to rank your own values helps you guide others through the hard choices.

ask: Why use physical cards rather than a written list?
What is the purpose of the eleventh card?

59.title: Reviewing logs and defining values
59.gist: After check-in and review of emergency strategies, members share their logs, then the group defines a value as something deeply meaningful. A pointer suggests having personal examples ready for members who struggle with the concept.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Abstract nouns like value can be hard for concrete thinkers. Tying the concept to something a member already said, like a GED, uses their own words as scaffolding.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Avoid using a member's real disclosure as an example without care: only use what they shared openly in group, and never something from their file.

ask: How do you make an abstract concept concrete without leading the person?
What would you do if a member said they value nothing?

60.title: The values card sort begins
60.gist: Members brainstorm values, use the worksheet categories, write up to ten on cards, rank them by importance, then write their substance of choice on an extra card.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Card sorting forces trade-offs, which a simple list never does. Ranking reveals priorities people may not have admitted even to themselves.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Warn members to include only what they are comfortable sharing. Then watch for the moment the substance card arrives; reactions tell you who is already feeling the tension.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to set aside their bottom card and notice whether they feel any loss. If not, it may not be a value at all.

ask: Why might the substance card be introduced only after ranking?
What does it mean if a member ranks money above family?

61.title: Placing the substance card
61.gist: Members slot the substance card into their value stack, showing what they would trade to keep using. A willing, insightful volunteer then walks through each value, saying how use helped and hurt it, while the facilitator blocks peer confrontation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking how use helped before how it hurt is a double-sided reflection setup. Hearing both sides in their own voice, people often do the math themselves, which is far more persuasive than a counselor's verdict.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Choosing the first volunteer is strategic: someone with some insight models honest weighing. A defiant first sharer can set a tone of bravado that others copy.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A card placed near the top is information, not failure, as the pointer says. Pushing that member risks shame and shutdown; note it and return to it gently over coming weeks.

ask: Why intervene when peers confront a member, even if what they say is true?
What would you reflect to someone who placed the substance card first?

terms.d: An MI reflection that names both sides of someone's ambivalence together.

62.title: Processing the values sort
62.gist: Each member reviews their stack, then the group reflects on what it was like to see everything at once and what they want to do next. Practice work asks them to list top values and how use helps or harms each.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Existential psychology, from Viktor Frankl onward, holds that people endure hardship when it serves meaning. Values work borrows that insight: change is easier when it is in service of something one cares about.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: End by asking each member to name one action this week that would honor their top card. A value becomes real when it gets a verb.

ask: What makes seeing all values at once more powerful than discussing them one by one?
How might you revisit this card stack at the end of the program?

63.title: CBA on antisocial behavior, and empathy
63.gist: Session 4 reuses the CBA, now aimed at changing antisocial behavior. It frames change as many small daily decisions and stresses that facilitator empathy reduces resistance and dropout.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The therapeutic alliance is one of the most consistent predictors of outcome across therapies, and warmth and empathy are tied to staying in treatment. The page's citations point the same way: a good early relationship keeps people in the room.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The page notes that others reinforce antisocial behavior and sometimes punish prosocial attempts, like peers mocking someone who goes to group. That is social learning (Bandura) and a reason CBI targets antisocial associates later.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what people around them do when they try to change. Naming the social punishment of change validates how hard it is and makes it a problem to solve.

ask: What social costs do your members pay for trying to change inside the unit?
How do you show empathy without seeming to approve the behavior?

terms.d: The working bond between helper and client: agreement on goals, tasks, and a trusting relationship.

64.title: Session 4 neutrality and flow
64.gist: The page repeats that there is no right answer in a CBA and the facilitator should steer toward self-discovery, adding gentle questions linking choices to values. The outline lists the sample CBA, a personal CBA, and practice work.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Neutrality here does not mean having no direction. MI calls itself directional: the counselor keeps the person's own goals in view while declining to argue. Asking how a choice affects family is a values bridge, not a lecture.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Prepare three values-linked questions in advance, built from what members shared last session. Ready questions keep you from defaulting to opinions under pressure.

ask: Can a facilitator be both neutral and directional? How?
What risks come with linking CBA items to someone's family?

65.title: Values review and the wish to change
65.gist: After a capped ten-minute check-in and review of values, members share their Living Your Values practice work. The facilitator then asks if anyone has ever woken up wanting their life to be different.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The ten-minute cap protects teaching time. Note concerns that need follow-up on paper so members see they will be addressed later, not dropped.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: William Miller wrote about quantum change, sudden life-altering shifts. The opening question invites those stories, but the next page argues most change is gradual. Both kinds exist; the program builds the gradual kind.

ask: Why ask about wanting change before teaching the tool?
What do you do when a member says they decided to change yesterday and needs no help?

66.title: The fork in the road is a myth
66.gist: The facilitator draws a fork labeled change and don't change, then questions it: change is usually many small decisions, not one. The group discusses choices that felt good at the time but hurt later, and short- versus long-term consequences.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Seeing recovery as daily decisions undercuts the abstinence violation effect described by Marlatt: the belief that one slip means total failure. If change is many choices, one bad choice does not erase the road.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Aristotle argued that character is built by repeated actions: we become just by doing just acts. The fork drawing becomes a picture of habits forming virtue or vice, step by step.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw a path with many tiny forks instead. Ask members to name three small forks they faced today in the unit.

ask: How does seeing change as daily decisions affect someone after a lapse?
What small forks do members face every day inside?

terms.d: After a slip, feeling like a total failure and then giving up entirely (Marlatt).

67.title: Teaching the CBA again, adjusting for veterans
67.gist: The group discusses past decisions driven by short-term payoffs, then the facilitator draws and explains the CBA. A pointer says to elicit the tool from members who learned it in pre-treatment and use them as co-teachers.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Having experienced members explain a tool uses the protégé effect: teaching something deepens one's own learning. It also creates peer models, more credible than staff.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Point out that consequences include benefits, not just punishment. Many members hear consequences only as sanctions, which makes the word itself a trigger.

ask: What changes when a peer, rather than staff, explains a tool?
Why might the word consequences carry baggage for justice-involved people?

68.title: Sample CBA: skipping group
68.gist: The page gives a model CBA on skipping treatment group, listing short-term gains like saving bus fare and seeing friends against costs like probation trouble. It suggests neutral examples like a night shift job or a new pet.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This sample is a community-supervision example. Notice how most benefits of skipping are immediate and social while costs are delayed and institutional, a pattern that delay discounting predicts will favor skipping.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For incarcerated members, swap in skipping a class or refusing a job assignment. Keep the structure but match the setting, a basic responsivity move.

ask: Why might social benefits like being with friends outweigh distant legal costs?
How would you adapt this example for a prison housing unit?

69.title: Sample CBA Part 2, first Success Plan sheet
69.gist: Part 2 of the sample shows benefits of attending group, mostly external, and costs like bus fare and boredom. The CBA worksheet is the first piece marked for the Success Plan.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Many sample benefits, such as making the officer or counselor happy, are external. That is a realistic starting point, but self-determination theory suggests lasting change needs internal reasons too. Ask what members would get for themselves.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Highlight the Success Plan symbol and explain why the sheet must be saved. The first marked document sets the habit for all the others.

ask: How can external motivation evolve into internal motivation?
What is the risk if a member's only reasons to change involve pleasing authorities?

terms.d: Doing something for outside rewards or to avoid punishment rather than for its own sake.

70.title: Personal CBA on a using situation
70.gist: Members choose a real situation involving substance use, list its benefits and costs of continuing, then name a replacement behavior. Facilitators circulate with open questions, never supplying answers.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The pointer says people would not do risky things if they gained nothing. That is functional analysis: every behavior serves a purpose. Naming the payoff tells you what the new behavior must also deliver.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Link costs to last session's values cards: how does this behavior affect the card on top? That bridge turns abstract costs into personal ones.

ask: What is the function of the target behavior your members most often choose?
Why must the replacement behavior be chosen before its costs are listed?

terms.d: Examining what triggers a behavior and what payoff keeps it going.

71.title: Weighing the new behavior and scoring items
71.gist: Members finish Part 2 with costs and benefits of the new behavior, then share insights while the facilitator marks shared themes. An option lets higher-functioning groups weight items 1 to 3.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Weighting items reflects a basic point from decision research: counting reasons misleads, because one heavy reason can outweigh many light ones. The scoring option teaches that subtlety.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Frame barriers on the CBA as the work ahead, as the script does. That turns a gloomy list into a syllabus: these are the things the program will help with.

ask: When might weighting items make a CBA worse rather than better?
How does calling barriers future work change the mood of the room?

72.title: Changes and Goals in Module 1
72.gist: The CBA is tied to values and personal goals, and members complete the Changes and Goals sheet with a goal and at least three steps. The review asks why short- and long-term consequences both matter.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Combining CBA, values, and goals layers three sources of motivation: consequences, identity, and aspiration. Each reaches different people; together they cover more members.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If a goal is huge, like owning a business, keep it and shrink the steps. Never shrink the dream; shrink the first move.

ask: Which motivational layer, consequences, identity, or aspiration, moves your members most?
How do you respond to a goal that seems unrealistic without crushing it?

73.title: CBA practice work on another behavior
73.gist: Members take home another CBA on a substance-related behavior they might change, linked to a personal goal, and are reminded that watching thoughts is the first step in changing actions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Repeating the CBA on different behaviors builds transfer: using a tool in new situations is what makes it a skill rather than a one-time exercise.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to do the homework CBA on a behavior they actually face this week, not a past one. Present decisions keep the tool alive.

ask: Why does doing the CBA on new behaviors matter more than perfecting one?
How would you know a member is using the CBA outside of group?

74.title: Goal setting as a motivational engine
74.gist: Session 5 has members set goals for the program and life, noting goals may change. It cites research that goals strongly regulate motivation and recommends repeated self-talk about reasons for change.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Locke and Latham's goal-setting research found that specific, challenging goals generally lead to better performance than vague ones, when people have the skills and commitment. Without skills, hard goals can backfire into discouragement.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Goals help because they make future rewards feel present, countering the pull of immediate costs of effort. That is self-control as a bridge between today's self and tomorrow's.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Goals set inside prison often depend on things outside one's control after release, like housing or employer attitudes. Help members separate goals they control from outcomes they hope for.

ask: Why might very challenging goals discourage someone with a history of failure?
How does repeated self-talk change importance and confidence?

75.title: Why are you here? Honest goals
75.gist: After check-in, members share their top value and what changing would gain them there. The group then brainstorms reasons for attending, and the facilitator accepts compliance with supervision as a legitimate starting reason.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Accepting compliance as a valid reason meets people where they are, a core stage-matched idea. People often begin for external reasons and develop internal ones along the way; demanding sincerity at the door just teaches people to fake it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When someone says they are here only because they have to be, reflect it plainly and ask what they might as well get out of the hours. It turns the mandate into an opportunity without arguing.

ask: Is a compliance-only goal a problem or a starting point?
What reasons for attending would you hear if members felt safe to be honest?

76.title: Writing a realistic, positive goal
76.gist: Members write a short-term goal related to substance use that is realistic and harms no one, using the Preparing for Change worksheet. The group then names barriers that could block goals like getting a job or staying off cocaine.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Naming barriers right after setting a goal mirrors Gabriele Oettingen's mental contrasting: imagining the goal then the obstacles tends to increase follow-through compared with positive fantasy alone.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask why writing goals down helps and let members answer. Then check each goal against the two rules aloud: can you do it in the timeframe, and does it hurt anyone, including you?

ask: Why might pure positive visualization weaken effort?
What makes a goal realistic for someone facing release with few resources?

terms.d: Imagining a desired future, then the obstacles in the way, to strengthen commitment (Oettingen).

77.title: Costs, benefits, reasons, and strengths
77.gist: Members write what happens if barriers win, what good comes from meeting the goal, their strongest reasons, and personal strengths that can help. The pointer asks facilitators to spread participation beyond the eager few.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking for personal strengths is a strengths-based move. Desistance research (for example, Maruna's work on redemption narratives) suggests people who see a good core self are better able to leave crime behind.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members struggle to name a strength. Offer evidence you have seen in group, like showing up on time or helping a peer, and ask if it fits. Let them accept or reject it.

ask: Why might naming strengths matter as much as naming risks?
How do you draw out quieter members without putting them on the spot?

terms.d: The process by which people stop offending over time.

78.title: Supporters and one task before next week
78.gist: Members identify supportive people and their qualities, including staff or officers if their own circle is thin, then commit to one specific task they can finish before the next session.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A single doable task builds a mastery experience, the strongest source of self-efficacy. Small completed steps tend to raise confidence more than big plans.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Suggesting a parole officer as a supporter is realistic but complicated, since the same person can sanction them. Acknowledge that tension rather than pretending the role is purely helpful.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Test each task: could you do it inside the facility this week? If not, shrink it until the answer is yes.

ask: What makes a person supportive of change, versus simply nice?
How do you handle the dual role of supporter and enforcer?

79.title: The thought-behavior link and why CBT
79.gist: Session 6 teaches the core idea of the program: to change behavior, target the thoughts beneath it. It cites research that structured, skill-based cognitive-behavioral programs reduce recidivism and introduces the iceberg metaphor.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Meta-analyses of correctional CBT programs generally find meaningful reductions in reoffending compared with no treatment or less structured approaches. The size varies widely, and well-implemented programs serving higher-risk people tend to show the largest effects.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The cognitive model goes back to Beck and Ellis: situations do not directly cause feelings and actions; interpretations do. Ellis put it in his ABC model, where beliefs about an activating event shape the consequence.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Thoughts drive behavior is a useful simplification. Behavior is also shaped by environment, habit, biology, and poverty. Overselling the cognitive story can sound like blame for structural problems.

ask: Where does the thought-behavior model fall short for someone returning to an unsafe neighborhood?
Why might structure and skills matter more than insight for reducing reoffending?

terms.d: Ellis's model: an Activating event, Beliefs about it, and emotional or behavioral Consequences.

80.title: Session 6 materials and flow
80.gist: The outline covers the iceberg group worksheet, a feelings chart, iceberg practice work, and steps from check-in to a thoughts-versus-beliefs activity.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This is the most conceptual session in Module 1. Draw the iceberg large and leave it unlabeled at first, so members build it with you rather than copying it.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Run your own iceberg on a recent moment you snapped at someone. Having a personal example ready makes the model feel lived.

ask: Why might thoughts versus beliefs be the hardest distinction for members?
How could the feelings chart help members who say they just feel fine or mad?

81.title: The program's main goal and target behaviors
81.gist: After check-in and goal homework, the facilitator asks what the program aims to accomplish, landing on reduced use and no new crime, then has the group list behaviors that would need to change.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Listing concrete behaviors first sets up the iceberg: those behaviors are the visible tip. Starting with what people do, which they can see, makes the shift to invisible thoughts more natural.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note that the script blends substance use and crime goals. Members may object that their crime was the drug use itself. Explore how use and other behavior feed each other rather than debating labels.

ask: Why start with behavior before thoughts when teaching CBT?
How do substance use and other offending reinforce each other?

82.title: The speeding example builds the chain
82.gist: The facilitator sets up a speeding scenario with a radar gun ahead. The group lists behaviors like braking or speeding up, then the feelings behind each, working right to left on the board.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Working backward from behavior to feeling to thought reveals that the same situation produces different reactions. The difference must lie inside the person, which is the key CBT insight made visible.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The cocky option, speeding up, often gets laughs and nods. Do not scold; it is the most useful row, because it shows how bold thinking produces risky action.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: If driving is unfamiliar for long-term residents, swap in an officer approaching during a shakedown. Keep the structure, change the scene.

ask: Why does one situation with different reactions prove the role of thinking?
How would you adapt this example for people incarcerated for many years?

83.title: Thinking controls behavior
83.gist: Thoughts are matched to each feeling and behavior, completing the chain, and the board reads that thinking controls behavior. The hopeful twist: if thoughts drive action, changing thoughts gives control.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Epictetus wrote that people are disturbed not by things but by their opinions about things. Ellis and Beck both credited Stoic ideas as forerunners of cognitive therapy.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Thoughts are not the only driver; emotions and urges can arrive before conscious thought, and some research shows quick reactions precede deliberate reasoning. Present the model as a powerful lever, not a total explanation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Emphasize the hopeful part. For people who feel controlled by courts and staff, the idea that they control their own thinking can land as real freedom.

ask: Is it ever true that feelings come before thoughts? How would you teach that honestly?
Why might this message feel especially empowering in custody?

84.title: Drawing the iceberg
84.gist: The facilitator draws an unlabeled iceberg and asks what part is visible and what tip of the iceberg means. Behavior is written at the tip, and the group starts discussing internal versus external.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
