deeper.text: Metaphors aid memory and transfer because they map a new idea onto a familiar image. The iceberg gives members a portable picture they can recall in a crisis without remembering any jargon.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The iceberg is often linked to Freud's model of the mind, but here the hidden layers are thoughts and beliefs that can be brought to awareness and changed, closer to Beck than to psychoanalysis.

ask: Why leave the iceberg unlabeled at first?
How is this iceberg different from a psychoanalytic one?

85.title: Feelings, body signs, and thoughts
85.gist: Below the waterline the facilitator writes feelings, body signs, and thoughts, defining each and handing out the Feelings Chart. A scenario is posted outside the iceberg: people at a sister's house start smoking weed.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on bodily maps of emotion (Nummenmaa and colleagues, 2014) found people across cultures report similar body locations for emotions, supporting the idea that body signs are useful early warnings.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Naming emotions precisely, called affect labeling, seems to reduce their intensity somewhat. A feelings chart expands vocabulary beyond mad, sad, and fine, which helps regulation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Family scenarios hit hard. A sister offering weed puts love and risk in the same room; expect strong reactions and let members say how close it is to their own life.

ask: Why might cravings be classed as a physical sensation here?
How does a richer emotional vocabulary help self-control?

terms.d: Putting feelings into words, which tends to dampen their intensity.

86.title: Charting the iceberg at a sister's house
86.gist: The group fills the iceberg for the weed scenario: thoughts like this will be the last time, body signs like a racing heart, feelings like excitement and nervousness, and the behavior of joining in.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Thoughts like just this once and nobody knows I am quitting are classic permission-giving thoughts. Relapse prevention calls related patterns seemingly irrelevant decisions and rationalizations that pave the way to use.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which single thought, if changed, would most change the behavior. That question previews cognitive restructuring and shows members the leverage point.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rewrite one thought in the chart and trace how the feelings and behavior change. One edit, a different ending.

ask: Why is this will be my last time such a dangerous thought?
How do excitement and nervousness together signal a craving?

terms.d: A thought that justifies a risky action, like just this once.

87.title: Beliefs: the base of the iceberg
87.gist: Beliefs are added at the bottom: global, always-on assumptions about self and the world that feed specific thoughts. Members practice by discussing beliefs like needing control or taking what you can get and how they might lead to use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Beck distinguished automatic thoughts from deeper core beliefs and schemas. Thoughts are situation-specific; beliefs are the lenses that generate them across situations, which is why changing beliefs has a wider effect.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Yochelson & Samenow described criminal thinking patterns, and later measures of criminal thinking build on similar ideas. Beliefs like the person with money has the power fit those patterns.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The always test is useful: if you can put always in front of it, it is likely a belief. Also note that a belief like I am who I am can protect identity as well as block change.

ask: Can a belief be both protective and risky? Give an example from your groups.
Why might changing a belief be harder but more powerful than changing a thought?

terms.d: A deep, general assumption about self, others, or the world that shapes specific thoughts.

88.title: Module 1 wrap-up and iceberg homework
88.gist: The module review recaps crisis strategies, values, goals, and the thought-behavior link, and previews Module 2's focus on risky thinking. Practice work is an iceberg on a behavior that got the member in trouble.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Applying the iceberg to one's own past behavior is the first step of self-monitoring, the backbone of CBT. A model only becomes useful once a person maps their own life onto it.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name one thing from Module 1 they would keep if they could only keep one. Their answers show you what actually landed.

ask: What would tell you Module 1 succeeded for a given member?
Why build risky thinking skills only after values and goals?

89.title: Participant Agreement and Group Expectations
89.gist: Members write why attending matters to them, review seven standard expectations including arriving sober and keeping confidentiality, add their own, and sign.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Commitment research, going back to Cialdini's work on consistency, suggests that a freely made, written, public commitment tends to shape later behavior more than a verbal nod. The reason line makes it personal, not just procedural.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief the blank lines 8 to 10: what members add tells you what they fear in a group, often respect or gossip. Those additions are cohesion data.

ask: What makes a signed commitment feel owned rather than coerced?
What would members' added expectations reveal about trust in your unit?

90.title: Introductions worksheet
90.gist: Members describe a typical week, who they spend time with, who matters most and what those people think of the program, past reasons for illegal behavior, and their importance and confidence ratings.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Quietly, these questions screen several RNR need areas: associates, family, leisure, and attitudes. A get-to-know-you sheet doubles as an informal needs assessment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The worksheet tells members not to use identifying names, which protects others. Model this yourself when sharing examples. Treat answers about reasons for crime with curiosity, not correction, this early.

ask: Which answers here would most inform your treatment planning?
How do the views of important people predict a member's engagement?

terms.d: Changeable factors linked to reoffending, such as antisocial peers, attitudes, and substance use.

91.title: Confidence Rating on group expectations, 1-5
91.gist: Members rate from cannot do it to can do it all the time how well they can stick to each expectation, starting with punctuality, respect, participation, homework, and an open mind.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rating specific behaviors rather than general willingness gives finer data. Self-efficacy is domain-specific: someone can be sure about respect yet unsure about homework.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by focusing on the lowest rating and asking what would raise it by two points. Small, concrete improvement targets beat promises to do better.

ask: Why is self-efficacy measured per behavior rather than overall?
What would you do with a member who rates everything a 10?

92.title: Confidence Rating on group expectations, 6-10
92.gist: The sheet continues with confidentiality and coming to group sober, then leaves room for members to rate any extra expectations the group added.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A low rating on arriving sober is a frank disclosure of active use. Treat it as a clinical signal for follow-up, not just a rule issue.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Confidentiality ratings show how much members trust themselves to keep group talk private. Discuss what makes keeping confidences hard on a unit, such as boredom, gossip, and leverage.

ask: How should you respond, clinically and procedurally, to a low sober-attendance rating?
Why might confidentiality be harder to keep in prison than outside?

93.title: Emergency Strategies reference sheet
93.gist: A take-away summary of the four craving facts and the five strategies: distraction, progressive muscle relaxation, deep breathing, pleasant imagery, and positive self-talk, with steps for each.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A one-page cue card supports recall under stress, when working memory shrinks. External reminders are a standard aid in skills training when the internal habit is not yet automatic.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to star their top two strategies and keep the sheet where they will see it daily. A sheet buried in a binder is no help during a 2 a.m. craving.

ask: Which strategy here is most realistic in a cell, and which least?
How could you make this sheet more personal for each member?

94.title: Emergency Plan Log
94.gist: A daily log where members note an urge, which strategies they used, and rate the urge before and after, then reflect on what works best for them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Before-and-after ratings turn each urge into a small experiment. Seeing a drop from 8 to 4 is direct evidence that urges pass and skills help, which builds self-efficacy far more than reassurance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In debrief, look for patterns across days: time of day, setting, mood. Those patterns are the first map of personal triggers for later modules.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to log a non-drug urge, like anger or junk food, if they had no cravings. The skill is the same; the practice still counts.

ask: What does a strategy that never lowers the rating tell you?
How could the log become a trigger map?

95.title: What's Important in My Life
95.gist: Members circle ten values from a list grouped under relationships, learning and skills, environment, and emotions, or add their own, as the base for the card sort.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A menu lowers the barrier for people who struggle to name values from scratch. Grouping into domains also shows whether someone's values cluster in one area, like security, or spread across life.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Watch for items like standing up for myself or making money; they can serve prosocial or antisocial ends. Ask what the value looks like on a good day versus a bad one.

ask: What does a list of values circled mostly under environment tell you?
How can the same value lead toward or away from crime?

96.title: Living Your Values practice work
96.gist: Members pick a substance-related behavior that got them in trouble, list four top values, and write how use helps and hurts each, following an example about stealing and parenting.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The two columns make ambivalence explicit for each value. Writing it by hand slows thinking enough for discrepancy to register, which a quick conversation can miss.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The example shows that use may not help a value at all. Accept members who write that it helps; ask how long that help lasted. Duration is often the turning point.

ask: Why might writing about values move people more than talking about them?
What would you ask a member who says use helps every value?

97.title: CBA Part 1 for Module 1
97.gist: The Module 1 copy of the cost-benefit grid for continuing a target behavior, now aimed at substance use rather than treatment participation. It is a Success Plan document.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Since this sheet feeds the Success Plan, its short-term benefits column becomes a list of needs the plan must meet another way. In relapse terms, these are the payoffs a high-risk situation promises.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Compare this CBA with the one members did in pre-treatment, if they did. Shifts in what they list are a quiet measure of growth.

ask: How would you turn this column of benefits into Success Plan content?
What does it mean if a member's CBA looks identical to their earlier one?

98.title: CBA Part 2 for Module 1
98.gist: The matching grid for a replacement behavior, listing short- and long-term benefits and costs of changing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Listing costs of change honestly is a form of coping planning: knowing what will be hard lets people prepare responses. Plans that skip costs tend to collapse at the first obstacle.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask whether the new behavior is available both inside and after release. A replacement that only works in one setting needs a second option for the other.

ask: What makes a replacement behavior durable across settings?
Why do honest costs strengthen rather than weaken a plan?

99.title: Changes and Goals for Module 1
99.gist: Members name a personal goal they are considering and at least three steps toward it, drawing on their values worksheet.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Linking goals to the values list ensures goals are anchored in what matters, not just what staff want to hear. Value-congruent goals tend to be pursued with more persistence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which value the goal serves. If the member cannot say, the goal may be borrowed; help them find their own version.

ask: How can you tell a borrowed goal from an owned one?
What step could a member take this week, inside the facility?

100.title: Preparing for Change worksheet
100.gist: Members set a short-term goal for life without substance use, with examples, then answer six questions on barriers, costs of failure, benefits, helpful traits, supporters, and one task before next session.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The six questions combine mental contrasting, decisional balance, self-efficacy, social support, and implementation in one page. It is a compact motivational plan that later modules expand into the Success Plan.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief question 6 first next session: did the task happen? Completed tasks earn specific praise; missed ones become a barrier to problem solve, never a scolding.

ask: Which of the six questions do you expect members to answer most weakly, and why?
How does this sheet foreshadow the final Success Plan?

101.title: A vocabulary for what you feel
101.gist: This chart hands members a broad list of feeling words sorted under happy, sad, angry and other. It widens a vocabulary that, for many men inside, has shrunk to 'fine' and 'mad', so later behavior chains can name the real emotion.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Affect labeling: putting a precise word to an emotion tends to lower its intensity. Neuroimaging work by Lieberman and colleagues linked naming feelings to reduced amygdala response, which is part of why emotional granularity is a regulation skill, not a soft extra.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Anger often sits on top of shame, fear or hurt. Ask members to circle the word they show the world, then the one underneath. Debrief by noticing how many 'angry' circles hide an 'embarrassed' or 'disrespected'.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member pick one word they have never said out loud about themselves and use it in a sentence about this week. Normalize the awkwardness; it is the point.

ask: Why might a narrow feeling vocabulary be adaptive in prison but costly after release?
Is anger a primary emotion, a secondary one, or does it depend on the person and moment?

terms.d: The ability to tell similar feelings apart precisely, such as irritated versus humiliated, rather than lumping them together.
Putting a feeling into words, which often softens its intensity.

102.title: The iceberg, blank template
102.gist: A blank iceberg diagram for members to fill in. The visible tip is behavior; below the waterline sit the feelings, body signs, thoughts and beliefs that drive it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The iceberg is a visual version of Beck's cognitive model: surface actions rest on automatic thoughts, which rest on deeper core beliefs. The picture makes an abstract hierarchy concrete and memorable.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Freud also used an iceberg-like image for the mind, but CBT's version is different: the hidden layers are accessible through questioning, not buried beyond reach. That difference matters, since it says change is learnable.

ask: What does a visual metaphor gain, and what does it oversimplify, compared with the linear behavior chain?
Where would you put a craving on the iceberg: body, feeling, or thought?

103.title: Diving under one costly behavior
103.gist: Members pick a behavior that brought unwanted consequences, ideally substance-related, and fill each layer: behavior, feelings, body signs, thoughts and beliefs. It turns the iceberg from a concept into a personal map.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to fill the tip easily and stall at beliefs. Use the downward arrow: 'And if that were true, what would it mean about you?' Two or three rounds usually reach a core belief like 'I can't count on anyone.'

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Body signs sit on the iceberg because physical arousal often arrives before conscious thought. Learning one's early bodily cues gives a person an earlier exit ramp than waiting to catch a thought.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which layer would have been easiest to change in that moment, and which would change the most if it shifted.

ask: Why might it be safer for members to analyze a past behavior than a current one?
How would you tell a genuine core belief from a rationalization offered for the group?

terms.d: A CBT questioning technique that follows a thought to its deeper meaning until a core belief appears.

104.title: Module 2 opener: changing thinking
104.gist: The divider page for Module 2, Cognitive Restructuring, listing its four sessions: behavior as a choice, risky situations, countering risky thinking, and putting it together. It marks the shift from awareness to active change of thoughts.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The sequence follows a classic CBT arc: first map the link between thoughts and actions, then find where risk arises, then learn to talk back to the thoughts, then rehearse the whole loop.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A module framed around 'behavior is a choice' can sound like blame to people shaped by poverty, trauma or addiction. The strongest facilitators hold both truths: context shaped you, and you still have choices now.

ask: Is it accurate to call addictive behavior a choice? In what sense yes, and in what sense no?
Why might the program teach risky situations before replacement thoughts rather than the reverse?

105.title: Why thoughts are the target
105.gist: This overview explains that Module 2 teaches the behavior chain and cognitive restructuring as core tools, grounded in cognitive theory and correctional research. It also warns that motivation fluctuates, so engagement techniques must continue throughout.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The cited lineage blends two streams: Meichenbaum's self-instructional training and Ellis's rational emotive work, plus Yochelson and Samenow's criminal thinking patterns. CBI merges a clinical model with a criminological one.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Meta-analyses of correctional programs, including work by Andrews, Bonta and Gendreau, consistently find that cognitive-behavioral approaches targeting criminogenic needs reduce recidivism more than punishment-oriented ones, though effects depend heavily on fidelity.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Yochelson and Samenow's work drew on a small, unusual sample and portrayed offenders as fundamentally different thinkers. Many scholars today see antisocial thinking as learned and common, not a separate criminal personality.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The note that motivation is transient is the key line here. Treat a member who was engaged last week and closed today as normal, not as failure; roll with it rather than confronting.

ask: What is lost if cognitive restructuring is taught without any attention to environment and opportunity?
How would you measure whether a skill has transferred to real life, not just the group room?

terms.d: Spotting unhelpful thoughts, testing them, and replacing them with more accurate or useful ones.
Discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs or acting against one's beliefs, which pushes people to change one side.

106.title: Module 2 worksheet roadmap
106.gist: A list of the worksheets used in Sessions 7 to 10, from the behavior chain to high-risk situations, replacement thoughts and goal progress. It lets the facilitator plan copies and see how practice builds across the module.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Notice the repetition: the behavior chain appears at the start and end. Spaced, repeated practice of one tool is how a skill moves from effortful to automatic.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Practice work between sessions is where change happens. Plan how members will complete it on a unit with little privacy or time, and what you will do when it comes back blank.

ask: Why might homework completion predict outcomes in CBT, and what does that imply in a correctional setting?
Which worksheet here would you cut if you had to, and why?

107.title: The behavior chain, link by link
107.gist: Background for Session 7 lays out the behavior chain: situation or trigger, thoughts and beliefs, feelings, behavior, and consequences. Its core claim is that interpretation, not circumstance, drives action, so changing thinking changes feelings and behavior.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is Ellis's ABC model in correctional dress: an Activating event, the Belief about it, and the emotional and behavioral Consequence. The trigger is not the cause; the appraisal is.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Epictetus wrote nearly two thousand years ago that people are disturbed not by things but by their views of things. Ellis and Beck both credited Stoicism. Members often respect an idea more when they hear it survived prison walls in antiquity too; Epictetus was born a slave.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Saying thoughts 'directly' cause feelings is a teaching simplification. Emotions can arise fast and bodily before deliberate thought, and feelings also shape thoughts. The loop runs both ways.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Calling the trigger an 'invitation' is a powerful reframe: an invitation can be declined. Use it when members say 'he made me do it.'

ask: If thoughts drive behavior, why do people so often act against what they think?
How would you explain to a skeptical member the difference between taking responsibility and taking all the blame?

terms.d: A person, place, thing or situation that sets off risky thoughts or cravings.
A deep, long-held assumption about oneself, others or the world that shapes how situations are read.

108.title: Consequences inside and out, plus agenda
108.gist: The page finishes the consequences idea, internal versus external and positive versus negative, then lists Session 7's materials and steps. The arc runs from a neutral example to a risky one before members try the chain themselves.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Moving from neutral to risky material is graded exposure for thinking: members learn the tool on low-stakes content before applying it where emotions run hot and defenses rise.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Internal consequences like self-respect are what behaviorists call intrinsic reinforcers. Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan) argues these sustain change longer than external rewards or punishments.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often list only external, negative consequences because that is what the system has taught them. Ask deliberately for an internal positive one, such as pride at a sober night, and write it big.

ask: Why might internal consequences matter more for long-term recovery than fear of re-arrest?
What makes a 'neutral' example truly neutral for someone with a violent or traumatic history?

terms.d: A result felt inside, such as pride, guilt or relief, rather than something that happens out in the world.

109.title: Check-in and the train switch
109.gist: The session opens with a thumbs check-in, a review of the iceberg, and practice-work sharing with praise for completion. It then introduces the train-switch image: seeing the collision ahead, you can pull the lever and change track.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Reinforcing homework completion out loud is operant conditioning applied to the group: the behavior you praise is the behavior you get more of. Andrews and Bonta's core correctional practice stresses a high ratio of reinforcement to correction.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The train metaphor quietly echoes the trolley problem in moral philosophy, but here no one is sacrificed. It frames choice as timing: the switch only works before the collision, which is why early recognition matters.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will say the engineer had no time to react. Agree, then use it: that is exactly why we practice spotting the other train sooner.

ask: What would a member's thumbs-down check-in teach you that a worksheet never would?
Is the train metaphor too mechanical for how cravings actually feel?

110.title: Two drivers, one spilled coffee
110.gist: The traffic example shows one event read two ways producing different feelings and actions. Then the group builds a risky chain on spilled coffee, with the facilitator writing members' own words for thoughts and one-word feelings.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The 'he did that on purpose' thought is hostile attribution bias, studied by Kenneth Dodge in aggressive youth: ambiguous acts get read as deliberate attacks. It is one of the most reliable cognitive predictors of reactive aggression.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Writing members' exact words matters: it signals respect and keeps the chain theirs. Asking permission before shortening a phrase models the collaborative stance of motivational interviewing.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After the coffee chain, ask how sure each member is that it was on purpose, from 0 to 100. Then ask what evidence would change that number.

ask: Where does hostile attribution come from: temperament, environment, or survival learning in dangerous places?
When might assuming bad intent actually be accurate and protective?

terms.d: A tendency to read ambiguous actions by others as deliberately hostile.

111.title: Short-term wins, long-term costs
111.gist: The group lists positive and negative consequences of the risky reaction and sorts them into now versus later. Then the same coffee scene is rewritten with calmer thoughts like 'it was an accident' to build a contrasting chain.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Defining a positive consequence as anything that makes a behavior more likely is the technical behaviorist meaning. Fighting can be reinforced by status and relief even while it destroys a life, which explains why it persists.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Delay discounting research shows people with substance use disorders tend to devalue future outcomes more steeply than others. Sorting consequences into now and later directly trains attention toward the discounted future.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: In some settings the 'later' cost of not responding to disrespect is real, such as being targeted. Acknowledge the code before asking members to weigh it against their goals.

ask: Why does a consequence that is certain and immediate beat one that is severe but distant?
How might you respect the prison code without endorsing it?

terms.d: Valuing a reward less the further away it is in time.

112.title: The replacement chain pays off
112.gist: With the new thoughts, members name softer feelings and a different action, such as reassuring the person who spilled it, and compare the consequences. The contrast shows that a changed thought ripples through feelings, behavior and outcomes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will hear 'forgiving' as weakness. Offer a middle replacement such as 'this is annoying, but not worth my freedom'. A replacement thought must be believable to the person, not just pleasant.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Side-by-side chains work like a controlled experiment: same situation, one variable changed. That design makes the causal role of thinking visible in a way a lecture cannot.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Viktor Frankl, writing about the camps, described a space between stimulus and response where freedom lives. The two chains literally draw that space on the board.

ask: What makes a replacement thought credible enough to work under stress?
Can a person act calmly while still thinking hostile thoughts, and does that count as success?

113.title: From coffee to the bar invitation
113.gist: The facilitator ties the calmer chain to members' goals and values, then moves to a substance case: a man trying to stay sober is invited to a bar by an old friend. Thoughts are written in present tense and linked to core beliefs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Tying the behavior to values is a motivational move from Miller and Rollnick: change sticks when it serves what a person already cares about, not what the facilitator cares about.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Insisting the situation is external keeps members from writing 'I wanted to drink' as the trigger. The craving belongs in thoughts or feelings; keeping the boxes clean is what makes the tool usable later.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask why present tense matters. Thoughts happen now, in the moment; writing them as now helps members recognize them when they actually show up.

ask: Is an old friend really a 'situation', or part of the person's identity and support network?
How would you handle a member who says the bar is the only place his community gathers?

114.title: Finishing the bar chain, handing out tools
114.gist: The group completes the bar example's feelings, behavior and consequences, probing for hidden costs like family impact. Members then get their own Behavior Chain sheet and learn every chain they write feeds their success plan.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When members list only fun outcomes of drinking, resist lecturing. Ask about specific people: who picks up the phone at 3 a.m., who visits on Sunday. Concrete faces generate consequences abstract warnings never will.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Telling members their chains become part of a success plan gives the worksheet a future use. People invest effort in work that accumulates toward something they own.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Group members may write safe, sanitized chains because staff read them and records can follow them. Honesty depends on trust about confidentiality limits, so be clear what is and is not reported.

ask: What would a facilitator lose by supplying the negative consequences instead of drawing them out?
How do confidentiality limits in corrections shape what a behavior chain can capture?

115.title: Members write their first real chain
115.gist: Members write their own substance-related chain: a specific external situation, at least five thoughts before acting, one-word feelings, the exact behavior, and consequences. The group then works one shared example on the board.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking for five thoughts pushes past the first, polished answer to the automatic thoughts underneath. The third or fourth thought is often the honest one.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Choosing someone who did the chain correctly to present is modeling, a key mechanism in Bandura's social learning theory. Peers learn more from a similar person succeeding than from the facilitator.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: If a member freezes, have them replay the moment like a film: where were you standing, who spoke first, what was the very first sentence in your head?

ask: Can people accurately recall the thoughts they had before past behavior, or do they reconstruct them afterward?
What risks come with putting one member's real chain on the board?

terms.d: Quick, reflexive thoughts that pop up in a situation without deliberate effort, often unnoticed.

116.title: Practice outside the room
116.gist: The session closes by assigning two personal behavior chains as practice, with members filling in the situation boxes before leaving so the facilitator can check them. Specific, picture-able situations are stressed.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Starting homework in the room lowers the barrier to finishing it, a small version of implementation intentions: a concrete start makes follow-through more likely.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Across CBT research, homework completion is generally associated with better outcomes, though it is hard to separate cause from the fact that motivated clients do more homework.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Checking situation boxes before members leave catches the most common error early: writing a feeling or a vague category instead of a scene.

ask: Why would a vague situation make it harder to recall automatic thoughts?
What practical barriers in a housing unit could you design around for homework?

terms.d: A specific if-then plan for when and how to act, which makes following through more likely.

117.title: History, lifestyle, and risky moments
117.gist: Session 8's background zooms in on the situation box and introduces a three-level map: life history factors, current lifestyle factors, and specific high-risk situations. Sensitive history is explored privately and may call for mental health services.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The distal-to-proximal structure mirrors Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention model: background vulnerabilities set the stage, lifestyle imbalances raise exposure, and the high-risk situation is the immediate test.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The example of using marijuana after nightmares is the self-medication hypothesis, associated with Edward Khantzian. It reframes use as an attempt to solve pain, which invites compassion and a better solution, not just abstinence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Keeping trauma history out of group discussion is protective: disclosure in a mixed prison group can expose someone to exploitation. Offer a private follow-up path.

ask: Where is the line between a cognitive-behavioral group and trauma treatment, and who should hold each?
Which lifestyle factors can a person realistically change after release, and which are structural?

terms.d: An ongoing condition of current life, like a stressful job or drug-heavy neighborhood, that raises exposure to risk.
The idea that people often use substances to relieve specific painful feelings or symptoms.

118.title: A situation you can picture
118.gist: High-risk situations are defined as the specific prompting event right before a choice, contrasted with vague descriptions. The page also previews the first two steps of the Success Plan: naming life factors, then the situations tied to them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Specific episodes are encoded with context, and context cues recall. A precise scene unlocks the automatic thoughts that a generic label like 'bad friends' hides.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Memory research on overgeneral autobiographical memory, studied by Mark Williams, links vague recall of personal events with depression and poorer problem-solving. Practicing specificity may be a skill in its own right.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Use the camera test: could a camera have filmed it? If not, it is a thought, feeling or category, not a situation.

ask: Why might people default to vague situations: avoidance, shame, or habit?
How might spotting patterns across many specific situations change what a person decides to change in life?

119.title: Session 8 materials and flow
119.gist: The outline lists worksheets on life history, defining and identifying high-risk situations, and the session steps. It moves from distinguishing lifestyle factors and situations to members naming their own risks.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Four worksheets in one session is heavy. Decide in advance which parts get full discussion and which can be quick, so the personal high-risk work is not rushed at the end.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The flow goes general concept, shared examples, personal application. It is the classic I do, we do, you do scaffold from instructional design.

ask: What would you protect if a lockdown cut this session to half its time?
How could you check that members truly grasp the difference between a factor and a situation?

120.title: Reviewing chains, opening risk talk
120.gist: After check-in, members recall the chain's five parts and which ones they control, then each presents a practice chain for correction and praise. The facilitator frames today's focus: the history and lifestyle that feed risky situations.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Correcting a first attempt is delicate. Praise the specific thing done right first, then shape one error, and leave other mistakes for later. Overcorrecting early teaches members that sharing is punished.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Shaping, from Skinner's work, reinforces closer and closer approximations of a target skill rather than waiting for perfection. A clumsy first chain is a step, not a failure.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Saying we always control thoughts and feelings overstates it; feelings especially are only partly controllable. Influence is a more honest word than control, and members who have tried and failed will notice the difference.

ask: Is it true we always control our thoughts? What does research on intrusive thoughts suggest?
How would you correct a member's chain in front of peers without costing him face?

121.title: What can't change versus what can
121.gist: The facilitator builds a three-column chart and draws general examples of life history factors, like childhood abuse or a jailed parent, then current lifestyle factors, like idle time or using friends. Personal trauma is gently routed to private follow-up.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The Adverse Childhood Experiences research by Felitti, Anda and colleagues found a graded link between childhood adversity and later problems, including substance use. Many listed history factors are classic ACE items.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking in general terms ('what might lead a person') is a classic distancing technique. It lets members speak about themselves safely in the third person, which often produces more honesty, not less.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Labeling history as unchangeable is true of events but not of their meaning. Trauma-informed work suggests how a person makes sense of the past can change a great deal, which is itself a cognitive target.

ask: If history can't be changed, can its influence? Through what routes?
What signs would tell you a member's brief mention of trauma needs same-day follow-up?

terms.d: Childhood abuse, neglect and household problems that are linked, as a group, to later health and behavior risks.

122.title: From family history to Saturday night
122.gist: Members privately list their own life history and lifestyle factors on a worksheet kept for the Success Plan. The facilitator then defines high-risk situations as specific triggers and walks through how a parent's use links to a family that still uses.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The chart is a causal ladder: past events shape present habits and networks, which generate specific invitations. Seeing the ladder helps members target the middle rung, which is changeable and has the most leverage.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Family systems thinking, from Murray Bowen and others, treats substance use as embedded in family patterns across generations. A person returning home re-enters a system that may pull him back into an old role.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Circulating while members write lets you catch who is stuck because of literacy rather than resistance. Offer to scribe quietly; never make reading a public test.

ask: How can someone protect recovery without cutting off a family that still uses?
Why might the middle column, lifestyle, be the best place to intervene?

123.title: Charting one woman's ripple effect
123.gist: Using the sample chart, the group links one history factor to a lifestyle factor and then to concrete risks, such as a holiday invitation from a mother who uses. Members generate more situations that branch from the same root.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: One root, many branches: a single history factor can spawn several lifestyle factors and dozens of situations. This is why rules like 'avoid bad people' fail; risk has to be mapped at the level of specific moments.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Holidays are a loaded example for incarcerated people, mixing longing and danger. Expect emotion; acknowledge that wanting family and fearing them can live in the same chest.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name one holiday or family ritual and silently rate its risk from 1 to 10. Then ask what a lower-risk version of that ritual might look like.

ask: How could the program help a member plan a safe visit rather than simply avoiding family?
Is a risky situation the same for everyone, or does the chart prove risk is personal?

124.title: Scoring personal risk situations
124.gist: Members complete the two risk-situation worksheets, which the facilitator scores using an Excel sheet that charts each person's risk profile. Practice work asks for four specific personal high-risk situations.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A self-rated risk inventory personalizes relapse prevention. Marlatt's model holds that high-risk situations differ by person, and Annis developed situational confidence measures on the same idea.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Returning a printed graph next session is a strong engagement hook: people are curious about data on themselves. Present it as a map to discuss, not a score to judge.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Self-report in a correctional setting is shaped by what members think staff want. Low scores may mean low risk, low insight, or low trust; ask about surprises rather than taking numbers at face value.

ask: What could make a member rate a situation as low-risk when it clearly is not for him?
How would you use a risk graph to start a conversation instead of ending one?

125.title: Countering risky thinking: the roots
125.gist: Session 9 introduces cognitive restructuring in three steps: notice thoughts objectively, pick out the risky ones, and replace them. It places the approach between Yochelson and Samenow's thinking errors and Jack Bush's Cognitive Self Change.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Jack Bush's Cognitive Self Change, developed in Vermont corrections, teaches people to observe their own thinking almost as a detached reporter. Self-observation comes before self-change.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Labeling thinking errors such as 'victim stance' can make members feel diagnosed and defensive. Downplaying labels in favor of rewriting thoughts is arguably a strength, keeping the focus on what to do instead.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Mindfulness traditions also start with noticing thoughts without fusing with them. Steven Hayes's Acceptance and Commitment Therapy calls this defusion; it offers an alternative to arguing with thoughts.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Calling thoughts 'recordings' is useful: an old tape plays automatically, but you can learn to hear it as a tape and choose not to follow it.

ask: Is replacing a thought always better than noticing it and letting it pass, as ACT suggests?
What is gained and lost when a program stops naming specific thinking errors?

terms.d: Habitual distortions, like blaming or minimizing, that Yochelson and Samenow linked to criminal behavior.
Jack Bush's correctional program teaching people to observe and replace the thinking that leads to offending.

126.title: Session 9 plan: rehearsing counters
126.gist: The outline for Session 9 lists the returned risk graphs, two replacement-thought worksheets, and a sequence ending in partner practice and peer feedback. The design moves from understanding counters to saying them out loud.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Building in peer feedback before facilitator feedback is deliberate. Praise from fellow members carries social weight in a prison culture where staff approval can look suspect.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Peer feedback often drifts into 'that was good'. Coach a format: one specific thing the partner said that sounded believable, and why.

ask: Why might rehearsing a thought aloud work better than writing it?
What could go wrong with peer feedback in a group with an informal hierarchy?

127.title: Returning each member's risk graph
127.gist: After check-in and a review of lifestyle factors versus situations, the facilitator hands back each member's scored risk graph and lists section scores on the board. Comparing patterns across members makes the data a group conversation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Posting scores on the board invites comparison, which can motivate or shame. Offer the option to share a pattern rather than exact numbers, and highlight that every profile is different, not better or worse.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Personalized feedback is a core ingredient of Miller and Rollnick's motivational enhancement approach: people respond more to their own data reflected back than to general warnings.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to predict their highest category before seeing the graph. The gap between prediction and result is often where insight starts.

ask: What does it mean if a member's graph shows no high-risk category at all?
How could group comparison support normalizing rather than ranking?

128.title: Three steps for changing thinking
128.gist: Members discuss whether their top risk scores surprise them, then learn the three steps of changing thinking: observe thoughts objectively, identify risky ones, replace them. Observing means noticing without judgment, often by writing thoughts down.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing thoughts down creates distance: on paper a thought becomes an object to examine rather than a truth to obey. Beck's thought records rely on exactly this effect.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Non-judgmental observation borrows from mindfulness and from Linehan's DBT, where observing and describing come before changing. Judging a thought as 'stupid' tends to trigger shame and hide the next one.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Asking people to watch their thoughts without judgment is hard when the program also labels some thoughts risky. Frame it as two separate moves: first notice, then evaluate.

ask: Can someone observe a thought neutrally while it is driving a craving?
Why might judging thoughts make people less honest about them?

129.title: The grocery aisle rationalization
129.gist: A man trying to stay sober stands in the liquor aisle telling himself he will buy some just in case a friend comes by. The group lists his other risky thoughts and learns one test: is this thought likely to get me into trouble?

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt called choices like this apparently irrelevant decisions: small, innocent-seeming steps that move a person toward relapse while preserving the story that he never chose to drink.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The test question is practical, not moral. It sidesteps arguments about whether a thought is true; 'it's legal to drink' can be accurate and still risky for someone on probation.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members for their own version of buying for a friend: the cover story they used before using. Most have one, and naming it often draws a knowing laugh.

ask: Why does the mind work so hard to keep a self-image of not choosing to relapse?
What separates a rationalization from a genuine reason?

terms.d: Small choices that seem unrelated to use but quietly set up a relapse; also called seemingly irrelevant decisions.

130.title: Two rules for a good counter
130.gist: Replacement thoughts must lead away from the risky behavior and be realistic. The page shows how the just-in-case thought lets the man buy alcohol while still feeling committed, and asks members to counter each risky thought.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Realism matters because the mind rejects counters it doesn't believe. A slogan like 'I'll never want a drink again' collapses at the first craving; 'I don't have to decide about forever, just leave this aisle' survives.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Stimulus control, a behavioral principle, explains the refrigerator question: once the cue is in the house, the decision is made over and over. Winning once at the store is cheaper than winning nightly at home.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may offer preachy counters to please you. Ask, 'Would you really say that to yourself at 11 p.m. on a Friday?' Keep only the ones that pass.

ask: Why is it easier to avoid a cue than to resist it repeatedly?
What makes a counter feel like your own voice rather than the program's?

terms.d: Changing your environment to remove or avoid the cues that trigger a behavior.

131.title: Counters built on what you value
131.gist: The sample chart pairs each of the man's risky thoughts with a realistic counter, and members learn that values-based counters, like children or hard-won sobriety, can be the strongest. Members then begin the Creating Replacement Thoughts worksheet.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Values counters work differently from logical ones. Logic disputes the thought; values reconnect to motivation. Both matter, but under strong craving, a felt reason like 'my kids' often outlasts an argument.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The counter that grudgingly accepts probation rules is gold: it validates resentment of the PO while still choosing compliance. Members trust counters that admit their frustration.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Family-based counters can backfire for members who are estranged or whose family harmed them. Help them find values beyond family, such as self-respect, freedom, or faith.

ask: Is a counter rooted in fear of the PO as durable as one rooted in values? Why or why not?
How would you help a member who says he has nothing left to lose?

132.title: Shoulder voices: rehearsing the argument
132.gist: Members write counters for each risky thought, then play the angel-and-devil game: a partner reads the risky thought and they answer with a counter on the spot. Whichever voice is stronger tends to win the choice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Spontaneous counters build retrieval fluency. Answering under mild pressure, without the paper, is closer to the real moment than writing, and practice under pressure transfers better.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Inner dialogue as a contest of voices goes back at least to Plato's chariot, with the charioteer reining in two horses. Psychology has its own versions, from Freud's structures to dual-process theories of thinking.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will play the risky voice with gusto and make the group laugh. Allow it: a vivid tempter makes the counter practice more real, as long as the counter gets the last word.

ask: Is it accurate that the stronger set of thoughts determines behavior, or are habits sometimes stronger than any thought?
Why might saying counters out loud matter more than writing them?

terms.d: The view that thinking runs on a fast, automatic system and a slower, deliberate one.

133.title: Rating confidence in new thoughts
133.gist: The facilitator asks how realistic and usable the new thoughts feel and how confident members are in them. Practice work asks them to use counters daily in real or imagined risky situations and record them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking 'how confident are you' taps self-efficacy, Bandura's term for belief in one's ability to act. In relapse prevention, low self-efficacy in a high-risk situation is a key predictor of a lapse.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Use a 0 to 10 confidence ruler, then ask the MI follow-up: why a 4 and not a 2? The answer makes members argue for their own strengths.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Inside, few drinking situations exist, so imagined rehearsal is the main practice. Encourage vivid mental rehearsal; imagery practice of a behavior can strengthen later performance.

ask: Is confidence a cause of success or mostly a result of past success?
How can practice inside a facility prepare someone for cues that only exist outside?

terms.d: A person's belief that they can carry out a specific action successfully.

134.title: Session 10: the whole loop
134.gist: Session 10 rehearses cognitive restructuring from start to finish. Its key message is that situations become risky because of the thinking they set off, and that recognizing choice over thoughts is empowering.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Locating risk in thinking rather than in the situation is a big claim: it means no place is safe or unsafe by itself. The practical takeaway is portable skill, because no one can avoid every trigger after release.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Relapse prevention research also shows environment matters a lot; cue exposure can drive craving with little conscious thought. Both are true, so pair thinking skills with avoiding cues where possible.

ask: If situations are risky only because of thinking, why do treatment programs still tell people to change playmates and playgrounds?
Where does empowerment end and self-blame begin?

135.title: Session 10 materials and steps
135.gist: The outline calls for six Behavior Chains per member, a Goal Readiness and Progress sheet, facilitator modeling of risky versus replacement thinking, personal role plays and a feedback protocol. Four chains go home as practice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Model, rehearse, feedback, homework is the core sequence of skills training in correctional CBT, drawn from Goldstein's structured learning approach. Each step targets a different part of learning.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Six blank chains can look like a mountain of paperwork. Frame them as two pairs, before and after, so members see a tight purpose rather than volume.

ask: Which of model, rehearse, feedback or homework would you never skip, and why?
How might the volume of worksheets affect members with limited literacy?

136.title: Review: three steps and counters
136.gist: After check-in, members recall the three steps, how to tell a risky thought, and what a counter is, then share real counters from practice. The facilitator sets up today's task: using the chain to both find and change thinking.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking what situations members actually met this week turns homework into real-world data. Celebrate any real use, even partial, more than polished worksheets.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The page mentions thought stopping. Research on thought suppression, notably Daniel Wegner's work, suggests that trying hard not to think something can make it rebound. Stopping a thought works best when quickly followed by a replacement or action.

ask: Why might thought suppression backfire while thought replacement helps?
What counts as success for a counter used once out of five tries?

terms.d: Interrupting a risky thought, often with a word like 'stop', before redirecting to another thought or action.

137.title: Same moment, rewritten
137.gist: Members pick a high-risk situation, write a chain for a specific instance, then fill a second chain on the same situation with replacement thoughts and new feelings, behavior and consequences. The facilitator then revisits the grocery aisle example.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The examples given, a job rejection, denied driving privileges, a cancelled visit, show that disappointment is a classic high-risk state. Marlatt's research found negative emotional states among the most common relapse precipitants.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A cancelled child visit is raw for incarcerated parents. If a member chooses it, slow down and validate before restructuring; rushing to a counter can feel like dismissing grief.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Debrief by asking members which box changed most between their two chains. Often it is feelings, which shows how much interpretation carries.

ask: Can a replacement thought honor a painful feeling instead of erasing it?
Why might disappointment be riskier than obvious triggers like seeing drugs?

138.title: The aisle, before and after
138.gist: Two complete chains show the grocery aisle scene with risky thinking, leading to buying and drinking, and with replacement thinking, leading to walking past. The facilitator then prepares to model the switch by thinking aloud with a hand at the head.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Listing no negative consequences for walking away is tidy but unrealistic: there may be boredom, craving, or friends teasing. Admitting those costs makes the choice more credible and prepares members for them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Feelings shift from excited and deserving to nervous and determined. Notice the new feelings aren't pleasant; recovery often means tolerating discomfort, not feeling good immediately.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Pointing to the head while thinking aloud makes the invisible visible. It signals to observers that this is inner speech, a technique called cognitive modeling, associated with Meichenbaum.

ask: Why might 'deserving' be one of the most dangerous feelings in recovery?
What negative consequences of the sober choice would you add, and why include them?

terms.d: A demonstrator speaks their thinking aloud so learners can see and copy the mental steps.

139.title: Thinking-aloud role play protocol
139.gist: The facilitator models the full inner debate, saying stop and switching to replacement thoughts before walking away. Each member then performs their own version, with the facilitator keeping it focused and closing with a four-step feedback routine.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Ending the role play right after the replacement thinking prevents members from rehearsing the risky thought in too much detail. Vividly dwelling on use can itself trigger craving.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Assign observers specific skill steps to watch. It keeps the audience engaged and turns them into coaches, which helps them learn the steps too.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Theater and psychodrama, from Jacob Moreno onward, have long used enactment to change behavior. Performing a new self in front of others makes it more real than imagining it alone.

ask: Why might performing a skill in front of peers produce more change than practicing it privately?
How would you handle a member who uses the role play to glamorize past use?

140.title: Closing Module 2, tracking goals
140.gist: Everyone completes a role play, the module is summarized, and members take home four chains to pair risky with replacement versions. A new Goal Readiness and Progress sheet asks them to update the short-term goal set in Module 1.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Planning thinking in advance is a form of pre-commitment. Deciding the counter before the moment means less willpower is needed when the moment arrives.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Goal-setting research by Locke and Latham found specific, challenging goals with feedback improve performance. Revisiting the goal each module adds that feedback loop.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name one moment this module when they felt proud of their work. Ending on owned progress strengthens commitment to the next module.

ask: What would a member's unmet short-term goal teach you about how the goal was set?
How do you know whether skill practice has changed real-world choices?

141.title: Blank behavior chain, first session
141.gist: The Session 7 behavior chain template: five linked boxes for situation, thoughts, feelings, behavior and consequences. Members use it to break one episode into parts and see where a different thought could have changed the ending.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A chain is a functional analysis in miniature: what came before, what happened, what followed. Behavior therapists use the same antecedent-behavior-consequence logic to find what keeps a habit alive.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief from right to left once in a while: start with the consequence and ask what thought made the behavior feel worth it. Reversing the direction surfaces hidden payoffs.

ask: Which box do members most often get wrong, and what does that tell you about how they understand their own behavior?
What does a linear chain miss about loops where consequences become new triggers?

142.title: Your history and your current life
142.gist: Members list the life events that shaped their substance use and the current habits and company that keep risk high. It becomes a Success Plan foundation and a quiet springboard for private case planning.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Separating what happened to me from what I do now draws a line between acceptance and action. It echoes the serenity prayer used in twelve-step groups: accept what can't change, change what can.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will list only history, which can become a story of why change is impossible. Gently ask for at least as many lifestyle items as history items.

ask: How might listing history factors help or hurt a member's sense of agency?
What would you do with a sensitive history item a member writes but doesn't want discussed?

143.title: Scoring risk by danger and frequency
143.gist: A party scene shows several high-risk moments stacked together, then the questionnaire instructions ask members to rate each situation on two scales: how often it happens and how risky it is for them. Frequency and danger together reveal priorities.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rating risk times frequency is basic risk assessment logic used in engineering and public health: a moderate danger met weekly can outweigh a severe one met yearly. Plans should follow the combined weight.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to rank the moments in the party scene: drugs visible, people having fun, a date flirting, an offer, a second push. Which is the real tipping point? Answers differ, which is the lesson.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Rating frequency is hard for people currently incarcerated, since many situations can't happen right now. Ask them to rate their life before custody, or how they expect life after release.

ask: Why might a stacked situation be more dangerous than any single trigger in it?
Should rare but very risky situations get special attention despite low frequency?

144.title: Five families of risky moments
144.gist: A facilitator guide defines the five scored categories: negative emotional or physical states, interpersonal conflict, social pressure, positive emotional states, and cognitions. Higher category scores point to where each member's Success Plan should focus.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: These categories closely follow Marlatt's relapse taxonomy, which found that negative emotional states, interpersonal conflict and social pressure accounted for a large share of relapse episodes in his early studies.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Positive emotions as a risk surprises many members. Celebration was often paired with use, so joy itself became a cue. Planning sober ways to celebrate closes a gap most people never notice.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The cognitions examples, like a job being beneath me, are thinking errors in disguise. Link them back to Session 9: these situations are really thoughts, and counters apply directly.

ask: Why would positive emotions be a relapse risk, and how could you plan for them?
Is 'cognitions' really a situation, or a different kind of category entirely?

terms.d: Tension or arguments with another person, one of the most common triggers for relapse.

145.title: Risk inventory, items 1 to 18
145.gist: The first page of the 50-item questionnaire lists feelings, conflicts, social scenes and thoughts for members to rate on risk and frequency. Items mix sadness, anger, cues like smell or sight, good days and authority conflict.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Spreading categories across the list rather than grouping them reduces patterned responding, so members rate each item on its own instead of blanket-marking a section.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Item 14, an urge or craving, is worth pausing on: cravings are internal and often pass in minutes. Urge surfing, from Marlatt's mindfulness work, teaches riding the wave until it fades.

ask: Which items here would likely score higher in prison than outside, and why?
How might reading the list itself act as a trigger for some members?

terms.d: Observing a craving as a wave that rises, peaks and falls, without acting on it.

146.title: Risk inventory, items 19 to 37
146.gist: The questionnaire continues with stress, bad news, special occasions, confrontation, pain, boredom, unexpected money and the usual time of day for using. Members keep rating each for risk and frequency.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Item 35, a certain day or time, reflects classical conditioning: times become cues just as places do. Payday Friday can trigger craving before any conscious thought.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Physical pain as a trigger links to the opioid crisis. Many people's use started with legitimate pain treatment, which is a reason to pair this curriculum with medical care, not replace it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Boredom is often underrated by members and the program alike. Point it out as the bridge to Module 3, which builds healthy activities to fill empty time.

ask: How can a person rebuild a weekly rhythm so the old using times stop being cues?
Why might 'I deserve it' thoughts around money be so persuasive?

terms.d: Learning in which a neutral cue, like a time or place, becomes linked with an experience and starts to trigger responses.

147.title: Risk inventory, items 38 to 50
147.gist: The final items cover rejection, disrespect, accusation, feeling bad about oneself, deserving a reward, fitting in, family gatherings, unwinding and missing old using friends. Together the 50 items create a personal risk profile.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Missing old friends (item 50) names grief for a lost social world. Recovery often means losing a community, and that loss needs filling, not just avoiding.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Disrespect items will score high for many men inside, where respect is currency. Link them to the coffee example from Session 7; the skill is the same.

ask: What does it mean for treatment if a member's highest risks are about belonging rather than substances?
How could you help someone grieve a using network without romanticizing it?

148.title: Name four of your own risky moments
148.gist: Members write four specific high-risk situations from their own past, using their life factors or questionnaire results. Each should state just the facts of what happened right before the decision that led to trouble.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect vague entries like 'being stressed'. Ask, 'stressed where, by whom, on what day?' until the scene can be pictured. This specificity is what makes Session 9 counters possible.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Limiting the entry to facts keeps the situation box clean of interpretation, which is saved for the thoughts box. Separating them is what lets members see interpretation as changeable.

ask: Why is 'just the facts' so hard for people when describing their own trouble?
Could listing situations make some members feel cornered by their past?

149.title: Pair each risky thought with a counter
149.gist: Members recall a situation with unwanted consequences and write five risky thoughts next to five replacement thoughts. The example counters the belief that one can be around using friends without using.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The example targets the illusion of control, a classic relapse thought: overconfidence that leads a person into risky company to test himself. Marlatt described testing personal control as a relapse trigger.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by reading counters aloud and asking the group: would this work on you? Peer reality-checking weeds out counters that sound good on paper but fail at midnight.

ask: When is confidence healthy, and when does it become a set-up?
Why does the program ask for exactly paired thoughts instead of general positive self-talk?

150.title: Testing counters in real life
150.gist: Members write three more risky-and-replacement thought pairs, then rate how well the counters worked and how likely they are to use them again. The ratings turn practice into feedback.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rating effectiveness turns each counter into a small experiment. Beck called this collaborative empiricism: treating beliefs as hypotheses to test, not as truths to defend.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A low effectiveness rating is valuable data, not failure. Ask what the counter was missing: realism, emotion, timing. Then rewrite it together.

ask: What would a consistently high rating from a member with obvious struggles suggest?
How could you help members gather honest evidence about counters inside a facility?

terms.d: Therapist and client working as a team to test beliefs against evidence.

151.title: Behavior chain, rewrite edition
151.gist: The Session 10 chain template, used in pairs: one for a risky-thinking version and one for the replacement version of the same situation. Comparing the two shows the payoff of changing one link.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to place their two chains side by side and draw an arrow at the exact point where the paths split. That split point is the skill to rehearse.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Rewritten chains can become too neat, ending in perfect outcomes. Encourage realistic replacement endings that include some discomfort, so members aren't surprised when sober choices still feel hard.

ask: What makes the same tool useful for both analyzing a past behavior and planning a future one?
How many repetitions might it take before restructuring happens without the paper?

152.title: Goal check: importance and confidence
152.gist: Members restate their short-term goal, rate its importance and their confidence from 1 to 10, and list steps they took since last session. It repeats at each module's end to track motivation over time.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Importance and confidence are the two rulers from motivational interviewing. Low importance calls for exploring values; low confidence calls for building skills and small wins. They need different responses.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask why the number isn't lower. It invites members to voice their own reasons for change, which MI research associates with stronger commitment.

ask: What would you do differently for a member with high importance but low confidence versus the reverse?
Why measure motivation repeatedly instead of once at intake?

terms.d: A person's own statements in favor of change, which motivational interviewing seeks to draw out and strengthen.

153.title: Module 3 opener: building a life
153.gist: The divider for Module 3, Setting the Stage for Success, lists its sessions on past successes, cost-benefit thinking about relationships, social supports and healthy activities. The focus shifts from thoughts inside to the life around the person.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Opening with success history is a strengths-based move: it reminds people they have already done hard things, which builds self-efficacy before asking for more change.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Recovery capital, a term from William White and colleagues, names the personal, social and community resources that sustain recovery. This module is essentially about building it.

ask: Why might a program focus on thoughts first and relationships second?
What forms of recovery capital are hardest for returning citizens to build?

terms.d: The internal and external resources, like relationships, skills and housing, that help sustain recovery.

154.title: Why peers and lifestyle matter
154.gist: This overview argues that negative peers model and reinforce substance use and crime while positive peers support change. The module guides members to examine relationships and activities and motivates them to swap risky ones for prosocial ones.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Antisocial associates are one of the central eight risk factors in Andrews and Bonta's RNR model, consistently among the strongest predictors of reoffending. Peer influence is a well-replicated finding in criminology.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Edwin Sutherland's differential association theory held that criminal attitudes and techniques are learned from intimate groups. Social learning theory, developed by Akers, added reinforcement and modeling to that idea.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Asking people to drop old friends assumes new ones are available. Returning citizens face stigma, restrictive supervision rules and few prosocial spaces. Treatment should help build new networks, not just prune old ones.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Talk of replacing friends can sound like disloyalty. Frame it as adjusting distance, not betrayal: some people move to the outer circle, not out of life entirely.

ask: Is peer influence mostly selection (choosing similar friends) or socialization (becoming like them)?
How would you help someone build a prosocial network when supervision rules forbid contact with many people they know?

terms.d: The major risk factors for reoffending identified in RNR research, such as antisocial attitudes, associates and substance use.
Behavior or relationships that benefit others and follow social norms.

155.title: Module 3 worksheet roadmap
155.gist: A list of Module 3 worksheets, from success history and cost-benefit analysis to mapping important people, support systems and healthy activities, ending with an action plan and goal check. It shows the module's arc from reflection to concrete plans.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The sequence moves from looking back (success history) to evaluating present ties to designing the future. That past-present-future arc also appears in many motivational and narrative therapies.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Plan ahead for members with very thin support networks. Have examples ready of community-based supports, peer recovery groups and faith or reentry organizations.

ask: Which worksheet here might bring up the most emotion, and how would you prepare for it?
How would you adapt support-system work for a member who will be released far from home?

156.title: Mining past sober stretches
156.gist: Session 11 shifts attention from relapses to times members stayed sober, to find what helped and reuse it. Facilitators stay neutral, highlighting change-pointing patterns without offering personal opinions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This borrows from solution-focused brief therapy, developed by de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg, which asks about exceptions: times the problem didn't happen. Exceptions hold clues people already own.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Addiction is widely understood as a chronic, relapsing condition for many people, and relapse rates have been compared to other chronic illnesses. Framing relapse this way reduces shame without excusing it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Neutrality here is hard when a member describes a success that involved something you would never recommend. Reflect what worked without judging; the point is his pattern, not your approval.

ask: Why do people remember failures more than successes, and how might that bias recovery?
Is a sober period that ended in relapse a success or a failure, and why does the answer matter?

terms.d: A solution-focused question about times the problem was absent or smaller, to uncover what already works.

157.title: Opening the door to past sobriety
157.gist: After check-in and a review of risky versus replacement thoughts, including one about not wanting to be in group, members share their paired chains. The facilitator then invites stories of any sober stretch, however short.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The review prompt about not wanting to be here is a smart move: it lets members voice resistance openly and practice countering it on the spot. Resistance named is resistance half-managed.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to recall a sober stretch and name one sensory detail from that time: a smell, a song, a morning. Concrete memory brings back the feel of capability.

ask: Why might people inside have trouble recalling any sober time in the community?
Does sobriety in custody count as a success history? What are its limits?

158.title: Five questions per sober period
158.gist: Members fill the Success History worksheet for each sober or attempted period: when it began, why they stopped, what helped, how long it lasted, and what led back to use. Discussion highlights jobs and supportive people.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Marlatt described the abstinence violation effect: after a slip, people who see it as proof of total failure are more likely to keep using. Remembering past success directly counters that spiral.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The five questions form a mini life chart. Patterns across periods, such as always relapsing after job loss, show which supports to protect and which risks to plan for.
