deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Validate short periods equally. Hours of sobriety can be a real achievement for someone in heavy use, and dismissing them teaches people their efforts don't count.

ask: What would it tell you if every sober period started for an external reason, like probation?
How might mapping patterns across relapses change how a member views himself?

terms.d: The guilt and all-or-nothing thinking after a slip that makes a full relapse more likely.

159.title: What ended each sober stretch
159.gist: Members explore what led to each relapse, such as a celebration, job loss or a fight, and repeat the five questions for up to five periods. Practice work turns one relapse into a behavior chain for next session.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Turning a relapse into a behavior chain reframes it as an event with steps, not a character flaw. That shift from 'I am weak' to 'here is what happened' is the heart of relapse prevention.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Attribution theory, from Bernard Weiner, distinguishes stable, global causes from changeable, specific ones. People who explain setbacks as specific and changeable tend to persist longer.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Check the situation boxes before members leave. Relapse chains often get the trigger wrong, writing 'I was depressed' instead of the event that came right before.

ask: How does seeing a relapse as a chain of events affect guilt and responsibility?
What risks come with asking members to recall vivid details of past use?

160.title: Weighing changes to your circle
160.gist: Session 12 brings back the Cost-Benefit Analysis, now applied to changing one's social network. Facilitators must recognize how hard it is to distance from longtime friends or family and stay neutral while members discover their own ambivalence.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The CBA is a decisional balance, a tool from Janis and Mann's decision theory adopted in Prochaska and DiClemente's stages of change. It makes ambivalence visible so it can be resolved by the person, not imposed.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on decisional balance suggests pros of change tend to rise and cons fall as people move through stages. But Miller and Rose found that pushing decisional balance on people who aren't considering change may sometimes strengthen commitment to the status quo.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Withholding opinion is the hard part. When a member defends a friend who clearly supplies drugs, reflect both sides back: 'He's been there for you, and he's also part of your using.' Let the tension do the work.

ask: Why might voicing the benefits of staying the same help someone change?
When is neutrality not appropriate, for example when someone is in danger?

terms.d: Weighing the pros and cons of changing versus staying the same.
Feeling two ways about a change at once, normal and central in motivational interviewing.

161.title: Session 12 flow
161.gist: The outline runs check-in, review, a group example of the Cost-Benefit Analysis, then a personal analysis on changing antisocial behaviors, with practice work to follow. The group example comes first to lower the stakes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Choose a group example close to members' lives but not about anyone present, such as a fictional person deciding whether to stop seeing an old crew. Distance invites candor.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Practicing the tool on someone else first is the same scaffolding as the neutral behavior chain: learn the form before applying it to your own heated material.

ask: What makes a good group example for a CBA about relationships?
How might group dynamics shape what members admit as benefits of old friends?

162.title: Benefits and costs revisited
162.gist: After reviewing why success and relapse history matter, members share relapse chains and the facilitator reintroduces the Cost-Benefit Analysis. The key reminder: consequences include both benefits and costs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Admitting benefits of risky behavior is what makes the CBA honest. If members can't name what they get from old friends, like loyalty, fun or protection, they can't plan to replace it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members without homework, follow the behavior management system calmly and briefly. Lengthy public correction costs group time and can shame; a quiet word afterward often works better.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Economists would recognize this as opportunity cost: every choice gives up something else. Naming what change costs is not pessimism but accounting.

ask: What needs do risky relationships meet that prosocial ones must also meet?
Why might people resist admitting any benefit of a behavior they've been punished for?

163.title: A group CBA on the bar crew
163.gist: After defining costs and short versus long-term outcomes, the group links relapses to friends or family, then fills Part 1 of a CBA on going to the bar with using friends. The benefits listed are honest: fun, company, not being bored.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Listing boredom as a benefit of the bar shows that relapse often meets ordinary needs. If a sober life can't solve boredom and loneliness, the old network will keep winning.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When members share a relapse involving a relative, listen for loyalty conflicts. It is easier to name a friend as risky than a mother or brother, so go slower with family examples.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Johann Hari popularized Bruce Alexander's Rat Park experiments, in which rats in enriched social cages consumed less morphine than isolated ones. The study is debated, but its point about connection fits this page.

ask: What is the real cost of telling someone to avoid friends who are also their only community?
How would the CBA change if the risky person were the member's partner?

164.title: Part 2: trying a new behavior
164.gist: The group picks a replacement, a night bingeing a show at home with a partner, and fills Part 2 with its benefits and costs. The facilitator notes prosocial choices tend to pay less now and more later, while risky ones do the reverse.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This short-versus-long-term asymmetry is the core of self-control research: impulsive choices win because rewards arrive first. The tool makes the delayed rewards concrete enough to compete.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A cozy night with a partner assumes a stable, sober partner and a home. Many members leave prison to shelters or halfway houses. Generate replacements that fit real reentry circumstances.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Affirming that members may still choose differently is genuine MI: autonomy support. People argue less against a choice they feel is theirs to make.

ask: What replacement behaviors would be realistic for someone in a halfway house with a curfew?
Why does respecting autonomy often increase rather than decrease change?

terms.d: Respecting a person's right to choose, which tends to strengthen their own motivation.

165.title: Your own CBA on a risky tie
165.gist: Members choose a behavior with a high-risk person, such as calling a brother who will invite them to use, and list its short and long-term benefits and costs. Facilitators must not supply answers; the benefits and costs have to come from members.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-generated reasons are more persuasive than ones given by others. Social psychology calls this the self-persuasion effect, and MI builds on it: people believe what they hear themselves say.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Linking costs to values from earlier sessions is a powerful prompt. Asking how a behavior affects what someone cares about turns an abstract cost into a personal one.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: If a member stalls on benefits, ask what he would miss most if that person vanished tomorrow. The answer is usually the real benefit.

ask: Why would facilitator-suggested costs make the activity less effective?
How could cultural values about family loyalty shape this CBA?

terms.d: Being convinced by arguments you generate yourself, which tends to last longer than being persuaded by others.

166.title: Imagining the alternative
166.gist: Members name a new behavior that would cost less and fill Part 2 with its costs and benefits, again without facilitator suggestions. The closing question asks what the exercise reveals about their relationships.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Listing costs of the new behavior first is unusual and smart: it brings barriers to the surface before enthusiasm masks them. Plans that anticipate barriers are more likely to survive.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The final question is the money question. Give silence after asking; insight about a relationship often arrives slowly and quietly.

ask: Why might naming costs of change first make the decision more durable?
What would you do if a member concludes the risky relationship is worth keeping?

167.title: Motivators, barriers, and weights
167.gist: The group charts shared discoveries and sorts CBA items into motivators and barriers. An optional step weights items 1 to 3 to show which matter most, and practice work repeats the CBA on another relationship and goal.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Weighting matters because a single heavy benefit, like belonging, can outweigh many light costs. Counting items treats them equally, which misreads how people actually decide.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Benjamin Franklin described a similar method he called moral or prudential algebra: listing pros and cons, then striking out items of equal weight to see which side remains.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Check marks for items several members share turn private struggles into group norms. It shows a barrier is common, not shameful.

ask: Why might weighting be reserved for higher-functioning groups, and could a simpler version work for everyone?
Can rational weighing capture emotional loyalties?

168.title: Relationships that block goals
168.gist: Session 13 asks members to identify risky relationships and how they block or sabotage personal goals. Seeing someone as a barrier is meant to motivate gradual moves away from high-risk ties toward new ones.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Framing people as barriers to goals shifts the question from whether a friend is good or bad to whether a relationship helps where I'm going. Goal-based framing avoids moral verdicts on loved ones.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Not every risky person is sabotaging; some are simply struggling too. Framing them only as obstacles can feed isolation. Consider which relationships could change, not only end.

ask: Can a relationship be both supportive and risky? How would you help someone hold both?
What signs suggest someone is actively sabotaging versus passively risky?

169.title: How people shape our choices
169.gist: After check-in and a review of how the CBA aids decisions and goals, members discuss their relationship CBAs. The facilitator recalls the bar-versus-home example and asks for real situations where friends or family were involved in use.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Social network research by Christakis and Fowler suggested behaviors like drinking and smoking cluster and spread through networks. The causal claims are debated, but clustering itself is well documented.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Start broad, how do people influence us, before personal. Members often describe others' influence more readily than their own, and that discussion can soften defenses.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to think of one person who made them better simply by being around. What did that person do? It seeds the support-system work ahead.

ask: Is influence a one-way street, or do members also influence risky friends?
How might social media extend or change peer influence after release?

170.title: Family, friends, acquaintances
170.gist: The facilitator sorts relationships into family, friends and acquaintances, defining each and noting that even loose ties can present risk, like a coworker using at work. Members are reassured they are not being asked to snitch.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The snitching reassurance is essential inside, where naming others can carry real danger. Say plainly that the point is for members to know their circle, not for staff to collect names.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 'strength of weak ties' showed that acquaintances often bring new information and jobs. Weak ties can be risks, but also bridges into new, prosocial worlds after release.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Defining family broadly, including chosen and adoptive kin, fits how many members actually live. It also widens the pool for possible positive supports.

ask: How could acquaintances become a route to new prosocial networks, not just a risk?
What does 'friend' mean in a setting where trust can be dangerous?

terms.d: Casual acquaintances outside close circles, who often connect people to new opportunities and information.

171.title: Mapping who matters, rating risk
171.gist: Members list important people, using initials if they prefer, then for each note why they matter and rate how much substance risk they pose from 0 to 3, with reasons. The final columns tie each person to a current goal.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rating people from 0 to 3 rather than safe or unsafe allows nuance. Most relationships are mixed, and graded ratings let members keep some ties at a distance instead of choosing all or nothing.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The anger example is telling: some people are risky not because they use, but because of how they make you feel. Encourage members to rate emotional triggers as well as substance exposure.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which rating was hardest to write and why. The hesitations often mark the relationships that matter most.

ask: Why might someone who never uses still be a high-risk relationship?
What privacy safeguards would you want for this worksheet in a correctional file?

172.title: Does each person help my goals?
172.gist: Members decide whether each listed person moves them toward or away from their goal, regardless of risk rating, then share one example. Practice work: two behavior chains about trouble involving a risky person from the list.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The pointer about a goal of a healthy bond with one's children is worth noting: the person who blocks that goal may be a co-parent. Explore carefully; these are among the most charged relationships.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Judging relationships against one's own goals keeps evaluation internal. It aligns with MI's focus on the person's priorities rather than the program's verdict.

ask: What happens when a person who helps one goal hurts another?
How might the evaluation change after release, when members actually see these people daily?

173.title: Why social support protects recovery
173.gist: Session 14 helps members identify supporters from daily life, from family to employers to supervision officers, and outside resources when local ones are scarce. Research cited suggests support buffers stress, reduces relapse and spreads coping skills.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Social support is one of the most consistent protective factors in health research, linked to lower stress and better recovery outcomes. Studies of mutual-help groups suggest gains in network support help explain part of their benefit.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cohen and Wills's stress-buffering hypothesis holds that support protects mainly by softening the impact of stress. For recovery, that means supporters matter most at precisely the moments risk is highest.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Listing a supervision officer as support is complicated: the same person can send someone back to prison. Members may reasonably see them as authority, not ally. Discuss what kinds of support each role can realistically give.

ask: Can an authority figure be a genuine support? What conditions make that possible?
Why might online recovery communities fill gaps for returning citizens, and what are their risks?

terms.d: The idea that social support protects health mostly by reducing the harm of stressful events.

174.title: Choosing the right person to call
174.gist: After review, the facilitator explains that different supporters suit different needs: a critical sister may be wrong for stress, while a grandmother who listens is right. Members are encouraged to build a network of several people.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Research distinguishes types of support: emotional, practical, informational and companionship. Matching support type to need is more effective than having one person who must do everything.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A network protects against a single point of failure. If the only support person moves away, gets sick, or relapses, the whole plan collapses. Ask: who is your backup to your backup?

ask: Which type of support do people leaving prison most often lack?
What happens to a recovery plan when the one support person relapses?

terms.d: Practical help, like rides, money or a place to stay, as opposed to emotional comfort.

175.title: Qualities of a helpful supporter
175.gist: The Choosing Support Systems worksheet asks members to list people in their daily life and judge whether each helps or hurts. The group discusses traits of good supporters: available, reliable, committed, honest, aware of one's patterns and warning signs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The list moves from logistics, like being available, to insight, like knowing your patterns. A support person who can spot early warning signs works as an external early-detection system for relapse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Having a volunteer read each trait and the group discuss it turns a lecture into a conversation. Ask for a story of someone who had that trait and how it mattered.

ask: Which of these traits would be rarest in a member's current network?
Can someone who has never seen you sober understand your patterns?

176.title: Honesty over comfort in supporters
176.gist: The discussion explores why follow-through, commitment, honest feedback and knowing one's patterns matter, then turns to qualities of people to avoid as supports, even those with good qualities otherwise.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Aristotle distinguished friendships of pleasure, of usefulness, and of virtue, where friends want the good for each other. A supporter who tells hard truths is closer to his third kind.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members prize loyalty above honesty, after years where honesty could get you hurt. Explore how honest feedback can be a form of loyalty, not betrayal.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to recall the last time someone told them something hard that turned out to be right. How did they feel then, and how do they feel about it now?

ask: Why might a person prefer supporters who agree with them, even when it hurts recovery?
How can someone ask for honest feedback without feeling attacked?

177.title: Who not to lean on
177.gist: The group reviews traits of poor supporters: those who feed risky attitudes, share the behaviors to avoid, are unreliable, dismiss wins and setbacks, are easily manipulated, or act as triggers. Each trait is discussed for why it undermines change.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: 'Easily manipulated into seeing things your way' is the sharpest item. A supporter you can talk into anything just amplifies your own rationalizations, which is the opposite of what recovery needs.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members may recognize themselves in this list, having been poor supports to others. That recognition can be turned into empathy and a goal: becoming a good support for someone else.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Codependency and enabling, terms from the family recovery movement, describe loved ones who protect the person from consequences. Enabling often comes from love, which makes it hard to name.

ask: Why might the most loving people in a member's life also be the most enabling?
How can a person tell an honest critic from someone who dismisses their successes?

terms.d: Actions by others, often well meant, that shield a person from consequences and make continued use easier.

178.title: Building a four-to-six person network
178.gist: Members are urged to pick supporters who help, to ask experts and community resources for new ones, and to list four to six realistic network members with reasons. Facilitators avoid exposing members with few options.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For members with almost no one, avoid public counting. Offer structured options they can list now, such as a peer recovery group, a reentry mentor or a faith community, so the sheet doesn't record emptiness.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Peer recovery support services, delivered by people with lived experience, have spread widely in reentry. Early research is encouraging, though study quality is mixed.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking experts for referrals widens a closed network. Many people leaving prison only know others from the same circles, so bridges to new circles have to be built deliberately.

ask: How would you prepare a resource list for members who are being released to different cities?
Why might a smaller realistic list be better than a longer idealized one?

179.title: Why a plan for support
179.gist: The session closes by asking why a support system matters, emphasizing that plans made in advance help when a person starts slipping. Support can be emotional, financial or practical, and can come from community resources and program staff.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Planning support ahead lowers the cost of asking when it matters. In a crisis, finding a number and making a call can feel impossible; a pre-made list removes those small barriers.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write the exact words they'd use to call a supporter when slipping. Rehearsing the opening line makes the call far more likely to happen.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Asking for help can feel like weakness in prison culture and in many masculine norms. Address that directly rather than assuming people will call just because they have a list.

ask: What makes asking for help hardest for the men you work with?
How could the program build help-seeking as a skill rather than just a list?

180.title: Session 15 materials and flow
180.gist: The outline for Session 15 lists the Healthy Lifestyle Activities and Developing an Action Plan worksheets plus a goal progress check. The session moves from reviewing supports to choosing new leisure activities and planning first steps.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Leisure appears in RNR's central eight as a risk factor: lacking prosocial leisure is linked to reoffending. Filling free time is not a soft extra but a criminogenic target.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prepare a list of activities that are actually available in your facility and in members' release communities, so the brainstorm ends with options they can act on.

ask: Why would leisure be a risk factor comparable to employment or family problems?
How do you build healthy leisure habits in a setting with very limited options?

181.title: What do you do with free time?
181.gist: After reviewing supports, the session shifts to current lifestyle factors, especially leisure time, defined as time free from obligations. The facilitator names common leisure traps like happy hours, casinos and parties.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavioral economics of addiction suggests substance use drops when rewarding alternatives are available. Community Reinforcement Approach, developed by Azrin and later Meyers, builds this into treatment by enriching a sober life.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The philosopher Josef Pieper argued leisure is not idleness but a condition of the spirit. For many members, free time has meant boredom or danger; reclaiming it as meaningful is a quiet transformation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what members did for fun before they ever used. Childhood interests, like drawing, sports or fishing, are often still alive and make credible starting points.

ask: Why might boredom be a stronger relapse driver than stress for some people?
What makes a leisure activity rewarding enough to compete with substances?

terms.d: A treatment that reduces substance use by making sober life more rewarding through work, family, and leisure.

182.title: Choosing activities worth trying
182.gist: Members list activities they want to try, have tried, or that match their values, share ideas, and circle four realistic, accessible ones to try in coming weeks. The Action Plan sheet comes next.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Linking activities to values echoes behavioral activation, a well-supported treatment for depression that schedules value-driven activities. Doing meaningful things tends to improve mood, rather than waiting to feel like it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Sharing ideas aloud helps members with thin lists. Write the group's ideas on the board so anyone can borrow one without having to admit they had none.

ask: Why might 'realistic and accessible' be the most important filter?
How could you tell an activity chosen to please you from one a member truly wants?

terms.d: Scheduling meaningful, rewarding activities to improve mood and motivation, rather than waiting for motivation first.

183.title: An action plan for new leisure
183.gist: Members turn one chosen activity into a plan: why they want it, one action step for the next few weeks, and a support person to help. The module closes by summarizing healthy relationships and assigning three more activities plus a goal update.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing down why you want something is a motivational anchor. When obstacles appear, the reason is there to reread. Pairing it with a single next step lowers the start-up cost.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Check that action steps are truly doable this week: 'ask the chaplain about choir' is concrete, 'get into music' is not. Help members shrink steps until they're almost too easy to fail.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to imagine starting the activity today and list the very first physical action. This is a version of the 'next action' idea from productivity thinking.

ask: Why might involving a support person in leisure plans make follow-through more likely?
What happens to motivation if the first try at a new activity goes badly?

184.title: Success history grid
184.gist: A grid where members record each sober or attempted-sober period: when it started, why they stopped, what helped, how long it lasted, and what led back to use. Patterns across rows show what to rebuild and what to guard against.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Reading the grid down a column reveals patterns, like supports that keep recurring in 'what helped' or triggers that keep recurring in 'what happened'. Columns, not rows, hold the lesson.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which column was easiest to fill. Members usually find relapse causes easier than helpers, a sign of how we remember failures more vividly.

ask: What would you infer if 'why' is always an external pressure like court?
How could this grid inform a Success Plan in concrete steps?

185.title: Chaining a past relapse
185.gist: The Session 11 behavior chain template, used for homework: members pick one relapse from their success history and trace the situation, thoughts, feelings, use and consequences. It turns a painful memory into a learnable sequence.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Relapse chains can stir shame. Open the debrief by thanking members for looking at the hard moment at all, then focus on the earliest link where a different move was possible.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt's model holds that relapse is a process, not an event. A chain lets a member see the build-up, often hours or days long, rather than only the moment of use.

ask: How far back before the use should the 'situation' start?
What does a relapse chain reveal that a success chain cannot?

186.title: CBA part 1: staying the same
186.gist: Members name a behavior they're thinking about changing and fill a four-box grid of short and long-term benefits and costs of continuing it. Owning the benefits honestly is what gives the later costs their weight.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Starting with benefits of staying the same respects ambivalence. MI holds that people move when their own reasons for change outweigh their reasons not to, and both must be voiced first.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which box was emptiest. An empty long-term benefits box often speaks louder than any lecture.

ask: Why might long-term benefits of staying the same be so hard to name?
When could listing benefits of risky behavior strengthen it instead?

187.title: CBA part 2: the new path
187.gist: Members write the alternative behavior and list short and long-term benefits and costs of changing. Comparing it with Part 1 shows how risky and prosocial choices trade immediate pleasure against later payoff.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Naming costs of change, like losing friends or feeling bored, prepares members for real obstacles. Expecting difficulty reduces the shock that can push people back to old patterns.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to put both parts side by side and circle the single item on either sheet that matters most to them. That one item often decides the choice.

ask: How might the short-term costs of change be reduced in practice?
Why do people underestimate how much short-term costs will hurt?

188.title: Private list of important people
188.gist: A private sheet where members list family, friends and acquaintances, using first names, initials or nicknames. It is the raw material for rating relationships and choosing supports, with no requirement to share.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Stressing privacy is essential where information can travel. Honor it: don't collect or read these sheets unless members choose to show them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Network mapping is used in social work and community psychology to visualize a person's ties. Some practitioners draw concentric circles with the person in the center, a visual variant that members may find easier.

ask: Would a circles diagram reveal more than three columns?
What does it tell you if the acquaintances column is the longest?

189.title: Rating your five key people
189.gist: Members circle their five most important people and, for each, note what they like, a risk rating from 0 to 3, why they're risky, and whether they help reach goals. The example shows a fun friend who is also high risk.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The example deliberately pairs fun with high risk. Recognizing that someone can be enjoyable and harmful at once is the core ambivalence this module works on.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking how members felt writing 'no' in the goals column for someone they love. Sit with the discomfort before moving to solutions.

ask: Why limit the list to five people?
How could a member reduce a person's risk without ending the relationship?

190.title: Support system checklist
190.gist: A one-page guide listing possible supporters, traits of helpful and unhelpful support, and steps: pick supporters who keep you steady, ask an expert, and list four to six network members. It summarizes Session 14's teaching.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Turning the session into a single reference page supports transfer: members can reread the criteria months later, after release, when choosing who to call.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to test one person against both lists. Most real people fit some of each; the question is which side dominates when it matters.

ask: How would you weigh a supporter who is honest but often unavailable?
What expert, besides a PO or counselor, might help members find new supports?

191.title: Scoring six possible supporters
191.gist: Members list six possible supporters and check which helpful traits each has: available time, commitment, follow-through, honest feedback, understanding patterns, recognizing trouble. The checks show who fits which kind of need.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A trait grid makes strengths and gaps visible across the network. If no one has 'recognizes when you're in trouble', that's a gap to fill, perhaps with a sponsor or counselor.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which trait column has the fewest checks. That column tells you what kind of new support to look for.

ask: Is it fair to judge loved ones on a checklist?
How could members tell supporters which traits they need from them?

192.title: Five healthy lifestyle areas
192.gist: The worksheet describes diet, exercise, spiritual development, mental health support and meditation as healthy activities linked to mood and coping, then asks which members want to explore. It widens the idea of recovery beyond avoiding substances.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Exercise has fairly solid evidence for improving mood and reducing stress, and some studies suggest it can ease cravings briefly. Meditation research is promising but uneven in quality, so claims of 'brain changes' deserve modest framing.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Twelve-step traditions place spiritual development at the center of recovery, and William James wrote about conversion experiences in alcoholism. Members who aren't religious can explore meaning, purpose or nature instead.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Diet advice can feel out of reach inside, where food is chosen for you. Focus on what members can control now, like timing, water or commissary choices, and what they'll do after release.

ask: Which of these areas are realistic inside a facility, and which only after release?
How strong is the evidence that diet affects relapse risk?

193.title: Four activities, four plans
193.gist: Members pick four activities for the next month and, for each, record why they chose it, one action step, and a support person to involve. It converts good intentions into concrete, social plans.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Combining a reason, a step and a partner hits three drivers of follow-through: motivation, a clear first action, and social accountability.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Next session, ask who tried something, not who finished the sheet. Reinforce attempts heavily, even failed ones.

ask: What would make a member's action step too big to start?
How could support people be involved without becoming pressure?

194.title: Goal check after Module 3
194.gist: The end-of-module check: members restate their short-term goal, rate importance and confidence from 1 to 10, and list steps taken since last session. Comparing with the Module 2 check shows motivation trends.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Repeated ratings create a simple time series. A drop in confidence after relationship work, for example, may signal that members now see the real size of the challenge, not that they're failing.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to compare this rating with their last one and explain any change in one sentence. The explanation is more useful than the number.

ask: How would you interpret rising importance but falling confidence?
What would you do with a member who rates both at 10 every time?

195.title: Module 4 opener: managing feelings
195.gist: The divider for Module 4, Emotion Regulation, lists nine sessions from recognizing feelings and coping by thinking or doing to urges, self-control, anger, stress, and rejection and failure. The focus moves from thoughts to emotions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Coping by thinking and coping by doing mirror Gross's process model, which distinguishes reappraisal, changing how you see a situation, from strategies that change your response or situation.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Emotion dysregulation is strongly linked to substance use problems and aggression. Many people use substances to manage feelings, so building regulation skills targets a core driver.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Linehan's DBT, originally for chronic suicidality, shares much of this content and has been adapted for substance use and corrections.

ask: Why might emotion regulation come after cognitive restructuring in this program?
Which of these sessions will likely meet the most resistance from men in prison, and why?

terms.d: The ways people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they experience and express them.

196.title: Why feelings get their own module
196.gist: The overview sets out Module 4's path: emotion regulation steps, recognizing feelings, the chain applied to emotions, coping skills, urges and mindfulness, then anger, anxiety and rejection. It notes sessions can be expanded for members with mental illness.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Landenberger and Lipsey's 2005 meta-analysis found CBT programs for offenders reduced recidivism on average, with stronger effects for programs including anger control and interpersonal problem-solving, and for well-implemented programs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Urge surfing and grounding come from mindfulness-based relapse prevention, developed by Bowen, Chawla and Marlatt. They teach tolerating feelings rather than only changing them, a useful complement to restructuring.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Treating emotions mainly as risks to manage can miss their information value: anger can signal real injustice, sadness real loss. Good regulation uses feelings, not just suppresses them.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The note on mental illness matters: many members have co-occurring disorders. Coordinate with mental health staff rather than stretching a skills group to cover clinical treatment.

ask: What is the difference between regulating an emotion and suppressing it?
How should a skills group adapt for a member with untreated depression or PTSD?

terms.d: Having a substance use disorder and another mental health condition at the same time.
Techniques that bring attention to the present moment through the senses, to reduce overwhelming emotion.

197.title: Module 4 worksheet and skill-card list
197.gist: A roadmap of Module 4 worksheets by session, including feelings charts, double behavior chains, coping strategies, urges, and skill cards for recognizing feelings, self-control, anger, stress and rejection. Skill cards give members pocket reminders.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Skill cards are memory aids designed for the moment of need. Under strong emotion, working memory shrinks, so a short written step list can stand in for what the mind can't recall.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Plan how members can keep skill cards: some units restrict papers. A card that gets confiscated or lost teaches nothing; ask about rules in advance.

ask: Why might pocket cards help more during emotional moments than during calm ones?
Which skill in this list would you expect members to use most after release?

198.title: Three steps: notice, name, manage
198.gist: Session 16 introduces emotion regulation in three steps: paying attention to emotions, labeling them, and managing them. It ties emotions back to the behavior chain and links better coping to less reoffending.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Noticing and labeling come before managing for a reason: you can't regulate what you haven't registered. This order matches Gross's process view, in which awareness opens the door to strategy choice.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Alexithymia, difficulty identifying and describing feelings, is more common among people with substance use disorders. For them, the first two steps are a real skill gap, not a formality.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Contrasting 'rational thought' with 'emotional dysregulation' can imply emotions are irrational. Modern emotion science, including Antonio Damasio's work, shows emotions are essential to good decisions.

ask: Can you manage a feeling without naming it first? What does research on implicit regulation suggest?
Why might people with long substance histories struggle to identify feelings?

terms.d: Difficulty recognizing, naming and describing one's own emotions.

199.title: Session 16 plan
199.gist: The outline lists the Steps to Emotion Regulation sheet, a feelings chart, a behavior chain and an emotions practice sheet, and moves from the link between feelings and antisocial behavior to the three steps and emotions in the chain.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The feelings chart returns from Module 1. Ask members if their vocabulary has grown since then; noticing progress itself builds motivation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Placing emotions inside the chain links new content to a known tool. Linking new learning to existing knowledge, called elaboration, helps it stick.

ask: How would you show members that their feeling vocabulary has grown?
What risks come with opening discussion of emotions with men who have learned to hide them?

200.title: How substance use tangles with feelings
200.gist: After reviewing leisure work, the facilitator introduces how years of use can dull emotions and how people use to escape pain or boost pleasure. Board examples begin with using to escape sadness over lost custody and to cope with anger.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Escaping bad feelings and amplifying good ones map onto negative and positive reinforcement. Over time, Koob's research on addiction suggests the negative side dominates: people use less to feel good and more to stop feeling bad.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Emotional numbing after long use links to neuroscience findings that substances can blunt the brain's reward response to everyday pleasures, which can make early recovery feel flat. That flatness tends to ease with time.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Warn members that feelings may grow louder as recovery continues. If they expect it, a surge of emotion reads as healing, not as a sign that sobriety isn't working.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to finish one sentence: 'Before I used, I usually felt...' Then: 'After I used, I usually felt...' The gap between them shows what the substance was doing.

ask: Why does relief from pain become a stronger driver than pleasure over time?
How might emotional numbness after long use affect a person's relationships early in recovery?

terms.d: A behavior becomes more likely because it removes something unpleasant, like using to stop sadness.

201.title: Emotions as information, not enemies
201.gist: Session 16 names why people use (to escape, amplify, or numb feelings) and then reframes emotions as signals with survival value, introducing fight-or-flight. It sets up the module's core stance: the goal is coping, not deleting feelings.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Functional views of emotion, going back to Darwin, treat feelings as rapid appraisals that prepare the body to act. Fear readies escape; anger readies confrontation. Using substances to change a feeling is, in this frame, shooting the messenger.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Stoics distinguished first movements (involuntary jolts) from assent (what we do next). That maps neatly onto fight-or-flight versus the choice point the Behavior Chain later trains.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Men who survived on the street often see fear as weakness. Reframe hypervigilance as a body that learned well in a dangerous place and now needs updating for a different one.

ask: If emotions are information, when is the information simply wrong, and how would a member tell?
Which of the three motives (escape, enhance, numb) predicts the hardest relapse pattern, and why?

terms.d: Automatic stress response (adrenaline, faster heart, tense muscles) that prepares the body to confront or flee a threat.

202.title: Three steps: notice, name, manage
202.gist: The facilitator rejects the idea of bad emotions and lays out the three-step regulation sequence: pay attention to the body, identify the emotion, then manage it. A modeled angry outburst makes body cues visible.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: A Finnish study by Nummenmaa and colleagues (2014) had people map where they felt emotions on body silhouettes, producing fairly consistent maps across cultures. It supports teaching body cues as an entry point to emotional awareness.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Gross's process model places regulation at different points: choosing situations, shifting attention, reappraising, or adjusting the response. Noticing early widens the menu; once rage peaks, only response-level tools remain.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When you model anger, debrief right away and out of role, so no one wonders if it was real. Ask members to name what they saw in your hands, jaw, and voice before anyone names the emotion.

ask: Why might the body be a more honest first clue than thoughts for this population?
Is there a cost to telling people there are no bad emotions when some feel shame as corrosive?

terms.d: The ways people influence which emotions they have, when, and how they experience and express them.

203.title: Building a richer feelings vocabulary
203.gist: Step two is labeling: members review the Feelings Chart, expand beyond mad, sad, glad, and scared, and circle feelings tied to their own use. Each person is treated as the authority on their own emotions.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on affect labeling (Lieberman and colleagues) found that putting feelings into words can dampen amygdala response. Work on emotional granularity suggests finer distinctions go with more flexible coping, though much of it is correlational.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Alexithymia, difficulty identifying and describing feelings, is more common among people with substance use disorders. A chart is a scaffold for a skill some members never had modeled at home.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to pick the feeling word closest to anger that is not anger, such as humiliated, cornered, or disrespected. Underneath words often point to better coping options.

ask: How do you balance 'each person is the expert' with noticing a member who mislabels hurt as anger?
Why might physical states like hungover or exhausted belong on a feelings chart?

terms.d: Ability to tell similar feelings apart precisely, for example frustrated versus resentful, rather than lumping them as 'bad'.

204.title: Coping by thinking, coping by doing
204.gist: Step three divides management into cognitive tools and behavioral tools, both forms of self-control, then returns to the Behavior Chain with Daniel's argument over money. It links feelings to the thoughts that interpret a situation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This mirrors CBT's two levers: change the appraisal (Beck, Ellis) or change the action and body state (behavioral activation, relaxation). Thinking tools work best at low to moderate arousal; doing tools often must come first when arousal is high.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which tools members already use without naming them, such as walking off, praying, or calling someone. Validating existing coping builds self-efficacy, Bandura's key ingredient for change.

ask: At what level of arousal do thinking skills stop working, and how would you teach members to recognize that line?
Is a relapse ever a coping-by-doing strategy, and what does that imply for replacing it?

205.title: Emotion as fuel and as trigger
205.gist: The group builds Daniel's chain from his partner's comment to thoughts, feelings, action, and consequences, then asks how emotion energized or justified his choice. It introduces mood itself, including boredom and overconfidence, as a trigger.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt and Gordon's relapse prevention model found negative emotional states among the most common high-risk situations. Note too the positive-mood trap: confidence after abstinence can lower vigilance.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Chains can make emotion look like a neat link, but in real arguments thoughts and feelings loop rapidly. Tell members the chain is a slowed-down replay, not a claim the mind moves in tidy steps.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask for the positive consequences honestly. Members trust a program more when it admits the problem behavior paid off in the short run.

ask: How does emotion work as a justification, not just a cause, in Daniel's case?
Why would feeling confident be a trigger, and what cognitive distortion hides inside it?

206.title: Boredom on a Saturday night
206.gist: The group builds a chain where boredom at home alone triggers hopeless, nostalgic thoughts, leading to resentment and restlessness and then a party with drugs. It shows how a quiet feeling escalates through thinking.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Boredom is widely reported as a relapse risk in early recovery, partly because old routines filled time with using. Building structured, rewarding activity is a core part of community reinforcement approaches.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Philosophers from Pascal to Heidegger treated boredom as a confrontation with empty time. For someone in reentry, boredom may hide grief for the lost life and identity of using.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The sample thoughts are classic all-or-nothing and fortune-telling. Have members spot which ones turn a dull evening into a verdict on their entire future.

ask: Is boredom an emotion, a state, or a signal of unmet needs, and does the answer change the intervention?
What would a replacement chain need beyond a new thought to beat a lonely Saturday?

207.title: Risky emotions and overcharged thinking
207.gist: Consequences of the boredom chain are weighed, then members are asked to identify risky emotions just as they did risky thoughts. Misread situations can inflate feelings, which cognitive restructuring can cool; the module's coming skills are previewed.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The point that misinterpretation intensifies feeling is Beck's cognitive model in miniature. Hostile attribution bias, seeing threat in ambiguous acts, is a well-documented pattern in aggressive behavior research (Dodge).

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When someone shares a time they misread a situation, ask what information they lacked at that moment. It keeps the lesson about missing data rather than about being stupid.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rate one memory's anger at the time and now, 0 to 10. The gap often shows how much the original story fueled the feeling.

ask: When is an intense feeling accurate rather than inflated, and how do you avoid invalidating real injustice?
Why list the positive consequence 'I avoided feeling lonely' at all?

terms.d: Tendency to read hostile intent into others' ambiguous actions.

208.title: Practice work: tie a feeling to use
208.gist: Session 16 closes by assigning the Identifying Your Emotions worksheet plus a risky and replacement Behavior Chain built around an emotion that has led to use. The Feeling Faces sheet backs up members who struggle to name feelings.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Homework is a defining element of CBT; it moves skills from the group room into real situations. Studies in CBT generally link homework completion with better outcomes, though the direction of cause is debated.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Literacy varies widely inside. Offer that members can draw, dictate to a peer, or use the faces chart, so the assignment tests self-awareness rather than writing ability.

ask: What would make practice work feel useful rather than like a compliance task on a unit?
How would you respond to a member who writes the same emotion every week?

209.title: Session 17 setup: Recognizing Your Feelings
209.gist: The background for Session 17 explains that members will practice the first two regulation steps through a structured skill with role plays. Facilitators must define, model, and rehearse with a prosocial, relevant demonstration.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Structured skill training (define, model, role-play, feedback, generalize) comes from Goldstein's Structured Learning and Bandura's social learning theory: people learn by watching a credible model and then practicing with feedback.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prepare your demonstration with a scenario members actually face, such as a phone call with a parole officer or a disappointing visit, not an office conflict. Relevance drives imitation.

ask: Why practice recognizing feelings as a behavioral skill instead of just discussing it?
What makes a model credible to men who distrust staff?

210.title: Check-in and reviewing emotion homework
210.gist: Members rate their mood with a thumbs gesture, review group expectations, recall the three regulation steps, and share an emotion and chain from practice work. It anchors the new skill in last session's material.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The thumbs check-in is itself emotional awareness practice. Push gently for one feeling word beyond 'good' or 'straight,' turning a routine opener into live rehearsal.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Eliciting review with open questions rather than lecturing uses retrieval practice, one of the best-supported findings in learning science: recalling information strengthens memory more than rereading it.

ask: How could the check-in itself become data on group climate over weeks?
What do you do when a member's check-in reveals a crisis that could derail the session?

211.title: Why naming feelings protects recovery
211.gist: The facilitator opens Session 17 by discussing what goes wrong when people miss their feelings, then posts three thinking steps: tune in to the body, link the situation, name the emotion. Members label each step as thinking or action.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Sequencing body before situation before label is a bottom-up route to awareness. It suits people whose first signal of trouble is physical tension rather than a clear thought.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Interoception, the sense of the body's internal state, is a growing topic in neuroscience; the insula is heavily involved. Some research links weaker interoceptive awareness with addiction, though the field is still young.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask about periods of numbness, not just bad feelings. Many members will recognize years of using when they felt nothing, which makes the skill personal.

ask: Why does the order body, situation, emotion matter, and when might another order work better?
What is lost if a skill has only thinking steps and no visible action?

terms.d: Perception of signals from inside the body, such as heartbeat, breathing, and gut tension.

212.title: Modeling the feelings skill aloud
212.gist: Members review steps two and three, then the facilitator models the skill out loud in a scenario where a spouse yells about a paycheck spent on drugs. Observers are assigned steps to watch, and pointing to the head marks spoken thoughts.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Thinking aloud makes covert cognition observable, a technique Meichenbaum used in self-instructional training. Assigning observers keeps attention active, which Bandura identified as the first step of observational learning.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Choose a model scene that hurts a little, like the paycheck example. A sanitized scene teaches the steps; a familiar, painful one teaches that the skill works when it counts.

ask: Why repeat the full wording of each step every time, and when could that backfire?
What does pointing to your head add that simply saying 'I think' would not?

213.title: Setting up personal role plays
213.gist: Each member names a specific time and place they could use the skill, ideally from their homework chain, and volunteers begin role plays. Because the skill is internal, members may practice without a partner.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Skill transfer improves when practice uses situations close to real life, a long-standing finding in training research. Generic scenarios produce performance in group that fades outside it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If a member cannot find an example, ask about the last time they felt their jaw tighten on the unit. Recent, small moments are easier to retrieve than dramatic ones.

ask: How specific must a scenario be before it truly helps the skill transfer?
What risks come with role-playing scenes close to real trauma, and how would you guard against them?

214.title: Feedback protocol and closing Session 17
214.gist: Role plays end with applause and a set feedback order: co-actor, observers by step, main actor, then the facilitator's praise. The session closes by linking the skill to the first two regulation steps and assigning practice work.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The fixed order lets peers reinforce before the authority figure speaks and has the actor self-evaluate, building internal standards. Specific praise tied to behavior is a core reinforcement principle from behavioral psychology.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Applause after every role play can become hollow. Make praise specific to what the person did, or reinforcement loses its value and members may see it as staff performance.

ask: Why does the co-actor speak first in feedback?
How would you give corrective feedback inside a protocol built mostly on praise?

215.title: Double Behavior Chain: why and when
215.gist: Session 18 background introduces the Double Behavior Chain, which pairs risky and replacement thinking without weighing consequences. Facilitators use it once members are motivated, keep two separate chains for ambivalent members, and stress intervening early.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is stage matching from Prochaska and DiClemente's model: people still weighing change need consequence work (decisional balance), while those in preparation or action need tools. Skipping consequences with an ambivalent member can trigger resistance.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Motivational interviewing (Miller and Rollnick) holds that pushing tools on someone not yet committed tends to evoke defensiveness. The manual's choice of chain formats builds that insight into the worksheet.

ask: How would you judge whether a member is motivated enough for the double chain?
Why might emphasizing risky feelings call for two separate chains?

terms.d: Weighing pros and cons of changing versus staying the same; used to work through ambivalence.

216.title: Session 18 materials and outline
216.gist: The outline lists the steps of Session 18: check-in, review, linking thoughts, feelings, and actions, introducing replacement thoughts as emotion regulation, completing and practicing a Double Behavior Chain, and assigning it as practice work.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is cognitive reappraisal, the regulation strategy Gross's research most often contrasts with suppression. Reappraisal is generally linked to better well-being, while habitual suppression is linked to worse outcomes.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Before group, write your own double chain from a recent frustration. Running the tool on yourself shows where members will get stuck.

ask: Does reappraisal risk teaching members to talk themselves out of legitimate anger?
Where in this outline is the riskiest point for losing the group's attention?

217.title: Reviewing Recognizing Your Feelings
217.gist: After the thumbs check-in, members recall the three regulation steps and the Recognizing Your Feelings steps, then share their practice situations. Struggling members can redo the skill in a brief role play.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what the body told them first in their homework situation. Stories about what happened are easy; the bodily detail shows whether the skill really ran.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Repeating review at the start of each session is spaced practice. Spreading learning over sessions produces more durable memory than cramming it into one.

ask: What signs would tell you that a member's homework was written in the hallway five minutes before group?
How long should review last before it eats into new learning?

218.title: Jade's layoff and the stop sign
218.gist: The facilitator introduces the Double Behavior Chain with Jade, who has just been laid off and spirals into resentful, fatalistic thinking. The stop sign marks the moment to interrupt risky thoughts and make room for new ones.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The stop sign echoes thought stopping, an older behavioral technique. Research suggests forcibly suppressing thoughts can make them rebound (Wegner's white bear studies), so the stop works best as a pause before replacement, not as an attempt to erase.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note the manual's point that a layoff can bring a flicker of excitement. Ask why: freedom, an excuse to use. Honest mixed feelings make the example believable.

ask: Which of Jade's risky thoughts are accurate, and how do new thoughts respect the true parts?
Why use a layoff rather than a typical prison-yard scenario?

terms.d: Trying hard not to think something can make that thought come back more often.

219.title: Runaway train of thought and feeling
219.gist: The group sees how Jade's new thoughts keep her calm and lead to a new action, while risky thoughts would likely have produced a lapse. Members then begin their own double chain on a situation where emotion led to use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The runaway train image describes a feedback loop: thoughts intensify feelings, which bias attention toward more justifying thoughts. Arousal also narrows attention, so early intervention matters before deliberate thinking weakens.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The new consequences include an honest negative: she still needs a job. Keep that. Replacement thinking that promises everything will be fine sounds like propaganda to people with hard lives.

ask: Is a lapse avoided by thinking alone, or does the new action do most of the work?
How would you explain the feedback loop to someone who insists anger just comes out of nowhere?

220.title: Completing and modeling the double chain
220.gist: Members write new thoughts and finish the replacement half of their chain while the facilitator checks each one. The facilitator then models Jade's situation aloud, voicing risky thoughts, then countering with new ones and stopping after the counter.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Check new thoughts for believability. Ask the member to rate, 0 to 10, how much they believe each one; a thought rated 2 will not hold in a real situation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Ending the model right after the counter keeps attention on the skill and not on the drama. It mirrors coping modeling, where showing struggle then recovery tends to teach better than flawless mastery.

ask: What makes a replacement thought believable rather than just positive?
Why might voicing risky thoughts aloud, even in a model, carry risk?

221.title: Practicing new thinking out loud
221.gist: Members practice by describing their situation, voicing risky thoughts, then new thoughts and feelings, and finally the new action. The facilitator cuts off overly detailed risky thinking and ends once the action is stated.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Calling thoughts old habits fits a habit-learning view: repetition strengthens automatic responses, and new responses need many reps to compete. Change is retraining, not one-time insight.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members enjoy telling war stories inside the risky thoughts. Pausing them is not censorship; dwelling on the details can rehearse craving rather than coping.

ask: Why might rehearsing risky thinking in detail strengthen it, and where is the line?
How many reps would a new thought need to compete with a decade of old ones?

222.title: Plan the new thinking in advance
222.gist: Session 18 closes by stressing that rehearsed new thinking is easier to use in a real risky moment, linking chains to members' Success Plans. Practice work is another double chain on a time emotions took over.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Implementation intentions, if-then plans studied by Gollwitzer, reliably improve follow-through across many goals. Pre-planned new thoughts act like if-then scripts for high-risk moments.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members compress their plan into one sentence: when X happens, I will think Y and do Z. Short scripts are easier to retrieve under stress.

ask: Why does planning ahead work better than relying on willpower in the moment?
How would a member keep a Success Plan alive after release, without the group?

terms.d: A specific if-then plan linking a situation to a planned response.

223.title: Why the body must calm first
223.gist: Session 19 background argues that managing activating emotions, mainly anger and anxiety, requires replacing risky thoughts, lowering physical arousal, and building interpersonal skills. This session targets the physical piece through relaxation, since intense arousal blocks clear thinking.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The cited work by Monti, Rohsenow and colleagues belongs to the coping-skills tradition in alcohol treatment. Relaxation alone shows modest effects; it tends to work best as one component of a broader skills package.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Arousal and reasoning trade off. Under high stress, prefrontal control weakens and habitual responses dominate, which explains why lowering arousal often must precede cognitive work.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The pointer to spend two sessions here is a dose decision. Skills learned once under calm conditions rarely hold up under real anger without repetition.

ask: Why might anger and anxiety be singled out rather than sadness or shame?
Should arousal reduction or thought work come first for a member with a trauma history?

terms.d: High-energy feelings like anger and anxiety that ramp up the body for action.

224.title: Session 19 materials and outline
224.gist: The outline runs from check-in and review through discussing how members already control their behavior, introducing the Coping Strategies worksheet, then teaching, modeling, and practicing each coping skill before assigning practice work.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Step 4, asking how members already control themselves, is a strengths move. Many have survived volatile settings by self-control nobody named; starting there signals respect.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Relaxation techniques can read as soft to men who equate calm with vulnerability. Frame them as performance tools used by athletes, pilots, and fighters to stay sharp under pressure.

ask: How would you frame relaxation for a group that values toughness?
Which existing coping strategies in a prison setting are risky but functional?

225.title: Check-in and double chain review
225.gist: Session 19 begins with a check-in that now adds a neutral gesture, reviews the three regulation steps and coping by thinking, and goes over members' Double Behavior Chains. A pointer urges two full sessions for practice.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The neutral option matters: forced binary ratings push people to exaggerate. Notice who always picks neutral; it may be honest, or it may be guardedness worth exploring privately.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: During homework review, ask which new thought a member actually used since last week, not just wrote. That separates paper learning from lived learning.

ask: What does adding a neutral rating change about the honesty of check-ins?
How would you tell a guarded member from a genuinely steady one?

226.title: Deep breathing as a brake
226.gist: The Coping Strategies worksheet is introduced, starting with deep breathing: in through the nose for five counts, out through the mouth for seven, for at least a minute. It links back to Module 1's emergency strategies.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Making the exhale longer than the inhale is thought to engage the parasympathetic nervous system, which slows heart rate. Controlled slow breathing has reasonable support for short-term stress reduction.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Breath control appears in yoga pranayama, Buddhist meditation, and military tactical breathing. Members may connect better to the soldier or athlete version than to a wellness one.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some people feel dizzy or anxious when focusing on breath, especially with panic or trauma histories. Let them keep eyes open and stop anytime.

ask: Why would a longer exhale calm the body more than a longer inhale?
How could deep breathing be done discreetly on a crowded unit?

terms.d: The branch of the nervous system that slows the body down: lower heart rate, rest, digestion.

227.title: Practicing calm with a mild trigger
227.gist: Members may close their eyes and picture a mildly unpleasant scene, then practice slow breathing to see if it lowers intensity. Debrief stays solution-focused on future use rather than processing the distressing memory.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Calling up a mild stressor before practice is a small dose of exposure. Practicing a skill under some arousal prepares it for real conditions better than practicing only when calm (state-dependent learning).

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Eyes-closed exercises can feel unsafe in a correctional group. Offer a soft gaze at the floor as an equal option, and watch for anyone who goes very still or tense.

ask: Why keep the debrief solution-focused instead of exploring the memory?
How would you recognize if a visualization tipped someone into a trauma response?

228.title: Pleasant imagery with all senses
228.gist: Members learn to mentally travel to a peaceful scene, free of drugs, violence, or sex, by describing what they see, hear, feel, smell, and taste. The facilitator models a waterside scene and guides silent practice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Multisensory detail makes imagery more absorbing, and absorption is what crowds out ruminative thoughts. Guided imagery is a common part of relaxation training.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Memory champions use vivid, multisensory scenes because the brain treats rich imagery almost like perception. The same property that aids memory makes a calming scene more effective.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some men have few safe memories to draw from. Let them invent a place or borrow one from a film or book; the scene need not be real.

ask: Why exclude drugs, violence, and sex specifically, and what might members choose instead?
Does escaping into imagery risk becoming the same mental checking out the module warns about?

229.title: Taking breaks and combining strategies
229.gist: Taking a physical break can release energy, but only if paired with replacement thinking, because brooding while active can escalate aggression or use. Members learn to combine strategies and use them early, and practice two at home.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on venting by Bushman found that hitting a punching bag while ruminating increased anger rather than reducing it. Physical activity helps when attention shifts away from the grievance, not when it rehearses it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what a break looks like on a unit where you cannot leave: going to the cell, reading, asking to step out. Breaks must fit the environment or they are fantasy.

ask: Why does catharsis feel like it works even when research suggests it can backfire?
What realistic breaks exist for someone who shares a cell?

terms.d: The popular idea that venting anger releases it; research largely does not support it.

230.title: Urges: accept, don't fight
230.gist: Session 20 background introduces mindfulness and acceptance approaches to cravings: feeling the urge without acting on it. Members will learn grounding to return to the present and urge surfing to ride out a craving.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Urge surfing was developed by Alan Marlatt and later built into Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention (Bowen, Chawla, Marlatt). It rests on the idea that urges peak and pass if not fed by action.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Mindfulness-based relapse prevention has shown some benefit in trials, particularly for reducing heavy use over time, though results vary and comparisons with standard relapse prevention are mixed.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (Hayes) and DBT's distress tolerance share this logic: struggle with an inner experience tends to amplify it.

ask: What is the difference between accepting an urge and giving in to it, and how would you explain it to a skeptic?
Why might acceptance work better for urges than reappraisal?

terms.d: Observing a craving's rise and fall with curiosity, without acting on it, like riding a wave.

231.title: Reviewing coping-by-doing practice
231.gist: Session 20 opens with check-in and review of the regulation steps and the coping-by-doing tools: counting backwards, pleasant imagery, deep breathing, and taking a break. Members share which strategies they practiced.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which strategy failed, not just which worked. Failures show where a tool does not fit a member's life and open real problem solving.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Counting backwards works partly by loading working memory. A busy mind has less room for the angry or craving thoughts that would otherwise fill it.

ask: Why might a strategy that works on the unit fail at home after release?
How would you help a member build a personal ranked list of tools?

232.title: Cravings are normal and time-limited
232.gist: Cravings are reframed as normal, common, time-limited, and a sign of change, often passing in roughly 20 minutes. Withstanding them weakens the trigger's link to use, and the session distinguishes avoiding triggers from responding to urges.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cue reactivity comes from classical conditioning: people, places, and things paired with use come to trigger craving. Each craving that passes without use is a small extinction trial, gradually weakening the link.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The 20-minute figure is a useful rule of thumb, not a law. Some cravings return in waves over hours, so say they usually pass rather than promising a fixed time.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Calling cravings a sign of change echoes the idea of extinction bursts: a response can briefly intensify when it stops being rewarded, before it fades.

ask: Why would a craving be a sign of change rather than a sign of failure?
What happens to extinction when a member lapses once in the middle of it?

terms.d: Craving and body responses triggered by reminders of past use.

233.title: Urge surfing step by step
233.gist: Urge surfing means observing a craving like a scientist instead of gritting your teeth, noticing sensations, feelings, and thoughts, and picturing the urge rise, crest, and fall. The facilitator teaches four steps and guides the group silently.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Taking an observer stance is cognitive defusion: the urge becomes something you have, not something you are. Labeling it creates a gap between impulse and action.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rate a remembered urge every 30 seconds during the exercise, 0 to 10. Seeing the number drop makes the wave visible instead of theoretical.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some will say it makes them think about using. Normalize that briefly: the goal is practicing being near the urge without obeying it, in a safe room.

ask: Is it risky to evoke cravings in a group setting, and how would you contain it?
How does observing like a reporter differ from suppressing?

terms.d: Stepping back from thoughts or urges to see them as passing mental events rather than commands.

234.title: Grounding: from spin-out to present
234.gist: Overwhelm leads people to spin out or check out, rooted in fight, flight, or freeze; children who cannot escape may learn to dissociate. Grounding links the senses to awareness, keeping a person in the present during anxiety, anger, or urges.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Dissociation as a childhood survival response is well documented in trauma research. Grounding is a standard technique in trauma-informed care, including Najavits's Seeking Safety, which targets co-occurring trauma and substance use.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members will quietly recognize the checking-out pattern. Avoid asking them to describe childhood events in group; naming the pattern is enough, and individual referral may be warranted.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Polyvagal theory (Porges) is popular for explaining freeze, but its neurobiology is debated. The behavioral observation of freeze is solid even if the explanation is not.

ask: How might dissociation look like defiance or not listening in a group?
What is the difference between grounding and the escape that pleasant imagery offers?

terms.d: Mentally disconnecting from the present, body, or feelings, often as a response to overwhelming stress.

235.title: Mental, physical, and soothing grounding
