235.gist: The facilitator models three grounding types: mental (listing street names), physical (noticing each part of a step while walking), and soothing (focusing on music and a calming walk). Each pulls attention from risky thoughts to something neutral or concrete.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Teach the 5-4-3-2-1 drill: name five things you see, four you hear, three you can touch, two you smell, one you taste. It is portable and works in a cell or a courtroom.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Swap the sample street names for streets members know, in Miami or wherever they are returning. Familiar names engage memory and give a quiet sense of home.

ask: Which grounding type fits which emotion best, and why?
When could soothing grounding slide into avoidance?

236.title: Role-playing urge strategies
236.gist: Members choose a specific scenario and strategy, pick a co-actor who resembles the real person if needed, and practice. The standard feedback protocol follows, and facilitators are reminded that waiting out silence often brings volunteers.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The tip to tolerate silence is powerful: most people find silence harder than volunteering. Count to ten in your head before rescuing the group.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Choosing a co-actor who resembles the real person adds realism, which improves transfer. Ask the main actor to say aloud which strategy they will use, which rehearses the decision itself.

ask: How do you role-play an internal skill like urge surfing so others can observe it?
What does a member's choice of co-actor tell you about the real relationship?

237.title: Pulling tools into Using Self-Control
237.gist: Session 21 background recaps the module's tools: double chains, four coping-by-doing strategies, urge surfing, and grounding. This session combines them in one social skill, Using Self-Control, so members see how the techniques fit everyday life.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Separate techniques become usable when bundled into one decision routine. Cognitive psychologists call this chunking: a single skill with four steps is easier to retrieve under stress than seven loose tools.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Self-control framed as willpower has a shaky history; the ego-depletion idea (Baumeister) has struggled in replication. Present self-control here as a learned routine, not a fixed reserve of strength.

ask: Is self-control a trait, a skill, or a product of environment, and what does each view imply for reentry?
Which of the seven tools would you expect most members to abandon first, and why?

238.title: Review of urge strategies
238.gist: After check-in, members recall the two urge strategies and three grounding types, then share how they practiced managing urges in two high-risk situations from their homework.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to compare urge surfing with grounding in their own experience: which felt more natural? Personal fit predicts which tool they will actually use.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name one high-risk situation they expect in their first week after release. Linking practice to a concrete future scene builds prospective memory.

ask: Why might high-risk situations in a facility differ from those after release, and how do you bridge them?
What would honest homework look like from someone who had no urges that week?

239.title: Self-control: four steps
239.gist: The skill Using Self-Control is introduced through a discussion of times members lost control, then four steps: notice body cues, notice risky thoughts, list coping strategies, and pick the best one and use it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The steps follow a classic problem-solving model (D'Zurilla and Goldfried): detect the problem, define it, generate options, choose and act. Here the problem is internal arousal rather than an outside task.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Aristotle described virtue as a habit formed by practice; self-control in his view was built by repeatedly acting well until it became character. Role play is a modern version of that apprenticeship.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking for times members lost control can invite boasting about violence. Steer toward the cost: what did that moment take from you?

ask: Why is step 4 the only one with an action component, and is that enough?
How do you keep a discussion of losing control from glorifying it?

240.title: Walking through the self-control steps
240.gist: Volunteers read each step while the group discusses why it matters and marks it thinking or action. Step 3 lists the full menu of strategies learned so far, from double chains to grounding.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what happens if someone jumps straight to step 4. Usually the answer is a habitual strategy that is not the best fit, which shows why generating options matters.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Reflective listening, flagged again here, is the core of Miller and Rollnick's motivational interviewing. It keeps members talking and signals that their reasoning is taken seriously.

ask: Is a long menu of strategies a help or a burden under stress?
How would you teach someone to pick the best strategy quickly?

terms.d: Restating the meaning of what someone said so they feel heard and keep exploring.

241.title: Modeling self-control at work
241.gist: The facilitator models being unfairly criticized at work, with the urge to curse out the boss, quit, and get high, walking through body cues, risky thoughts, options, and choosing deep breathing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The scene shows how an injustice appraisal fuels anger and then a using plan in one breath. Linking anger directly to use mirrors relapse prevention findings that interpersonal conflict is a top relapse trigger.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The model ends once he calms down, but unfair criticism remains. Discuss what comes next, such as raising it later with the boss, so self-control is not confused with silent acceptance of mistreatment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For men facing job barriers due to a record, losing a job is a huge risk. Make the stakes real: one outburst can cost the job that satisfies parole.

ask: When does self-control become self-silencing, and how would you teach the difference?
Why include 'go get high' in a work scenario about anger?

242.title: Running self-control role plays
242.gist: Observers are assigned steps, the facilitator pauses role plays that go off track and points to the posted steps, and feedback follows a shorter protocol: observers, main actor, then praise. Every member takes a turn.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Pausing is a teaching move, not a correction. Say something like let's rewind to step 2, so the actor stays in the role and the group sees that mistakes are part of practice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking how likely members are to use the skill is a small commitment probe. Saying an intention out loud tends to increase follow-through, a theme in MI's attention to change talk.

ask: Why might this protocol drop the co-actor's feedback compared with earlier skills?
What do you do when a role play reveals a member's real plan to retaliate?

terms.d: A person's own statements in favor of change; MI aims to draw these out.

243.title: Anger can be changed
243.gist: Session 22 background acknowledges that some people are so conditioned to respond aggressively that change seems impossible, then argues that knowing anger's signs and using reasoning makes change possible. Members will practice the skill Dealing with Anger.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Meta-analyses of CBT for anger generally find moderate positive effects. Novaco's work on anger, building on Meichenbaum's stress inoculation, shaped many correctional anger programs.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Anger programs alone often show weak effects on violent recidivism unless they address broader criminogenic needs, per the RNR literature (Andrews and Bonta). Anger skills are one piece, not the whole picture.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Seneca's On Anger argued anger is a choice following a judgment of injury, and that delay is its best remedy. Two thousand years later, CBT says much the same.

ask: If aggression has been adaptive in someone's environment, what exactly are you asking them to give up?
Why might anger be tied to substance use more than other emotions in this population?

244.title: Review of self-control practice
244.gist: Session 22 opens with check-in, review of the regulation steps and the Using Self-Control skill, and sharing of practice work. The facilitator stresses that practice is what makes skills hold in hard moments.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When members share their homework, ask which step was hardest to remember in the moment. The answer usually points to step 1: noticing comes too late.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Practice builds automaticity. The goal is for the steps to fire with little effort, because effortful processing is what gets lost when arousal spikes.

ask: How would you know a skill has become automatic for a member?
What is the most honest reason members skip practice work?

245.title: Reading anger's early signals
245.gist: Self-control strategies are recast as anger management, with physical sensations and body language added to the Behavior Chain as early warning signs. Members list their own cues, since anger moves fast and early intervention prevents regret.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Anger arousal models often describe escalation in phases, from trigger to peak to recovery. Cues caught early sit before the point of no return, where reasoning still has room.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Build an anger thermometer on the board from 0 to 10. Members place their cues on it; low numbers are where the skills work best.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will say they go from 0 to 10 instantly. Explore what happened in the hour before, such as fatigue, hunger, or earlier slights, which lower the threshold.

ask: Why do some people perceive their anger as instant when research suggests there are usually earlier cues?
How do stress and sleep loss change anger thresholds?

terms.d: A 0-10 scale used to rate anger and match coping strategies to intensity.

246.title: Dealing with Anger skill steps
246.gist: Volunteers read and discuss the anger skill steps: identify the triggering situation, identify thoughts, body cues, and feelings, consider the consequences of possible responses, then choose a coping strategy. Each is marked thinking or action.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Adding consequential thinking, step 3, brings in a classic CBI target: thinking ahead before acting. Weak consequential thinking is linked with impulsivity in criminology research.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When members discuss consequences, have them include consequences for others, such as a child watching or a partner. This adds empathy to self-interest.

ask: Why include consequences in the anger skill but not in Recognizing Your Feelings?
Can one think about consequences when angry, or must that come after calming down?

247.title: Model: friend wrecked my car
247.gist: The facilitator models a friend wrecking his car: noticing disrespect and the urge to punch, weighing arrest or a dirty UA against calming down, taking a break with paced breathing, then returning to calmly arrange repairs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The model ends with assertive action, asking the friend to pay. This shows anger management is not passivity; the goal is to turn energy into a fair resolution.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Respect is a high-stakes currency in street and prison cultures, as Elijah Anderson described in Code of the Street. Disrespect triggers can feel like threats to safety, not just to pride.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect members to say that letting it go looks weak. Ask: who looks stronger, the man who gets arrested or the man who gets his car fixed?

ask: How would you adapt this model when the disrespect happens in front of peers?
Is respect a legitimate need to be met rather than a distortion to be challenged?

248.title: Rehearsing before the anger role play
248.gist: Actors may rehearse the scene privately first, directing the co-actor, while a co-facilitator assigns observer steps. The facilitator monitors, pauses when needed, ends at the final step, and reminds actors to point to their heads.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Private rehearsal lowers performance anxiety and keeps a co-actor from improvising an escalation. With anger scenes, it is a safety step too.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After a role play, ask the actor to rate their real anger during the scene. If it rose, they practiced the skill under true arousal, which is good preparation.

ask: When could realism in an anger role play become unsafe, and what are your stop signals?
Why might a member resist pointing to their head, and does it matter?

249.title: Stress, the brain, and relapse
249.gist: Session 23 background explains that many people use to cope with stress and anxiety, and that chronic use alters the brain's stress response, weakening regulation and impulse control. Coping skills plus prosocial lifestyle changes reduce both stress and relapse risk.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Rajita Sinha's research shows that stress and drug cues both increase craving, and that stress-induced craving can predict relapse. Chronic use appears to dysregulate the HPA axis, the body's main stress system.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model holds that stress depends on appraisal: whether a demand seems threatening and whether we feel able to cope. That is why the manual calls stress perception-based.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Telling people stress is perception can sound dismissive when reentry stress is objective: housing, debt, supervision. Address real stressors, not just appraisals.

ask: Which reentry stressors are objective and which are amplified by appraisal?
How does knowing about stress neurobiology reduce shame for members?

terms.d: The hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal system that releases cortisol and regulates the body's stress response.

250.title: Session 23 materials and outline
250.gist: The outline lists check-in, review, a Daily Stressors worksheet with group rating activity, introduction of the stress and anxiety skill, role plays, and practice work on dealing with anxiety and stress.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The group rating activity will expose different stress thresholds. Use it to show that the same event lands differently, then ask what explains the difference.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Holmes and Rahe's life events scale tried to rate stressful events numerically. Later research favored daily hassles (Lazarus) as stronger predictors of well-being, which this worksheet echoes.

ask: Why might small daily hassles predict relapse better than big life events?
What would you do if a member rates every stressor as maximal?

terms.d: Small, frequent irritations of everyday life that add up and affect stress and health.

251.title: Reviewing the anger skill
251.gist: Session 23 opens with check-in and a review of why Managing Anger matters and its steps, followed by members sharing where they practiced the anger skill and how they rated themselves.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Self-ratings tend to be generous. Ask for one step they would do differently next time; it invites honest self-assessment without making the review a test.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-monitoring, rating one's own performance, is itself a behavior change technique. Simply tracking a behavior often shifts it, a phenomenon called reactivity.

ask: How do you get honest self-ratings from people used to being evaluated by authorities?
What does a member's rating tell you beyond whether the skill worked?

terms.d: The tendency for a behavior to change simply because it is being monitored.

252.title: Stress is a response to demands
252.gist: Stress is defined as the body's natural response to demands, triggered even by positive or imagined change. Members list times stress led to use and complete the Daily Stressors worksheet, with high totals normalized.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Hans Selye distinguished harmful distress from eustress, the stress of positive challenges. A new job or release date can trigger the same body alarm as a loss, which surprises many members.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The Yerkes-Dodson principle suggests moderate arousal can improve performance while high arousal impairs it. Stress is not the enemy; overload and poor coping are.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Release is one of the most stressful positive events there is. Name it directly; members often feel ashamed that freedom feels frightening.

ask: Why might positive change, like release, trigger use as often as negative events?
What is the risk of normalizing high stress scores?

terms.d: Positive stress linked to challenges a person welcomes, like a new job.

253.title: Mapping stress: body, mood, behavior
253.gist: The facilitator builds a chart sorting members' stress signs into physical, emotional, and behavioral symptoms, identifies which ones most often led to use, and pairs each symptom with a matching coping skill.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Matching coping to symptom type is efficient: breathing for physical tension, reappraisal or talk for emotional load, scheduling and routines for behavioral drift. One-size coping fails because stress shows up differently.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to circle their earliest stress symptom on the chart. The first sign, often sleep or irritability, is the best place to intervene.

ask: Which category of symptom are members least likely to notice in themselves?
How might behavioral symptoms like isolating be mistaken for calm?

254.title: Healthy stress relief and mood surfing
254.gist: Members brainstorm healthy stress reducers such as exercise, journaling, meditation, leisure, and support, and weigh how likely they are to use them. Urge surfing is extended to mood surfing: letting anxiety pass without using.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Regular exercise has solid evidence for reducing anxiety and depressive symptoms. Expressive writing studies by Pennebaker found benefits for health and mood, though effect sizes vary.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Mood surfing mirrors DBT's distress tolerance and the Buddhist idea of impermanence: feelings arise and pass. Telling yourself it is just a feeling is a form of defusion.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking how likely members are to actually exercise or journal is wise. Plans that ignore real barriers, like no gym or low literacy, are wishful thinking.

ask: How do you make stress reduction realistic for someone with no money, transport, or free time?
When would allowing anxiety to pass be the wrong advice?

255.title: Dealing with Anxiety and Stress steps
255.gist: The skill Dealing with Anxiety and Stress has three steps: decide if anxiety or stress is present and what is causing it, identify coping strategies, then pick the best one and do it. Volunteers read and label each step.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking why in step 1 separates worry about solvable problems from free-floating anxiety. Problem-focused coping suits the first, emotion-focused coping the second, in Lazarus and Folkman's terms.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some men do not use the word anxious and say stressed or on edge instead. Accept their words; the label matters less than catching the state.

ask: Why is this skill shorter than Dealing with Anger, and what does that suggest about anxiety?
How would you tell problem-solving from rumination when someone is 'working through' stress?

terms.d: Coping by changing the situation causing stress, as opposed to managing the feelings it causes.

256.title: Model: job stress, breath, and imagery
256.gist: The facilitator models a work-stress scene, choosing to work through it, then combining deep breathing with a vivid forest-stream visualization. Members then name specific situations, with a person, time, and place, for their own role plays.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have backup scenarios ready for members who draw a blank: a crowded parole office, a job interview where the record comes up, a first family dinner after release.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Combining a body strategy with an imagery strategy targets two channels at once. Stacking techniques is common in stress inoculation training.

ask: Why might the record coming up in an interview be the most important stress scenario for this group?
What makes a backup scenario good enough to engage someone who resists?

257.title: Stress spills into every area of life
257.gist: After feedback, the wrap-up notes that stress leads not only to use but to trouble in relationships and jobs that later raises risk. The next session previews rejection and failure, and practice work is assigned.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Stress proliferation, a sociological concept from Pearlin, describes how one stressor spawns others: a lost job brings debt, then family conflict. Reentry is a textbook case.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Draw one stressor in the middle of the board and have members map what it can cause. Seeing the spread motivates early coping.

ask: How does stress proliferation change where you would intervene first?
Which life area do you think most often carries stress back to substance use for your members?

terms.d: How one major stressor tends to generate further stressors in other areas of life.

258.title: Rejection, failure, and self-definition
258.gist: Session 24 background notes that early in a new lifestyle, rejection and setbacks around jobs and relationships can be devastating. The session teaches learning from failure, keeping perspective, and coping, since labeling oneself a failure predicts quitting.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Carol Dweck's growth versus fixed mindset work captures the self-definition point: seeing ability as changeable supports persistence. Note that mindset interventions have shown small and inconsistent effects in large replications.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Marlatt's abstinence violation effect describes how a lapse, read as proof of personal failure, can become a full relapse. Rejection can trigger the same all-or-nothing self-verdict.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Labeling theory in criminology (Becker, Lemert) argues that being labeled a criminal can push someone into that identity. Self-labeling as a failure works similarly from the inside.

ask: How does a criminal record turn ordinary rejection into a confirmation of a deeper story?
What separates useful learning from a failure from self-punishment?

terms.d: After a lapse, guilt and seeing oneself as a failure make full relapse more likely.

259.title: Session 24 materials and outline
259.gist: The outline covers check-in, review, the stressors activity, introducing and role-playing the rejection and failure skill, and assigning both the skill practice work and the Goal Readiness and Progress worksheet.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Pairing the rejection skill with goal tracking is deliberate: setbacks matter because they threaten goals. Keep the goal visible during role plays so members practice coping in its service.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The outline repeats the Daily Stressors activity from last session; it may be a carryover. Decide whether to rerun it or use the time for a fresh rejection inventory.

ask: Why connect emotional coping to goal progress rather than teaching it alone?
How would you adapt this session for someone who just received bad news, such as a denied parole?

260.title: Reviewing stress and anxiety practice
260.gist: After check-in, members review how managing stress and anxiety keeps them on track toward goals and the skill steps, then share where they practiced the skill and how each step went.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Tie review to goals as the manual does. Ask what goal the stress threatened; it keeps skills purposeful rather than abstract.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask the group to name one stressor they noticed earlier this week than last. Earlier detection is the real sign of progress.

ask: How do you measure progress in a skill that works invisibly?
What would you do if most members did not practice this week?

261.title: Four steps for setbacks
261.gist: The Rejection and Failure skill has four steps: decide whether you feel rejected or set back, consider ways to manage the feeling, pick a calming strategy and use it, and think about how to succeed next time.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step 4 adds forward planning that earlier emotion skills lacked. It moves from regulating the feeling to learning from the event, which is what turns failure into feedback.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Self-compassion research by Kristin Neff suggests treating one's own failures with kindness is linked with greater motivation to improve, not less. It counters the belief that harshness keeps you sharp.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Men may deny feeling rejected. Ask what happened in the body the last time a door closed on them, like a no from a job or a family member's unanswered call.

ask: Why might rejection be harder to admit than anger in this population?
Is step 4 safe to do while still upset, or should it wait?

terms.d: Treating oneself with kindness and understanding during failure, rather than harsh self-criticism.

262.title: Model: lectured for being late
262.gist: The facilitator models a boss lecturing him for lateness: feeling like a failure, noting the urge to use, choosing muscle relaxation and a call to his sister, then setting an earlier alarm to prevent repeat lateness.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The model accepts the criticism as partly fair and turns it into a plan. That shows the difference between shame (I am a failure) and guilt (I did something to fix), which Tangney's research links to more constructive behavior.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Calling a support person is an action step many members lack. Help them name an actual person and plan for when that person is unavailable.

ask: Why does the model include accepting fair criticism rather than only coping with feelings?
What if a member has no one to call?

terms.d: Shame targets the self (I am bad); guilt targets a behavior (I did bad) and more often motivates repair.

263.title: Rehearsing rejection role plays
263.gist: As with the anger skill, actors may rehearse privately, observers get assigned steps, the facilitator pauses when needed and ends at the final step, and actors point to their heads for thinking steps.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Rejection scenes can touch raw wounds, such as a partner leaving or a child refusing contact. Let members choose a smaller rejection for practice and save the big ones for individual sessions.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask the co-actor to deliver the rejection calmly and briefly. Harsh delivery turns the role play into a test of anger rather than of coping with loss.

ask: How do you judge whether a rejection scenario is too raw for group?
What does step 4 look like when the rejection is permanent?

264.title: Practice rejection skill and update goals
264.gist: Session 24 closes by assigning the Rejection and Failure practice sheet, with the top half filled in group, and an update on the Goal Readiness and Progress worksheet, setting a new short-term goal if one was met.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Setting a new goal right after one is met keeps momentum, consistent with Locke and Latham's goal-setting research: specific, challenging goals with feedback tend to improve performance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Celebrate small completed goals publicly. For people with long histories of failure, visible wins build the self-efficacy that buffers future rejection.

ask: How short should a short-term goal be for someone in a facility?
What do you do when a member's goal stalls because of things outside their control?

265.title: Steps to Emotion Regulation handout
265.gist: This sheet lays out the three regulation steps with a body map from head to feet for noticing physical reactions and body language, then lists coping-by-thinking and coping-by-doing tools members will use through the module.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A head-to-toe map turns vague distress into a body scan, which is easier for people who do not think in feeling words. It makes step one concrete and checkable.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking each member to mark the one body zone that alerts them first. Over the module, return to that zone; it becomes their personal early warning light.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Thought stopping is listed among tools, but suppression research suggests it can backfire alone. Teach it as a pause that leads straight into a replacement thought.

ask: Why split body cues into inside reactions and outside body language?
Which tools on this list carry the most risk of misuse, and how?

266.title: Feelings Chart vocabulary sheet
266.gist: A grid of feeling words grouped under happy, sad, angry, and other, from accomplished to withdrawn, gives members vocabulary beyond the basics and is used to circle feelings linked to their own substance use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Grouping words under four families helps people move from a broad category to a precise word. That two-step search mirrors how emotion wheels, such as Plutchik's, are used clinically.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which words members have never used about themselves. Words like supported or thankful can be surprisingly hard to claim, and that is worth noticing.

ask: Why do angry words outnumber calm words for many members, and what does that reveal?
What feelings are missing from this chart that matter in prison, like humiliated or numb?

267.title: Behavior Chain with positive feelings
267.gist: A blank Behavior Chain (situation, thoughts, feelings, behavior, consequences) sits beside a list of pleasant feeling words, prompting members to map how positive moods, not just painful ones, can lead to use.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Marlatt and Gordon's taxonomy of relapse situations included positive emotional states and celebrations, not only negative ones. Good moods can lower vigilance and invite reward-seeking.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief with a celebration example, like a birthday, a release date, or a first paycheck. Members often recognize that their worst runs started on good days.

ask: Why might positive-emotion relapse be harder to prepare for than negative-emotion relapse?
How does a positive feeling become a justification for using?

268.title: Identifying Your Emotions homework
268.gist: Members list at least three feelings tied to their substance use or illegal behavior and, for each, the physical reactions inside and the body language others could see. It builds the personal cue list used throughout the module.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking what others can see adds a social mirror: members learn how their emotions read from outside, which matters in settings where misread body language can escalate conflict.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief in pairs: one member shows the body language without words, the partner guesses the feeling. It makes the sheet active and tests whether signals are as clear as members think.

ask: What does it mean if a member's body language contradicts the feeling they named?
Why link feelings to illegal behavior rather than only to use?

269.title: Recognizing Your Feelings practice sheet
269.gist: A two-part practice form: in group, members write the skill name, steps, and when they will try it; afterward, they describe the situation, rate their performance, and note what they would change.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Planning before, reviewing after is a plan-do-review cycle. Writing when and how you will practice is an implementation intention, which raises the odds of actually doing it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief on the last question, what they would do differently. It shifts attention from success or failure to adjustment, which is how skills actually improve.

ask: What would make this form feel less like school for members with bad school memories?
How can you tell from the after section whether the skill was really tried?

270.title: Double Behavior Chain: cousin's party
270.gist: This Double Behavior Chain carries a filled-in example: a cousin's party invite, old thoughts about fun and getting high, a stop sign, new thoughts about probation and sobriety, a movie invite instead, and honest consequences including the cousin's possible distance.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The example keeps a painful cost on the list: the cousin may stop hanging out. Recovery often means losing people tied to the old life, and naming that keeps the plan honest.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking whether the new feelings, nervous and scared alongside focused, fit the new thoughts. Mixed feelings after a good decision are normal, not a sign of failure.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Social network research in recovery (for example, Longabaugh's work on network support) suggests changing who you spend time with is one of the strongest predictors of staying sober.

ask: How would you help someone grieve a relationship that recovery costs them?
Is offering the movies a real alternative, and what would make it more likely to be accepted?

271.title: Coping Strategies step sheet
271.gist: This handout gives step-by-step instructions for deep breathing, counting backwards from above 20 (by twos or threes for a challenge), pleasant imagery with all senses, and taking a break by leaving and redirecting.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Counting backwards by threes is effortful on purpose: it occupies working memory so rumination has less room. Making a task harder makes it a better distraction.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by having members rank the four tools for three settings: the unit, a family visit, and the street. Fit depends on context, and ranking makes that visible.

ask: Which of these tools could look suspicious to staff or peers if done openly?
Why does taking a break begin with deciding if the situation is risky?

272.title: Coping Strategies practice ratings
272.gist: Members practice at least two of the four coping-by-doing strategies, check whether they completed every step, and rate on 1-to-5 scales how useful each was and how likely they are to use it again.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Separating usefulness from likelihood of reuse is smart: a tool can work but feel awkward. The gap between the two numbers shows where barriers, not effectiveness, block use.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking about any strategy rated useful but unlikely. Problem-solve the barrier together, such as embarrassment, time, or setting.

ask: What would you do with a member who rates everything a 5?
How could ratings across the group guide which tools you emphasize?

273.title: Dealing with Urges handout
273.gist: This sheet lists urge surfing's four steps and grounding exercises: mental grounding (describe surroundings, recite your identity, name objects of one color, invent names for people), plus physical and soothing options for staying present.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Reciting your own name, age, and address is orientation, a simple way to reconnect with the present when dissociating. It is used in trauma care for the same reason.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which grounding exercise members could do unnoticed in a crowd. Inventing playful names for strangers can add humor, which itself loosens a craving's grip.

ask: Why might humor be an underrated grounding tool?
When could naming objects by color fail to work for someone?

terms.d: Awareness of who you are, where you are, and when it is; restoring it helps during dissociation.

274.title: Dealing with Urges practice ratings
274.gist: Members pick two high-risk situations likely to trigger urges, choose urge surfing or a grounding type for each, practice it, and rate usefulness and likelihood of reuse on 1-to-5 scales.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pairing each urge strategy with a named situation builds context-specific plans. Coping tends to transfer better when it is linked to the cue where it will be needed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking whether any member actually had an urge this week. If not, discuss imagined practice honestly; rehearsing without a real urge still builds the routine.

ask: How valid is a rating of a strategy practiced without a real urge?
Which high-risk situations do members list most, and what does that reveal about the group?

275.title: Using Self-Control practice sheet
275.gist: The standard skill practice form for Using Self-Control: steps and a planned practice time written in group, then the situation, a four-level self-rating, and what to change written after trying it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which coping strategy members picked in step 4 and why. The choice reveals whether they matched the tool to the situation or used a favorite by habit.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A four-level rating avoids a neutral midpoint, nudging members to commit to a judgment about their own performance.

ask: Is a self-rating useful when the stakes of looking good in group are high?
What follow-up question would reveal whether self-control held up later that day?

276.title: Managing Anger practice sheet
276.gist: The skill practice form for Managing Anger: members record the steps and when they expect to use them, then after practicing describe the situation, rate how well they followed the steps, and plan improvements.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking where members were on a 0-to-10 anger scale when they started the skill. Catching anger at 3 versus 8 shows whether early detection is improving.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Anger often flares around people members cannot avoid, like officers or family. Make sure debriefs include those, not only easy scenarios with strangers.

ask: How would you respond to a member who reports using the skill but still got a write-up?
Why might members avoid writing about anger at staff?

277.title: Daily Stressors checklist
277.gist: Members check stressors from the past month, from arguments with family and unstable housing to bill collectors, unsafe neighborhoods, job problems, and boredom, adding their own. The total shows how much load they carry.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cumulative stress matters more than any single item. Allostatic load, a concept from McEwen, describes the wear on the body from chronic stress, which links to health problems.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Many items reflect structural conditions like poverty and lack of resources, not personal failings. Naming that is a social justice point and helps reduce self-blame.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by sorting checked items into can change, can influence, and must accept. That echoes the Serenity Prayer, which many members already know from 12-step settings.

ask: How do you keep a stressor list from feeling hopeless?
Which items here are criminogenic needs in RNR terms, and which are not?

terms.d: Cumulative wear on the body from repeated or chronic stress.

278.title: Dealing with Anxiety and Stress practice
278.gist: The skill practice form for Managing Anxiety and Stress: steps and a planned practice in group, then a real situation, a self-rating, and what to change, completed after use.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking whether the stress came from a problem that could be solved or one that had to be tolerated. It shows whether members picked problem-focused or emotion-focused coping to match.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to note the time of day the stress hit. Patterns, like evenings or after phone calls, point to predictable triggers worth planning for.

ask: What does it mean if a member always reports stress from the same source?
How would you adapt this sheet for someone with severe anxiety symptoms?

279.title: Rejection and Failure practice sheet
279.gist: The skill practice form for Dealing with Rejection and Failure: members write the steps and when they will practice, then later describe the setback, rate how they did, and note what they would change.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief with focus on step 4: what did they learn for next time? Members who skip it may be coping with feelings but not growing from the event.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing about a failure gives some distance from it. Expressive writing research suggests that putting a hard event into a narrative can help people make sense of it.

ask: How do you debrief a rejection that is still fresh and painful?
What separates learning from a failure from finding someone to blame?

280.title: Goal readiness and progress tracker
280.gist: Members name a short-term goal, rate its importance and their confidence from 1 to 10, and list steps taken since last session. It tracks motivation and progress across the program.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Importance and confidence rulers come from motivational interviewing. Low importance calls for exploring values; low confidence calls for building self-efficacy and smaller steps.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking why a rating is not lower, for example why 6 and not 3. Members then explain their own reasons for change, which strengthens commitment.

ask: What would you do when importance is high but confidence stays low for weeks?
How might confidence ratings be inflated in a group setting?

terms.d: A 0-10 or 1-10 scale used in MI to rate importance of or confidence about change.

281.title: Skill cards: Recognizing Your Feelings
281.gist: Cut-out cards repeat the three thinking steps of Recognizing Your Feelings: tune in to the body, identify the connected situation, name the emotion. Members carry them as pocket reminders.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Portable cues support recall outside group. External aids reduce the memory load at the exact moment arousal makes remembering hard.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Suggest members keep the card where they will see it at risky times, like with their commissary list or by the phone schedule.

ask: Do pocket cards still get used after the first week, and how could you find out?
How else could the steps be cued in a facility where paper is limited?

282.title: Skill cards: Using Self-Control
282.gist: Pocket cards repeat the four steps of Using Self-Control: notice body cues, notice risky thoughts, list coping strategies, then choose the best one and do it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members write their top two coping strategies on the back of the card. A personalized card is more likely to be kept and used.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cards repeat the step wording exactly so that it becomes a script. Consistent wording across group, card, and homework strengthens memory.

ask: Is word-for-word recall of steps necessary, or is the gist enough?
How would you check whether a member could use the skill without the card?

283.title: Skill cards: Managing Anger
283.gist: Pocket cards repeat the four Managing Anger steps: identify the trigger, identify thoughts, feelings, and body cues, think about consequences, then pick and use a coping strategy.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members where they could glance at this card before a known flashpoint, like a call home or a meeting with a case manager.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: No one reads a card mid-rage. The card's value is in rehearsal before and review after; be honest with members about that.

ask: When is a skill card most useful in the anger cycle?
How might the consequences step differ for anger at a loved one versus a stranger?

284.title: Skill cards: Managing Anxiety and Stress
284.gist: Pocket cards repeat the three steps of Managing Anxiety and Stress: decide if anxiety or stress is present and what is causing it, identify coping strategies, and pick the best way and act on it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Encourage members to read the card on a calm day each morning. Daily rehearsal keeps steps available for stressful moments.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The 'and why' in step 1 is the key move: naming the source turns diffuse dread into a defined problem, which tends to reduce anxiety on its own.

ask: Why does naming the cause of stress often reduce it?
How would this card help someone with no identifiable cause for their anxiety?

285.title: Skill cards: Rejection and Failure
285.gist: Pocket cards repeat the four Rejection and Failure steps: notice the rejection or setback, consider ways to manage the feeling, pick one and act, and think about succeeding next time.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Suggest keeping this card with job application materials. Rejection in a job search is frequent, and the card reframes each no as data.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Thomas Edison is often credited with saying he found thousands of ways that did not work. Whether or not the quote is exact, the mindset behind step 4 is the same.

ask: How might repeated rejection during reentry wear down even good coping skills?
What support beyond a card does someone facing dozens of job rejections need?

286.title: Module 5 sessions at a glance
286.gist: The divider for Module 5, Social Skills, lists its eleven sessions from Introducing Social Skills and Active Listening through saying no, assertiveness, handling criticism, avoiding trouble, and celebrating a positive event. It moves the program from inner regulation to relationships.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The order roughly climbs from receptive skills (listening, empathy) to expressive ones (needs, assertiveness) and then to lifestyle (positive activities, celebrating). Receiving well comes before asserting well.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Placing celebration last is shrewd: positive events are a known relapse risk, so ending the module there prepares members for good days, not just bad ones.

ask: Why might listening be taught before saying no?
Which of these eleven skills do you expect your members to need most after release?

287.title: Choosing Behavior Responses: module aims
287.gist: The module description frames social skills training as a structured, evidence-based technique: learn communication skills, practice them in role play, then apply them in real life, moving from basic to advanced skills. Goals include empathy, conflict management, and avoiding trouble.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Lipsey, Landenberger, and Wilson's meta-analysis of cognitive-behavioral programs for offenders found meaningful average reductions in recidivism, with stronger effects for well-implemented programs. Implementation quality matters as much as the curriculum.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Many poor outcomes in reentry stem from skill deficits, not only from attitudes. Teaching skills fills a gap that lecturing about choices cannot.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Skills practiced in a facility may not generalize to neighborhoods with different norms. Booster sessions and community practice are often recommended but not always available.

ask: How would you tell whether a member's problem is a skill deficit or an attitude problem?
What makes a CBI program 'well-implemented' in practice?

terms.d: Structured teaching of interpersonal skills through modeling, role play, feedback, and real-world practice.

288.title: Module 5 worksheet list
288.gist: This page lists the worksheets and skill cards for each Module 5 session, from High Risk Areas and the Behavior Chain to cards for each skill and a final Goal Readiness tracker. It is a prep checklist for facilitators.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Before the module starts, sort the cards into labeled envelopes by session. It saves group time and avoids handing out the wrong card mid-role play.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Session 30 pairs Disclosing Key Information with Seeking Support, hinting at how to discuss a record or recovery status with employers and family, a central reentry challenge.

ask: Which worksheet here would you most want to adapt to Miami reentry realities?
Why might disclosing key information sit beside seeking support?

289.title: Session 25: skill deficit or thinking?
289.gist: Session 25 background asks members to identify risky situations across peers, work, family, and leisure, challenging the belief in a simple fix. Facilitators judge whether a lapse came from antisocial thinking, needing restructuring, or a skill deficit, needing practice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This distinction is a core assessment move: thinking problems call for cognitive restructuring, while knowing the right thing but failing under pressure calls for behavioral rehearsal. Matching method to cause is the responsivity principle in RNR.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members: did you want to say no and couldn't, or did you not want to say no? Their honest answer tells you which tool to use.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Real cases are usually mixed; peers' persistence also feeds risky thinking. Treat the split as a working hypothesis, not a diagnosis.

ask: What clues in a member's story signal a skill deficit rather than antisocial attitudes?
Why would believing in a simple fix be risky in recovery?

terms.d: RNR idea that treatment should match a person's learning style, abilities, and needs.

290.title: Session 25 materials and outline
290.gist: The outline covers check-in, review, generating risky situations linked to the module's skills with the Top 5 High Risk Situations worksheet, completing at least one Behavior Chain, and assigning another chain as practice work.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Limiting members to their top five risks forces prioritization. Ask what made number one beat number two; the reasoning shows insight.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Mapping risk before teaching skills gives each skill a target. People learn faster when they already know where they will use a tool.

ask: How might a member's top five change between now and release?
What risks do members tend to leave off their lists?

291.title: Opening Module 5 with check-in
291.gist: Session 25 starts with check-in, a quick review of how rejection and failure tie to substance use, and verification that everyone completed practice work, with points recorded where used. It then bridges from Module 4.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Recording points for completed homework is a token reinforcement system. Reinforcing completion consistently is more effective than occasional punishment for missing it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Points can shift motivation from learning to scorekeeping. Pair them with genuine interest in what members wrote so the practice feels valued, not just counted.

ask: Does recording points help or hurt intrinsic motivation in your group?
How would you handle a member who does homework only for points?

292.title: One fix is never enough
292.gist: Through Carlos, who thought a job was all he needed, the group sees that many risk areas operate at once. Members then list social situations that pressure them to use, including celebrations like a birthday, promotion, new baby, or finishing supervision.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Andrews and Bonta's Central Eight risk factors include antisocial associates, attitudes, family, work, and leisure. Addressing one, like employment, rarely changes outcomes if others stay untouched.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Employment programs alone have shown mixed effects on recidivism in research reviews. Jobs seem to help most when combined with other changes in peers, thinking, and support.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what members plan to do on the day supervision ends. That milestone is often celebrated with use, so a plan for it is valuable.

ask: Why is it tempting for clients and systems alike to believe in single fixes like a job?
How would you plan for a celebration that is worth celebrating?

terms.d: Andrews and Bonta's eight major risk factors for criminal behavior, such as antisocial attitudes, peers, and substance abuse.

293.title: Small changes, chained and countered
293.gist: Members pick their riskiest situation, check that it is a situation rather than an antisocial act, complete a Behavior Chain, share it, then pair up to write counter thoughts for each risky thought. Practice work extends the chain.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Separating situation from action is essential: if the situation is already the crime, there is no choice point to rehearse. The chain teaches that risk appears before the behavior.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Peer pairing for counter thoughts uses peers as coaches. Counter thoughts from a peer often sound more credible than from staff, which boosts acceptance.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The emphasis on many small changes echoes kaizen, the Japanese idea of continuous small improvement, and habit research showing small changes can be easier to sustain.

ask: Why might peers produce better counter thoughts than facilitators?
How do small changes add up in a life with very large risks?

294.title: Active listening as a foundation
294.gist: Session 26 background explains that listening is a core part of healthy communication, helping members build prosocial relationships and participate productively in treatment itself. Facilitators prepare to define, model, and role-play Active Listening.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Carl Rogers placed empathic listening at the heart of the helping relationship. Teaching members to listen gives them the same tool counselors use to build trust.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Point out that the skill improves the group itself: when members listen to each other, feedback becomes meaningful and peer support grows.

ask: Why might listening be undertrained in environments where people must be guarded?
How could improved listening change relationships with officers or POs?

295.title: Reviewing risk areas
295.gist: After check-in, members review why tracking high-risk areas matters and how social skills serve their goals, then share their practice Behavior Chains. Practice is framed as the engine of success in hard moments.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to name which social skill would have changed the outcome in their homework chain. It previews the module and links each skill to a real risk.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members listen to a partner's chain and summarize it before giving feedback. It quietly previews today's active listening skill.

ask: How could you use the review to show members their own progress since Module 1?
What signals that a member is copying the same chain each week?

296.title: Why listening matters; three steps
296.gist: Members discuss times poor listening caused problems and how listening affects relationships, then learn three Active Listening steps: look at the speaker, focus on what they say, and check in to confirm you understood.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Eye contact norms vary across cultures and settings; in some cultures and in prison, direct eye contact can signal challenge or disrespect. Offer looking toward the speaker or nodding as alternatives.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step 3, checking in, is paraphrasing. It catches misunderstandings early, before they turn into conflict, which ties listening directly to avoiding trouble.

ask: How would you adapt step 1 for someone for whom eye contact feels threatening?
What gets in the way of focusing on what someone says during conflict?

297.title: Walking through listening steps
297.gist: Volunteers discuss each Active Listening step, why it matters, and whether it is thinking or action, before the facilitator models the skill with assigned observers.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The script's Step 2 prompt repeats wording from Recognizing Your Feelings (identifying the connected situation) rather than the listening step of focusing on what is said. Read Step 2 from the skill card instead.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what could go wrong if you skip step 3: you act on what you thought you heard. Many fights start that way, which makes the step's value obvious.

ask: Why is focusing a thinking step rather than an action?
How could you show that someone is listening without speaking?

298.title: Model: listening to the PO
298.gist: The facilitator models a meeting where the PO stresses getting a job: eye contact and nodding, an inner summary of the PO's concern, then a paraphrase and a request for a job placement referral.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The model ends with a question that turns listening into action. Paraphrasing plus asking for help shows the PO engagement, which can build a cooperative supervision relationship.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on supervision suggests that a firm but fair, supportive relationship between officer and client is linked with better compliance and outcomes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members see the PO only as an adversary. Ask what they want the PO to believe about them, and how listening helps them get it.

ask: Is active listening with a PO genuine or strategic, and does it matter?
How does a member's view of authority shape their listening?

299.title: Active listening role plays and feedback
299.gist: Observers watch assigned steps, actors point to their heads for thinking steps, and the full four-part feedback protocol follows each role play, repeating until all members have practiced.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: In role plays, have the co-actor share something mildly personal. Listening is easiest to fake with neutral content and hardest with emotional content.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the co-actor whether they felt heard. Their answer is the real test of active listening, more than whether steps were ticked off.

ask: How can you tell genuine listening from performed listening?
Why does the co-actor's experience matter most for this skill?

300.title: Understanding others' feelings and trust
300.gist: Session 27 background explains that relating to others' feelings helps prevent conflicts that once led to use, and helps members see how their use affected family. Rebuilding trust with loved ones, who can support and hold them accountable, is central.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Empathy has cognitive (understanding another's view) and affective (sharing their feeling) parts. Programs mostly train cognitive empathy, which is more teachable and still useful in reducing conflict.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Family involvement in treatment, such as through community reinforcement and family training (CRAFT) or family therapy, has research support for improving engagement and outcomes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Facing harm to family can trigger shame. Pair awareness with a path to repair so the session builds hope instead of guilt alone.

ask: How do you build empathy for family without turning it into a shame session?
Why might cognitive empathy be easier to teach than affective empathy?

terms.d: Understanding what someone else is thinking or feeling, without necessarily sharing the feeling.

301.title: Session 27 materials and running order
301.gist: This page lists the supplies and the seven-part sequence for the empathy skill session: check-in, teach, model, rehearse, feedback, homework. The fixed order is the program's structured skill-training backbone, so members always know what comes next.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The teach, model, rehearse, feedback, assign loop comes from structured learning in the Goldstein tradition, built on Bandura's social learning theory: people pick up behavior by watching a credible model, trying it, and getting reinforced.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prep a model scene before group where you misread someone's emotion at first and then correct it. Showing the correction makes the empathy skill feel learnable rather than a talent some people simply have.

ask: Which part of this seven-step format would you cut first if you only had 40 minutes, and what would that cost?
Why might a predictable session structure matter more in a correctional setting than in outpatient therapy?

302.title: Opening the empathy session
302.gist: Check-in, a quick review of active listening, and a homework check lead into the new skill. The facilitator invites members to recall how their use hurt the people closest to them, which gives the empathy skill a personal reason to exist.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Empathy here is treated as a learnable skill, not a trait. Psychologists separate cognitive empathy (reading what another person feels) from affective empathy (feeling with them); this session mostly trains the cognitive side, which can be practiced step by step.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The prompt about hurting loved ones can trigger shame and shutdown. Normalize it quickly: the point is not to relive guilt but to notice that substance use blinds us to signals we would otherwise catch.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Adam Smith wrote of imagining ourselves in another's situation as the root of moral feeling, long before psychology existed. The session is a practical version of that old idea of perspective taking.

ask: Is guilt about past harm a useful fuel for change, or does it tip into shame that blocks learning? Where is the line?
Can someone with strong antisocial attitudes learn cognitive empathy and use it to manipulate better? How would you guard against that?

terms.d: Accurately recognizing what another person is thinking or feeling, without necessarily sharing the emotion.

303.title: Five steps for reading others' feelings
303.gist: The five skill steps are introduced: observe words and body language, name the likely emotion, stay calm and open, check your guess, then ask an open question. The example of a spouse angry about unemployment shows that surface anger often hides a different worry.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step 3 is the hinge. Under threat, people default to defending themselves; pausing to stay open-minded interrupts the automatic hostile reading that cognitive models of aggression describe.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on hostile attribution bias, associated with Kenneth Dodge's social information processing work, finds that aggressive people more often read ambiguous cues as hostile. A deliberate labeling step is one way to slow that misreading.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Show the group a neutral face photo and ask each member to name the emotion. The spread of answers proves why Step 4, checking your guess, is not optional.

ask: Body language reading varies by culture. How reliable are facial and posture cues across the cultures in your groups?
When anger masks fear or overwhelm, what does that suggest about how members interpret staff anger toward them?

terms.d: A tendency to interpret other people's ambiguous actions as deliberately hostile.

304.title: Checking the guess, then modeling it
304.gist: Steps 4 and 5 are explained: confirm the emotion you think you see and ask an open-ended question. The facilitator then models the skill with a brother angry about family stress, while observers each track one step.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Confirming the emotion is a reflection, a core motivational interviewing move (Miller & Rollnick). A tentative reflection lets the other person correct you, which lowers defensiveness on both sides.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Pointing to your head during thinking steps makes invisible cognition visible. Insist on it; it is how members learn that skilled behavior begins with an internal decision.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A scripted line like checking whether someone feels pressured can sound robotic outside the room. Encourage members to translate it into their own street or family language.

ask: Why is a reflection framed as a guess often more powerful than a correct statement delivered with certainty?
What is lost when a sibling's anger is answered only with empathy and no accountability for what caused it?

305.title: From model to member role plays
305.gist: The model ends with an offer of help, then each member names a real situation, ideally tied to their own risk for use, to rehearse. The page covers recruiting a first volunteer and letting them pick a realistic co-actor.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Behavioral rehearsal is one of the more consistently supported ingredients in skills training. Practice with personally relevant scenarios tends to transfer better than generic scripts, since the cues match real life.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: In a prison unit, volunteering first can feel like losing face. Frame going first as a status move, or quietly pre-arrange a respected member to break the ice.

ask: What makes a role play realistic enough to transfer but safe enough that nobody escalates?
How would you adapt this skill for a member whose main risky relationship is a parole officer rather than family?

306.title: Feedback round and empathy wrap-up
306.gist: A four-part feedback protocol follows each role play: co-actor first, then observers, then the actor, then praise. The session closes by linking empathy to fewer miscommunications and to finding the real issue, and assigns practice work.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking the co-actor first centers the receiver's experience, which is exactly the skill being taught. Ending on positive reinforcement follows operant principles: reward approximations, not only perfection.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Neuroscience on mentalizing points to networks such as the temporoparietal junction and medial prefrontal cortex. Heavy substance use is linked to weaker social cognition in some studies, a reason practice may need repetition.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to rate, 1 to 10, how likely they are to use the skill this week, then ask why not a lower number. It borrows an MI scaling move to surface their own reasons.

ask: Does praise from a facilitator mean the same thing to members who distrust authority? What reinforcer might work better?
How would you know, outside group, whether empathy skills actually changed behavior on the unit?

307.title: Session 28 overview: refusal skills
307.gist: The background frames refusal as knowing when and how to decline a risky situation, practiced across many scenarios so it generalizes. Materials and a six-part plan follow.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Refusal training is a classic element of relapse prevention (Marlatt & Gordon). Social pressure is among the high-risk situations commonly tied to lapses, so a ready refusal is a coping response prepared in advance.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: School programs that relied mainly on just-say-no messaging showed weak results. Refusal works better when paired with skill practice, identity, and real alternatives, which this session tries to include.

ask: Why do refusal skills need to be practiced in many different situations to generalize?
What makes an adult refusal program different from the school campaigns that disappointed?

308.title: Finding the moments to say no
308.gist: After the empathy review and homework check, members look back at episodes where use spun out of control and locate the points where a no was possible. It reframes relapse as a chain of small yeses.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt described apparently irrelevant decisions: small choices that seem harmless but walk a person toward a high-risk situation. This review helps members see the earlier, easier exits.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Draw a timeline on the board for one volunteer's story and mark each fork. Members usually find the cheapest no came hours before the drink or hit.

ask: At which point in a relapse chain is refusal easiest, and why do people usually wait until the hardest point?
How does seeing a lapse as a chain change the shame someone feels about it?

terms.d: Small, seemingly harmless choices that gradually set up a high-risk situation for relapse.

309.title: Four steps to a good refusal
309.gist: Steps are introduced: judge whether the situation is risky, brainstorm several ways to decline, pick and deliver the best one, and offer a safer alternative. Having more than one option prepared is stressed.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Generating several options before choosing mirrors problem-solving therapy (D'Zurilla and colleagues): brainstorming first, judging second, so stress does not lock you into the first idea.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members which refusals have actually worked on the street. Their own lines carry more credibility than anything the facilitator suggests.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Step 4 keeps the relationship while refusing the behavior. That separation of person from act echoes nonviolent communication and many ethical traditions.

ask: When is offering an alternative a mistake, for example with people who should be cut off entirely?
Why is Step 3 labeled both thinking and action?

310.title: Modeling a refusal at a party
310.gist: The facilitator models the skill with a work holiday party that has an open bar, weighing options aloud and choosing to explain honestly while offering a sober hangout. Members then name their own real situations.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The model assumes a workplace party, which may feel distant for many reentry members. A swap such as a cousin's cookout, or a friend offering a ride with something in the car, often lands better.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note that the model discloses not drinking. Ask the group whether disclosure is always wise; for some people a short no without explanation is safer and fully legitimate.

ask: Is honesty about recovery a strength or a risk in a reentry social circle? What decides it?
How does avoiding a situation entirely differ from refusing inside it, in terms of skill and risk?

311.title: Running the refusal role plays
311.gist: Practical guidance for role plays: a volunteer picks a co-actor, can rehearse first, observers get assigned steps, and the facilitator pauses scenes that drift. The aim is lots of repetition of the steps.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For refusal, coach the co-actor to push realistically, two or three times, then stop. Pressure that is too soft gives false confidence; pressure that is too hard turns practice into a fight.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-efficacy, Bandura's term for confidence in performing a specific behavior, grows most from mastery experiences. A successful refusal under mild pressure builds belief that a real one is possible.

ask: How hard should a co-actor push before practice stops being helpful?
What signals tell you a role play has become emotionally real in a risky way?

terms.d: Confidence that you can carry out a specific behavior in a specific situation.

312.title: Closing: a plan for saying no
312.gist: The wrap-up ties refusal to planning for high-risk situations and drawing limits with family and friends. Homework sends members to try it for real.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Implementation intentions, studied by Peter Gollwitzer, are if-then plans. Research generally finds that deciding in advance what you will do when a cue appears improves follow-through.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have each member write one if-then sentence for their riskiest person, such as if he offers, then I say my line and leave. Read a few aloud.

ask: Why might boundaries with family be harder than refusals with peers?
How would you check whether homework refusals happened or were invented to earn points?

313.title: Session 29 overview: stating needs
313.gist: The background positions this skill as the next step after starting conversations and listening: asking for what you need in a calm, non-combative way. Materials and a seven-part plan follow.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Assertiveness sits between passive silence and aggression. Assertiveness training, popularized in early behavior therapy by Joseph Wolpe and others, treats it as a learnable habit.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Norms on directness vary by culture and by setting. In a prison, open requests can signal weakness; members may need to judge where assertion is safe.

ask: Is unmet need a common trigger for use in your groups? How would you test that idea?
Where would assertiveness actually be dangerous for a member, and how should the skill account for it?

314.title: Opening the communicating-needs session
314.gist: Check-in, a review of the refusal skill, and homework sharing open the session. Discussion begins by recalling the communication skills built over recent sessions.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Use the homework review to spot who never practices. A brief, curious question about what got in the way usually gets further than reminders about points.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Each skill builds on the last, a scaffolding approach. Listening and reading feelings come before asserting needs because a request lands better when you have first understood the other person.

ask: Why might the program teach listening before asserting, rather than the reverse?
What does a member's homework pattern tell you about readiness, beyond compliance?

315.title: A formula for asking calmly
315.gist: The page names two failure modes, bottling things up or confronting while agitated, and offers five steps: calm timing, ask permission, describe facts then feelings, make a request the other can decline, and say thanks.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The facts-then-feelings-then-request order closely resembles Marshall Rosenberg's nonviolent communication and the DEAR MAN skill in Linehan's DBT.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Choosing a calm moment respects how emotional arousal narrows thinking. Many models of emotion regulation, including Gross's, show timing and situation selection are strategies in themselves.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rewrite a demand they once made into a request the other person could refuse. Notice how the sentence shrinks the threat.

ask: Why is permitting a no essential to a request being a request rather than a demand?
Is bottling up feelings always worse than venting badly? What does it depend on?

terms.d: A DBT skill for asking: Describe, Express, Assert, Reinforce, stay Mindful, Appear confident, Negotiate.

316.title: Objectivity, disappointment, and the model
316.gist: Steps 3 to 5 are unpacked: describe events objectively, accept a possible decline calmly, and thank the person. Strict guidance for modeling follows, including restarting the demo after any error.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Objective description separates observation from evaluation. Saying what happened rather than what the person is like reduces the blame that triggers defensiveness.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The rule never to let a member perform the model protects a clean demonstration. Restarting after a mistake also models accountability without collapse.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Read three statements, such as you always ignore me, and have members turn each into an observable fact.

ask: How objective can anyone be about a conflict they are part of?
Why might staying calm after a no be the hardest step for your members?

317.title: Modeling a request to a partner
317.gist: The model shows a person reopening yesterday's argument with a partner: asking for time, describing the fight, sharing sadness, requesting a fun outing, and thanking them. Members then choose real situations for their role plays.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: John Gottman's research on couples emphasizes gentle start-ups: how a hard conversation opens strongly predicts how it goes. The model is essentially a gentle start-up.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The scene is warm and low stakes. Push members toward harder cases, like asking a parole officer or a mother who has stopped trusting them.

ask: What changes when the person you need something from has power over you?
Is naming sadness easier or harder than naming anger for most men in your groups, and why?

318.title: Rehearsal and feedback for needs
318.gist: The rehearsal option, observer step assignments, and the five-part feedback protocol are repeated, with practice work given at the end. Every member should perform before the skill is considered covered.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Repetition of the protocol can feel monotonous. Vary who leads feedback, or let a member who has mastered the protocol run one round under your watch.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on skill acquisition broadly finds that spaced, repeated practice with feedback beats a single demonstration. The repetitive format is a feature, though it risks boredom.

ask: How could you keep the feedback routine fresh without losing fidelity to the model?
What does a co-actor's report of how it felt add that observers cannot?

319.title: Session 30 background: support networks
