319.gist: This background frames building a support network, linked to the list of supporters from Module 3. Engaging supporters may require fuller disclosure: offense history, relapse signs, triggers, antisocial thinking, and the success plan.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Prosocial support is linked to better reentry and recovery outcomes in much research, though the quality of the relationship matters more than the number of people.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: In the RNR model (Andrews & Bonta), antisocial associates are a central criminogenic need. Building prosocial ties is the flip side of reducing contact with antisocial peers.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Asking for full disclosure of offense history carries real risk of stigma or rejection. Members need help deciding how much to share with each person.

ask: How much disclosure is too much, and who should decide?
What happens to a support network when the most supportive person is also connected to the old lifestyle?

terms.d: A changeable risk factor linked to reoffending, such as antisocial peers or attitudes, targeted in treatment.

320.title: Session 30 materials and plan
320.gist: Supplies and a six-part plan for the support session: check-in, define the skill, model, role play, the disclosing worksheet, and support-seeking homework.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Worksheet 7 on disclosure is the most sensitive item in this session. Read it ahead and decide what you will do if a member discloses something reportable.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Erving Goffman's work on stigma described how people manage information about a discrediting mark. Deciding whom to tell is a skill the session makes explicit.

ask: What ethical limits apply when members disclose offense history in group?
Why put disclosure in a worksheet rather than leaving it to discussion?

321.title: Opening the support session
321.gist: Check-in and a review of communicating needs lead into the session's purpose: turning the supporters identified earlier into a working network. Members are invited to voice what makes asking for help hard.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Help-seeking reluctance is common, especially among men raised to value self-reliance. Naming the barriers first lets the group treat them as solvable rather than as character flaws.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to finish the sentence asking for help feels like... Collect the words on the board and look for patterns.

ask: How do masculinity norms in your population shape help-seeking?
Is the fear of being a burden based in reality for people who have burned bridges?

322.title: Barriers, then steps for seeking support
322.gist: Common fears such as being judged, doubting anyone can help, or past exploitation of others are validated. Five steps follow: notice what bothers you, choose a guide, share thoughts and intentions, listen openly, and plan together.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The fear of having used people before deserves direct respect. Reframe it: asking honestly is different from manipulating, and the difference shows over time.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Attachment theory suggests people with insecure histories may expect rejection when they reach out. Small, successful asks can slowly revise those expectations.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step 4 asks members to listen with an open mind, which guards against seeking support only to hear agreement.

ask: How can a member tell the difference between seeking support and seeking permission?
What would make a supporter trustworthy after someone has exploited past relationships?

323.title: Noticing distress and choosing a helper
323.gist: The facilitator walks through the first three support steps, asking how members know something is wrong, what blocks choosing a helper, and why sharing thoughts and intentions matters. It trains members to detect their own distress before it becomes action.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step 1 is interoception and self-monitoring: recognizing internal warning signs. In relapse prevention, early detection of emotional states gives more time to cope before a lapse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask about times they kept something to themselves. Many will describe isolation before past relapses or offenses, which becomes evidence for the skill.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sharing intentions, not just feelings, gives the helper a chance to intervene before a bad plan becomes a deed, a little like a pilot reading the flight plan aloud to the co-pilot.

ask: Why might disclosing an intended action feel riskier than disclosing a feeling?
What internal signals do your members most often miss before they act?

324.title: Taking advice without arguing
324.gist: Steps 4 and 5 address a familiar trap: asking for help, then rejecting or debating it. The last step pushes from complaining to a solution-focused plan, before the facilitator sets up the model.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The yes-but pattern is a classic sign of ambivalence. In MI terms, someone may seek help while sustain talk still dominates; arguing back usually strengthens the resistance.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Solution-focused brief therapy (de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg) shifts attention from problem talk to what would be different. Step 5 borrows that spirit.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Pair members. One asks for advice; the partner answers; the asker may only reply with a question or thanks. Debrief how hard it was not to argue.

ask: When is rejecting advice actually the healthy choice?
How do you, as a counselor, notice yes-but in yourself during supervision?

terms.d: Asking for help, then dismissing each suggestion; often a sign of mixed feelings about change.

325.title: Modeling support: a father and son
325.gist: The model shows a parent after treatment whose teenage son avoids him. He calls his brother, shares worry and a plan to force a fishing trip, hears the brother advise patience, and asks for options that respect the son's pace.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This model hits a nerve for many incarcerated parents. Expect emotion, and leave space; it often opens honest talk about repairing family ties after prison.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The model shows how a plan born of guilt, forcing contact, can backfire. A trusted helper offers an outside view that corrects a distorted urgency to fix things fast.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Family contact during and after incarceration is associated with better reentry outcomes in a range of studies, although the direction of cause is hard to prove.

ask: How might the father's need to make up for lost time be about his own guilt rather than his son's needs?
Who in a member's life can give honest feedback without being part of the old lifestyle?

326.title: Casting and staging support role plays
326.gist: Setup guidance repeats with an added tip: choose a co-actor who resembles or can convincingly play the real person. Optional private rehearsal and assigned observer steps keep the role play focused.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Stimulus similarity aids transfer: the more practice resembles the real situation, the more likely the learned behavior shows up there. Casting a realistic co-actor is a cheap way to boost that.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Watch for co-actors who play a family member too cruelly or too kindly. Coach them briefly to play it the way the person actually talks.

ask: What risks come with asking a peer to play someone's mother or child?
How would you judge whether a scene is realistic enough?

327.title: What to tell your supporters
327.gist: Once a supporter agrees, members use the Disclosing Key Information worksheet to note what that person needs to know. Extra ideas include sharing a values card, a letter to self on relapse costs, a photo collage, and a list of harms caused.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The letter and collage work like a Ulysses contract: you leave reminders with someone else for a future moment when your own judgment may be weaker.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Behavioral economists call this a commitment device, a choice made now to bind your future self. Odysseus tying himself to the mast is the classic image.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which item each person would actually hand over. The gap between what is useful and what feels safe to share is the real conversation.

ask: Can reminders of past harm backfire by triggering shame instead of resolve?
What should a supporter do with the letter if the person relapses anyway?

terms.d: An arrangement made now that makes it harder for your future self to act against your goals.

328.title: Support takeaways and homework
328.gist: Closing points: not everyone will agree to help, permission should always be asked, and a prosocial life depends partly on support. Homework is to actually invite someone or rehearse with a peer or staff member.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prepare members for refusals. A no from a family member can feel like proof they are beyond help; frame it as information about that person's capacity, not a verdict.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Inside a facility, members may have few chances to contact supporters. Rehearsing with staff is a reasonable fallback but does not test the real relationship.

ask: How would you help a member who has no one willing to join their network?
Is a paid professional a legitimate part of a support network, or a different category?

329.title: Session 31 overview: assertive communication
329.gist: The background defines assertiveness as confident, non-aggressive expression of thoughts and feelings, useful in conflict and when setting limits. The core format is a when you do this, I feel or think that statement.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: I-statements, popularized by Thomas Gordon, shift attention from accusation to one's own experience. They make it harder for the other person to argue, since you are reporting your reaction.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A formula can sound stiff or therapeutic. In tough settings, members may be mocked for using it; teach the principle so they can phrase it naturally.

ask: What separates assertion from aggression when the other person sees any challenge as disrespect?
Why does the program tie assertiveness to staying out of risky situations?

terms.d: A sentence that describes your own feeling or thought about a behavior instead of blaming the other person.

330.title: Opening the assertiveness session
330.gist: Check-in, a review of the support skill, and homework sharing lead into a question about times members felt taken advantage of. It anchors assertiveness in a remembered feeling.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Being taken advantage of can call up stories of victimization, including abuse. Be ready to contain disclosures and follow up privately if needed.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Many people swing between passivity and explosion: they stay silent until resentment builds, then lash out. Assertiveness breaks that cycle by speaking earlier.

ask: How often does a member's aggression begin as unexpressed resentment?
What is the difference between feeling disrespected and being disrespected?

331.title: Four steps to speak up assertively
331.gist: Members reflect on times their feelings were ignored and whether substance use shaped how they spoke up. Steps follow: see why conflict could arise, set your goal, brainstorm what to say, then choose and speak.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step 2, naming the ultimate goal, is the key. Under insult, people often switch from what they want to winning the moment; an explicit goal keeps the long game in view.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The pointer suggests a behavior chain. Build one with the group showing the aggressive path and the assertive path from the same trigger.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Stoic thinkers such as Epictetus urged separating what is up to us from what is not. Assertiveness focuses on your own words, not on controlling the other person.

ask: Why might intoxication make people both more passive and more aggressive, sometimes in the same night?
How do you decide if your goal is respect, safety, or the relationship when they conflict?

332.title: Modeling: weed in my car
332.gist: The model shows a person whose friend brings marijuana into his car despite knowing he is on probation and staying clean. He names his frustration and the legal risk, sets a goal of staying clean without a fight, and speaks up.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This scenario is real for many on supervision. Ask what members would actually say; some will insist on ejecting the friend, which opens a useful talk about boundaries versus relationships.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The model ties a feeling, disrespect, to a concrete consequence, a probation violation. Linking emotions to stakes makes assertion feel like self-protection, not weakness.

ask: Is assertiveness enough here, or should the person simply end the ride?
How does the risk of a violation change what counts as an overreaction?

333.title: Assertiveness role plays in practice
333.gist: Members pick situations where speaking up would have defused risky emotions linked to illegal behavior, choose co-actors, and briefly describe the scene. The stated aim is reducing antisocial behavior.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have each main actor say the goal aloud before starting. Observers can then judge whether the words served that goal rather than just the formula.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Social skills training is a common part of cognitive-behavioral programs for justice-involved people. Effects on reoffending appear stronger when skills target criminogenic needs, consistent with the RNR model.

ask: How might you tell whether an assertive role play was respectful or just aggression in calm clothing?
What makes the program's goal of fewer antisocial behaviors different from simply better communication?

334.title: Assertiveness wrap-up and practice
334.gist: The close links assertiveness to planning for high-risk situations and drawing limits with family and friends. Members get practice work and may rate how likely they are to use it.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member for one relationship where they are usually too quiet and one where they are usually too loud. The pattern often reveals who holds power over them.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The close repeats the same takeaways as the refusal session. You might add a distinct point, such as how assertiveness prevents resentment from building.

ask: Can assertiveness be learned without first feeling worthy of having needs?
How would you measure whether assertive communication reduced conflict on the unit?

335.title: Session 32 background: handling criticism
335.gist: This background explains why criticism is hard: people want approval, criticism often arrives harshly, and defensiveness can turn into aggression or use. The skill teaches staying calm, sorting constructive from demeaning criticism, keeping the useful part, and dropping the rest.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: In Beck's cognitive model, criticism can activate core beliefs like I am worthless. The reaction is often to that belief, not to the comment itself.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Psychologists studying shame, such as June Tangney, distinguish shame (I am bad) from guilt (I did something bad). Guilt tends to motivate repair; shame often drives anger and hiding.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Members get criticism from staff, courts, and officers who may be harsh or unfair. Labeling something derogatory still leaves a power imbalance the skill cannot fix.

ask: How do you separate a criticism's tone from its content when the tone is contemptuous?
Why might people in recovery be especially sensitive to criticism?

terms.d: Shame targets the whole self as bad; guilt targets a specific act. Guilt is more often linked to making amends.

336.title: Session 32 materials and plan
336.gist: Supplies and the six-part plan for the criticism session, including skill cards and the Responding to Criticism practice worksheet.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Plan a model where you are criticized for something partly true. It shows that the skill is not about proving the critic wrong.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Before the session, recall a time you took supervisory feedback badly. Use that memory to keep your model honest.

ask: What kind of criticism do you, as a facilitator, find hardest to take?
Should the model include unfair criticism, fair criticism, or both?

337.title: Opening the criticism session
337.gist: Check-in, a review of assertiveness, and homework sharing open the session. The facilitator frames criticism as something to handle in a way that keeps members on track with their goals.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The homework review is itself a feedback moment. Notice how members react when you point out an incomplete assignment; it is live data for today's skill.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Placing criticism right after assertiveness is deliberate: one teaches giving hard messages, the other receiving them. Together they cover both directions of conflict.

ask: How could you use your own correction of a member during review as a teachable moment without humiliating them?
Why do giving and receiving criticism tend to rely on the same underlying calm?

338.title: Praise versus put-down: noticing reactions
338.gist: Members compare their instant thoughts, feelings, and belief in two opposite comments from a neutral person after helping with a task. The contrast leads into staying calm, listening objectively, and sorting constructive from demeaning criticism.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on negativity bias, reviewed by Baumeister and colleagues, suggests that bad events and feedback generally weigh more on us than good ones of the same size.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The exercise reveals the automatic thought, the step before emotion in the CBT model. Members often find they believe the insult more readily than the thanks, which hints at underlying self-beliefs.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask who found the praise harder to believe. That question often surfaces low self-worth more honestly than asking about criticism.

ask: Why would someone believe a put-down more than praise from the same neutral person?
Is calling criticism derogatory sometimes a way to avoid hearing a true message?

terms.d: The tendency for negative information to have a stronger effect on thoughts and feelings than equally strong positive information.

339.title: Five steps for taking criticism
339.gist: The steps: hear the message over the tone, stay calm and pick out what is useful, repeat it back and ask questions, thank the person, and make helpful changes. The facilitator labels thinking and action steps with the group.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Separating message from tone is a form of cognitive reappraisal, a strategy Gross's model of emotion regulation links to lower distress than suppressing the reaction.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Thanking a critic who was cruel may feel false. Offer members an honest alternative, such as acknowledging the point without thanks, for cases where thanks would be dishonest.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Douglas Stone and Sheila Heen's work on receiving feedback notes we often reject a message because of who said it. Step 1 asks members to look past the messenger.

ask: When is tone itself the message, for example a threat?
What does repeating the criticism back accomplish that simply nodding does not?

340.title: Modeling: yelled at on day two
340.gist: After Step 5 is discussed, the facilitator models a new employee whose co-worker yells that he was rude to a customer. He calms himself, pulls out the useful point, and works through the steps.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A new job is a common reentry flashpoint, since one blowup can cost the position. Ask members what they would have done before treatment; it makes the stakes concrete.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The model shows the critic delivering a fair point in an unfair way. Members learn they can keep the content while declining to match the anger.

ask: How would the model change if the critic were a supervisor rather than a peer?
What thoughts might make a new employee with a record especially reactive here?

341.title: Setting up criticism role plays
341.gist: Members each name a real case, ideally connected to their substance use risk, then a volunteer picks a co-actor who resembles the real critic. The facilitator helps anyone stuck by asking prompting questions.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Criticism from family about past use is a rich scenario. Coach co-actors to use the exact phrases members hear at home; realism matters more here than in most skills.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Run the same scene twice, once with harsh tone and once calm, using identical words. Ask the actor whether the message felt different.

ask: How much harshness should a co-actor use in practice?
What would you do if a role play brings up a member's real anger at a family member?

342.title: Criticism wrap-up and practice
342.gist: The close asks where the skill applies: facing people who learn about one's record, lowering anger when told one is wrong, and picking up useful advice. Practice work is handed out.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The record example links to stigma research. Labeling theory in criminology suggests that being treated as a criminal can push people toward that identity; a calm response resists the label.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Studies on growth mindset suggest beliefs about whether abilities can change shape how people take feedback, though replication results have been mixed.

ask: How should a member respond when criticism about their record is factually true but used to exclude them?
Can learning to take criticism make someone too compliant with unfair treatment?

terms.d: The idea that being publicly labeled deviant can shape a person's identity and behavior toward that label.

343.title: Session 33 overview: peer pressure
343.gist: The background notes that trouble often comes from following antisocial peers, that avoidance is not always possible, and that many clients will not cut off using friends. The skill extends refusal into ongoing relationships.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Differential association theory (Sutherland) holds that criminal behavior is learned in close groups. In RNR terms, antisocial peers are among the strongest predictors of reoffending.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Admitting that clients will not end these relationships is honest harm reduction. Still, staying close to using friends carries real risk that refusal skills alone may not offset.

ask: When should a counselor push for ending a relationship rather than managing it?
Why might people keep risky friendships even when they see the risk?

terms.d: Sutherland's theory that criminal attitudes and techniques are learned through close relationships.

344.title: Opening: use as a social event
344.gist: Check-in, review of responding to criticism, and homework lead into an observation that for many people substance use happens with family and friends. That social context is what makes refusal so hard.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking about family who use can bring loyalty conflicts. Avoid framing relatives as villains; members will defend them and disengage.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Anthropologists note that sharing drinks or drugs often works as a ritual of belonging. Refusing can read as rejecting the person, which is why the skill needs warmth.

ask: What does a member lose socially by refusing, and how can that loss be replaced?
How would you handle a member whose parent is their main source of drugs?

345.title: Steps for saying no to friends
345.gist: Members review past ways they declined invitations and what worked, then hear why total avoidance is unrealistic. Four steps follow: spot the trouble, recall your goals, think of ways to decline, and tell the person you cannot join.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step 2 is goal priming. Calling long-term goals to mind before acting can tilt choices away from immediate rewards, much as delay discounting research describes.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: People with substance use disorders tend, on average, to discount future rewards more steeply than others. Recalling goals is one tactic for making the future feel closer.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Start with what already worked for members. Building from their successes respects their expertise, an MI principle.

ask: Why might recalling goals help in the moment, and when would it fail?
How does this skill differ from Session 28's refusal steps, and is the overlap useful?

terms.d: The tendency to value an immediate reward more than a larger one that comes later.

346.title: Modeling: a friend brings a bottle
346.gist: After Steps 3 and 4, the facilitator models a friend offering to come over with drinks. The person admits wanting the company but knows the bottle would tempt him.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The model separates two wants: the friend and the drink. Naming both honestly avoids pretending temptation is absent, which relapse prevention warns can leave people unprepared.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to list what they actually want from using with friends: laughter, belonging, relief. Then brainstorm sober ways to get each one.

ask: Why is admitting the desire to drink in the model more effective than showing indifference?
How can someone keep the friendship but lose the bottle?

347.title: Peer-pressure role plays
347.gist: Members describe real situations involving other people where trouble could arise, ideally linked to their substance use risks, and pick realistic co-actors. Observers watch assigned steps.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Group members may know the real people being portrayed. Remind the room of confidentiality and keep the role play about the situation, not gossip.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Practice in a treatment room lacks the intoxicating cues, music, and smells of a real party. Discuss with members how cue intensity will make the real thing harder.

ask: How could cue exposure be built into practice without being unsafe?
What signs show a member is rehearsing a refusal they never plan to use?

348.title: Peer-pressure feedback and wrap-up
348.gist: The four-part feedback protocol is applied, each member performs, and the close asks why it matters to avoid joining others in trouble. Practice work is assigned.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Repetition across sessions of nearly identical refusal skills builds overlearning: practicing past the point of first success so the response holds under stress.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: End with a speed round: you play a series of quick tempting offers, and each member gives a different refusal in under five seconds.

ask: Is overlearning worth the boredom it may cause?
How would you notice that a member's peer group has changed for the better?

terms.d: Continuing practice after a skill is first mastered so it holds up under pressure.

349.title: Session 34 overview: prosocial activity
349.gist: The background says that having few prosocial ties and pastimes raises crime risk, so avoiding risky settings must be matched with joining positive ones. Members used to lowered inhibitions may feel awkward socially sober, and practice reduces that anxiety.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Leisure and recreation is one of the central eight risk factors in Andrews and Bonta's RNR model. Empty time is a known risk, not just boredom.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Behavioral activation, developed for depression, schedules rewarding activities to rebuild positive reinforcement. Recovery often needs new sources of reward to replace what substances provided.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Social anxiety and substance use often occur together, and some people drink to cope socially. Sober exposure to social settings tends to reduce that anxiety over time.

ask: Why is replacing activities as important as avoiding risky ones?
What prosocial activities are realistic for someone on supervision with little money?

terms.d: A therapy approach that increases rewarding, meaningful activities to improve mood and reduce avoidance.

350.title: Opening the positive-activity session
350.gist: Check-in, a review of the peer pressure skill and its consequences if skipped, and homework sharing open the session before the new skill is introduced.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Review questions here ask what happens without the skill. Members often answer from experience; let one story stand as a reminder of why replacement activities matter.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members how they spent the hours they used to spend using. Many will say they have not replaced them, which sets up today's session.

ask: What happens psychologically to someone who quits a substance but fills nothing in its place?
Why might reviewing negative consequences motivate some members and deflate others?

351.title: Barriers and steps to joining in
351.gist: Members name what has stopped them from joining positive activities, then learn four steps: pick an activity, list ways in, choose the best time and route, and show up. The group brainstorms activities, drawing on the Module 3 list.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Three of four steps are planning. Much research on intentions suggests the gap between wanting and doing is closed by specifics: when, where, and how.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Barriers are often practical: transport, money, a record that bars some volunteering. List them honestly so the brainstorm produces options members can actually reach.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sociologist Robert Putnam wrote about the decline of community groups and the social capital they build. Positive activities are also doorways into networks.

ask: Which barriers are internal (shame, awkwardness) and which are structural, and does the skill address both?
How would you help someone whose only past social life revolved around using?

terms.d: The value of social networks, trust, and connections that help people get things done.

352.title: Modeling: volunteering at a soup kitchen
352.gist: The facilitator models hearing a co-worker describe church soup-kitchen volunteering, weighing ways to join, deciding to ask her at the next break, and asking whether the group welcomes newcomers.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Volunteering is associated with better wellbeing in many studies, though healthier people may simply volunteer more. Helping others is also a recurring theme in recovery traditions such as twelve-step service.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A church-based model assumes comfort with faith settings. Offer secular parallels such as a gym, a sports league, or a library program.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name one person they already know who does something positive, and draft the exact question they could ask to join.

ask: Why might asking a known person be easier than walking in cold?
How does helping others change how a person in recovery sees themselves?

353.title: Rehearsing a first step in
353.gist: Members each choose a real chance to join a positive activity, ideally one that replaces a risky routine, and act it out with a co-actor. The facilitator prompts anyone stuck.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This skill has little conflict, so role plays can feel flat. Add realism by having the co-actor ask an awkward question, like why the person was away so long.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Rehearsing the first contact targets anticipatory anxiety. Exposure research suggests that facing a feared situation, even in practice, tends to reduce avoidance.

ask: How should a member answer questions about their past when joining a new group?
What does a successful first visit look like, and what should count as progress?

354.title: Positive-activity feedback and homework
354.gist: The four-part feedback protocol runs for each member, then practice work asks members to actually try the activity before the next group.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to report next week not only whether they went but how it felt before, during, and after. Anticipated discomfort is usually larger than the real thing.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Work on affective forecasting by Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson finds people often overestimate how strongly and how long future events will affect them.

ask: How would you respond if a member's first try went badly?
What makes a new activity stick beyond the first visit?

terms.d: Predicting how you will feel in the future; people often misjudge intensity and duration.

355.title: Session 35 overview: sober celebrations
355.gist: The background notes that milestones like a raise or finishing supervision once invited celebrating with substances. The session teaches new ways to reward achievements without use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Relapse prevention recognizes that positive emotions can be high-risk, not only negative ones. Marlatt's taxonomy of high-risk situations includes pleasant states and celebrations.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Across cultures, toasting is woven into rituals of success. Sober celebration means inventing new rituals, not just skipping the old one.

ask: Why might good days be riskier than bad days for some members?
What rituals could mark a milestone with the same emotional weight as a toast?

356.title: Opening the celebration session
356.gist: Check-in, a review of why a range of positive activities matters and how they grow support networks, and homework sharing open the session.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask whether anyone has had a win since last group. Celebrating a real one in the room models the skill before it is taught.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Linking activities to support networks shows how prosocial behavior compounds: new activities bring new people, who bring more chances for positive reinforcement.

ask: How might the group itself serve as a place to celebrate members' progress?
Why do many people in recovery downplay their successes?

357.title: Three steps to celebrate safely
357.gist: Members consider what makes celebrating hard and how using can turn a great day into a terrible one. Three steps follow: decide whether to celebrate, pick a healthy reward that fits your goals, and reward yourself.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step 2 requires that the reward support the goal. That aligns reinforcement with values, so the celebration strengthens the identity behind the achievement.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to recall their best day ever that ended badly because of use. The contrast makes the risk vivid without lecturing.

ask: What counts as worth celebrating for someone whose wins have been rare?
Why might some people sabotage themselves after success?

358.title: Reward ideas and a probation milestone
358.gist: The group brainstorms healthy rewards such as a movie, a meal out, family time, new clothes, a trip, or a hobby day, and discusses why following through matters. The model shows finishing probation and celebrating by arranging a park day with a son.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-reinforcement is central in Bandura's social cognitive theory: people regulate behavior partly by rewarding themselves when they meet their own standards.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Positive psychology research on savoring suggests that consciously noticing and sharing good events can deepen and extend their emotional benefit.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The model needs a co-parent's permission. Point out that even a celebration can require communication skills from earlier sessions.

ask: Can a costly reward like new clothes become a financial risk for someone just released?
How is celebrating with a child different from celebrating for yourself?

terms.d: Deliberately paying attention to and prolonging enjoyment of positive experiences.

359.title: Celebration role plays
359.gist: After the model, members name real situations to celebrate, choose co-actors, and rehearse while observers watch assigned steps. Familiar guidance on pausing and ending role plays applies.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will struggle to name anything to celebrate. Help them find small milestones, like a month clean or completing this module.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Celebration role plays can turn light and jokey. Keep the link to risk explicit by including a scene where someone offers a drink to celebrate.

ask: How would you build temptation into a celebration role play without derailing it?
What does it say about a member if they cannot name any recent win?

360.title: Close of Module 5 sessions
360.gist: Feedback runs for each role play, then practice work is assigned along with an update to the goal readiness and progress sheet, setting a new short-term goal if the old one is met. This is the final session page of Module 5.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Ending a module with goal review loops back to motivation. Setting a new goal right after success keeps momentum and prevents the drift that often follows a finish line.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to name the Module 5 skill they use most and the one they avoid. The avoided one is usually the most needed.

ask: Looking across Module 5, which skills overlap so much that they could be merged?
What would a fair test of whether Module 5 changed behavior look like?

361.title: Top five high-risk situations
361.gist: A simple form where members list their five riskiest situations, from Session 25. It becomes the source of scenarios for every Module 5 role play.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Identifying personal high-risk situations is the foundation of relapse prevention (Marlatt & Gordon). Skills are only useful if matched to the situations where a person actually slips.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for specific entries: not parties but a cousin's birthday where everyone drinks. Debrief by ranking which situations are avoidable and which must be managed.

ask: How accurately can people predict their own high-risk situations?
Should the list be revisited as members' lives change after release?

362.title: Blank behavior chain form
362.gist: A five-column form tracing situation, thoughts, feelings, behavior, and consequences, from Session 25. Members use it to map how one event led to an outcome.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The chain reflects the CBT premise, rooted in Beck and Ellis, that thoughts mediate between events and actions. Seeing the links shows where a new thought could change the ending.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking members to circle the link they could most easily change. Then rewrite the chain with a new thought and compare consequences.

ask: Do feelings always follow thoughts, or can a strong feeling come first?
How could the chain be misused to blame someone for things outside their control?

363.title: Active listening practice sheet
363.gist: The standard practice form for Session 26: name the skill, write its steps, plan when to use it, then describe the real attempt, rate it, and note what to change. A stray line about support-network information appears on the page.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Planning ahead and reflecting afterward wrap the real attempt in two learning moments. Self-rating builds the habit of self-monitoring.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When debriefing, ask about the moment listening was hardest. A vague rating of good tells you little; a specific moment tells you everything.

ask: How reliable are self-ratings when points are awarded for completion?
What would make a member honest about rating themselves poorly?

364.title: Empathy skill practice sheet
364.gist: Session 27's practice form asks members to plan and then report a real use of understanding others' feelings, rate their step-following, and note improvements.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask whether the member's guess about the other person's emotion turned out right when checked. That single detail shows whether Step 4 happened.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members add one line: what emotion they would have assumed before this skill. The comparison makes growth visible.

ask: How can empathy practice be verified when the other person is not in the room?
What if checking someone's feelings made the situation worse?

365.title: Refusal skill practice sheet
365.gist: Session 28's practice form: members plan a refusal, try it in real life, describe the situation, rate themselves, and note changes.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members will say no situation came up. Treat that as information: either they are avoiding well or not noticing risk. Ask which.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing the planned refusal ahead of time turns an abstract skill into a concrete if-then plan.

ask: Inside a facility, where can refusal really be practiced?
How should a near-miss, where the member almost said yes, be scored?

366.title: Communicating needs practice sheet
366.gist: Session 29's practice form for planning and reviewing a real request using the calm-timing, permission, facts-and-feelings, request, and thanks formula.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what happened when the other person said no, if they did. Handling a refusal well is the real test of the skill.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write their opening sentence word for word before trying it, so the first line is already decided.

ask: How do you separate a poorly delivered request from one refused for reasons beyond the member's control?
What needs are hardest for your members to name?

367.title: What my supporters should know
367.gist: A grid for Session 30 where members list risky situations, thoughts, places, people, and feelings, plus signs they are slipping and how a supporter can help. It is the script for disclosure conversations.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Listing early warning signs for others to watch borrows from relapse prevention and crisis planning: supporters can see drift before the person admits it.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This resembles a Wellness Recovery Action Plan or a psychiatric advance directive, tools where people prepare instructions for helpers while well.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which boxes members would not share with family. That hesitation guides who gets which version.

ask: Who should hold this information, and what if a supporter misuses it?
How specific should the help section be to be useful?

368.title: Seeking support practice sheet
368.gist: Session 30's practice form for planning and reporting a real attempt to ask someone for help or to join one's support network.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask whether the member listened without arguing during Step 4. It is the step most often skipped in real life.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Actually asking someone turns a theoretical support list into a tested one. Each success strengthens the expectation that help is available.

ask: What if the person asked gave poor advice?
How many asks does it take before a support relationship feels real?

369.title: Assertive communication practice sheet
369.gist: Session 31's practice form: plan an assertive statement, use it, describe and rate the attempt, and note what to change.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to write the exact sentence they used. You can then check whether it described behavior and feelings or slipped into blame.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members note their goal from Step 2 and whether the conversation moved them toward it.

ask: How would you coach someone whose assertive attempt was received as aggression?
What setting is the safest place for a first real try?

370.title: Responding to criticism practice sheet
370.gist: Session 32's practice form for planning and reviewing a real moment of receiving criticism calmly and using what was useful.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask what change, if any, they made after the criticism. Step 5 separates real learning from polite listening.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing about criticism afterward gives a cooler second look, often revealing more useful content than seemed present in the heated moment.

ask: How can a member tell whether a criticism was fair after the fact?
Is a calm response with no change still success?

371.title: Avoiding trouble practice sheet
371.gist: Session 33's practice form for planning and reviewing a real refusal to join others in risky activity.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask how the relationship looked after the refusal. Members need evidence that friends can survive a no, or information that they cannot.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Add a line: what goal did you remind yourself of in Step 2? It shows whether the thinking step really happened.

ask: What should a member conclude if every refusal costs them a friend?
How would you score a refusal that worked only because the member left early?

372.title: Positive activity practice sheet
372.gist: Session 34's practice form for planning and reporting an attempt to join a positive activity.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: If members could not attend because of facility limits, ask them to complete the planning steps fully. Planning is part of the skill.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Recording the experience helps members notice reward from the activity, which strengthens the chance of returning.

ask: What counts as getting involved when options inside are limited?
How might you follow up on activities after release?

373.title: Celebration practice sheet
373.gist: Session 35's practice form for planning a healthy reward for a real achievement and reflecting on how it went.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask how the reward felt compared with how celebrating used to feel. Honest answers may reveal a gap that needs more work.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Encourage members to pick a small win this week so the practice actually happens.

ask: Can celebrating too often weaken its reinforcing power?
What is a fitting reward for a member with no money and few freedoms?

374.title: Goal readiness and progress check
374.gist: Members rate, on 1 to 10 scales, how important a short-term goal is and how confident they are, then list steps taken since last session.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Importance and confidence rulers come from motivational interviewing (Miller & Rollnick). Low importance calls for exploring values; low confidence calls for building skills and small wins.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask why the score is not lower. Members then argue for change in their own words, which MI calls change talk.

ask: What would you do with a member who scores 10 on importance and 2 on confidence?
Do these ratings predict follow-through, or mainly mood that day?

terms.d: A person's own statements favoring change, such as desire, ability, reasons, or need.

375.title: Active listening skill cards
375.gist: Cut-out cards repeat the three active listening steps: look at the speaker, focus on the message, and check your understanding. Members carry them as pocket reminders.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pocket cards are external memory aids. Cues present in the real environment can trigger a learned response the way a reminder note would.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Looking at the speaker is treated as universal, but eye contact norms differ by culture and in prison can signal a challenge. Teach flexibility.

ask: Where might a member actually look at a skill card in daily life?
How might you adapt the eye contact step for members from cultures where it signals disrespect?

376.title: Empathy skill cards
376.gist: Pocket cards repeat the five steps for understanding others' feelings, from watching words and body language to asking an open question.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to keep one card where they will see it before a likely tense talk, such as a phone call home. A cue placed at the right moment beats one buried in a folder.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Three of the five steps are internal. The card reminds members that most of empathy happens silently, before anything is said.

ask: Would a shorter card with a single cue word per step be more usable?
Which step on this card is most likely to be skipped under stress?

377.title: Refusal skill cards
377.gist: Cut-out cards list the four refusal steps: judge the risk, think of ways to decline, choose and deliver one, and suggest a safer alternative when it fits.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write their own best refusal line on the back of the card. A personal line is easier to retrieve under pressure.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A card is visible to others. In some settings, carrying a recovery card could invite teasing, so members may prefer to memorize it.

ask: Where could a member safely keep this card?
Which refusal line would you write on the back for your toughest group member?

378.title: Communicating needs skill cards
378.gist: Pocket cards repeat the five steps for stating a need: choose a calm time, ask permission, describe facts and feelings, make a declinable request, and thank the person.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The card encodes a sequence. Chunking a complex social act into ordered steps reduces load on working memory, which stress narrows.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which step members would most like to skip. Usually it is asking permission, which is exactly what keeps the talk from feeling like an ambush.

ask: Why is asking permission so rare in everyday conflict?
Does a card help in a heated moment, or only in preparation?

379.title: Seeking support skill cards
379.gist: Cut-out cards list the five support-seeking steps, from noticing that something is bothering you to working out a plan with the helper.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write the name of one real helper on each card. A named person turns a skill into a phone number.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Step 1 sits first because people cannot seek help for a problem they have not noticed. Self-awareness gates every other step.

ask: What if the person named on the card becomes unavailable?
How often should a member's list of helpers be reviewed?

380.title: Assertive communication skill cards
380.gist: Pocket cards repeat the four assertiveness steps: why conflict might arise, the ultimate goal, options for what to say, and choosing and speaking.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members add the when you do this, I feel that frame to the card so the format is at hand.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Keeping the ultimate goal in view echoes the military idea of commander's intent: when plans fail, people improvise toward the stated purpose.

ask: How does naming a goal change what counts as winning a conflict?
Which members might use this card most, the passive or the aggressive ones?

381.title: Responding to criticism skill cards
381.gist: Cut-out cards list the five steps for taking criticism: hear the message over the tone, stay calm, repeat back, thank the person, and make useful changes.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write one calming phrase on the card for Step 2, something they can say silently when criticized.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Repeating the message back buys a few seconds, which can help the initial surge of anger pass before responding.

ask: Which step do you personally find hardest when you receive feedback?
Is thanking a critic always genuine, or sometimes strategic, and does it matter?

382.title: Avoiding trouble skill cards
382.gist: Pocket cards list the four steps for avoiding trouble with others: recognize the risk, recall your goals, think of ways to decline, and say you cannot take part.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to write their main goal on the card. Step 2 works only if the goal is concrete and personal.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: This card overlaps heavily with the Session 28 refusal card. Help members see the difference: this one is about ongoing relationships.

ask: Do near-identical skills help reinforcement or cause confusion?
What goal would most reliably stop your members in a risky moment?

383.title: Positive activity skill cards
383.gist: Cut-out cards list the four steps for joining a positive activity: pick one, list ways in, choose the best time and approach, and get involved.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members write one specific activity and a date on the back. Specific plans are more likely to happen than general wishes.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The card treats joining as a skill rather than a matter of personality, which counters the belief that some people are just not social.

ask: How might an activity card help during the first weeks after release?
What would make someone keep an activity going after the first try?

384.title: Celebrating a positive event cards
384.gist: Pocket cards repeat the three steps for celebrating: decide whether the event deserves it, pick a healthy treat that fits your goal, then enjoy it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to list three rewards on the card ahead of time, so a milestone does not catch them without a sober plan.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Rituals in many cultures mark transitions: graduations, weddings, rites of passage. A planned sober celebration can serve as a personal rite of passage.

ask: Which milestones in reentry deserve a ritual of their own?
How might a planned reward prevent a spontaneous risky one?

385.title: Module 6 contents: problem solving
385.gist: This divider lists Module 6's five sessions: an introduction, defining problem and goal, brainstorming, planning and trying a solution, and putting it all together.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The module spreads one skill across several sessions, giving each step room for modeling and practice before combining them.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The steps mirror the scientific method: define the question, generate hypotheses, test, and evaluate. Members are learning to run small experiments on their lives.

ask: Why give each problem-solving step its own session rather than teaching all at once?
How does problem solving draw on the social skills from Module 5?

386.title: Why problem solving works
386.gist: The module introduction defines problem solving as a cognitive process for finding effective solutions, built on three steps. It cites D'Zurilla and Nezu, Goldstein, Linehan's DBT, and Thinking for a Change research on recidivism, and frames problems as external barriers, internal barriers, or conflicts.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Problem-solving training appears in many effective cognitive-behavioral programs for justice-involved people. Effects of single components are hard to isolate, since they are usually delivered as part of packages.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: D'Zurilla and Nezu distinguished problem orientation (attitudes toward problems) from problem-solving skills. A person who sees problems as threats may avoid them even with good skills.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Rational step models assume time and calm. In chaotic, low-resource lives, some problems are structural, and good steps cannot fix poverty or discrimination alone.

ask: Which kind of barrier, external, internal, or conflict, dominates your members' lives?
How would you separate poor problem solving from lack of resources?

terms.d: A person's general attitude toward problems, such as seeing them as challenges or threats.

387.title: Module 6 goals and the running problem
387.gist: Members carry one problem through all the in-group sessions and another through the practice work. Goals include group cohesion, trust in the process, learning the three steps, and applying them to personal risky situations.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Using the same problem across sessions shows how each step builds on the last and lets members see a full solution develop.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Help members choose problems with enough weight to stay interesting for five sessions but not so raw that they become crisis work.

ask: What makes a problem good for teaching versus good for therapy?
How might cohesion goals conflict with challenging members' thinking?

388.title: Module 6 worksheet list
388.gist: A list of Module 6 worksheets by session, from the problem solving wheel to the plan evaluation sheet, goal readiness form, and skill card.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note that several worksheets come three per participant. Print extras ahead of time to avoid stalling the session.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Before teaching, complete all the worksheets yourself on a real personal problem. It shows you where members will get stuck.

ask: Which worksheet do you expect members to struggle with most?
How might so many forms affect members with limited literacy?

389.title: Session 36: now versus later problems
389.gist: Problem solving is framed as an advanced skill that offers an alternative to using as a way of coping. The session distinguishes problems needing an instant answer from those allowing time, and teaches ways to convert the first kind into the second.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Dual-process models, popularized by Daniel Kahneman as fast and slow thinking, suggest quick decisions rely on habit. Buying time allows slower, deliberate reasoning to take over.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Neuroscience links stress to reduced prefrontal control. Delaying a decision gives the brain time to recover from an acute stress response.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The now versus later idea is easy to grasp and sticks. Use it as a shared shorthand on the unit for the rest of the program.

ask: Why is converting a now problem into a later one often the most powerful single move?
What problems truly cannot be delayed?

390.title: Introducing the three steps
390.gist: After check-in and a review of the celebration skill, the facilitator writes the three steps: define problem and goal, brainstorm and choose, then plan and try. The first step is introduced as deciding precisely what the problem is.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Defining a problem precisely is often the hardest part. Vague problems like my life is a mess produce vague solutions.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to state a problem in one sentence with no blame and no feelings. Watch how hard it is.

ask: Why do people often skip defining the problem and jump to solutions?
How could the problem definition itself contain a hidden thinking error?

391.title: Brainstorming, planning, and avoidance
391.gist: Steps 2 and 3 are explained: generate many options, weigh pros and cons, choose, then plan and test. Discussion links poor problem solving to substance use, noting that ignoring problems or using to avoid them usually makes things worse.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Using to escape a problem is avoidance coping. It brings short-term relief, which negatively reinforces the habit, while the problem grows.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Avoidant coping is associated with worse outcomes across many mental health and addiction studies, while active problem-focused coping tends to fare better, especially for controllable problems.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Lazarus and Folkman distinguished problem-focused coping from emotion-focused coping. Both have a place; the skill is matching the strategy to whether the problem can be changed.

ask: When is emotion-focused coping wiser than problem solving?
How does negative reinforcement explain why avoidance is so hard to stop?

terms.d: A behavior becomes more likely because it removes something unpleasant, such as stress relief from using.

392.title: Now problems and later problems
392.gist: The facilitator sorts examples on the board: being in a car where people light up or an old dealer recruiting you are now problems; losing a job or a using roommate are later problems. Buying time helps people think, seek help, and avoid rash moves.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to sort their own examples. Some will argue a problem is both, which is a good point: a later problem can contain many now moments.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The sorting builds metacognition, thinking about the type of problem before reacting to it.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Play a round where you read a problem and members shout now or later. Then ask how to move the now ones.

ask: Can a chronic later problem, like a using roommate, generate repeated now crises?
Why might some members treat every problem as a now problem?

terms.d: Awareness of and thinking about your own thinking.

393.title: Buying time: Isiah's party invite
393.gist: The group helps a fictional man, Isiah, whose old trouble-making friend calls with a party invite, find ways to exit the call. Earlier skills such as refusal, self-control, counter-thoughts, and pros and cons become delay tools.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This page knits the curriculum together: social, emotional, and thinking skills become tools for creating time, which problem solving then fills.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Delay works for an invitation but can become chronic avoidance if the later problem is never addressed. Stress the follow-through.

ask: How can a counselor tell healthy delay from avoidance?
Which earlier skill would you teach first if a member could learn only one delay tool?

394.title: Modeling a delay, then members try
394.gist: The model shows Isiah thinking aloud about the risk and replying that he is heading to the store and will text later. Members then each name a real now problem and pick a skill or simple stalling line to delay it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The model uses a small white lie. Discuss with members whether that is acceptable; some will value honesty, others see it as a practical safety tool.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Ethicists debate whether lying is ever justified to protect oneself. Kant held lying always wrong; most other ethical traditions allow some exceptions. The model opens that debate.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Encourage members to collect delay lines that are honest, such as I need to think about it, so they are not forced to invent excuses.

ask: Is a protective white lie a thinking error or a skill?
How could relying on excuses backfire with persistent friends?

395.title: Choosing three real problems
395.gist: Practice work asks members to pick three later problems for the module. Guidelines: no obvious solution, other people must be involved, ideally linked to substance use, and real in current life.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Requiring other people in the problem forces consideration of consequences for others, the perspective taking practiced in Module 5.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Members often choose problems with clear answers, like paperwork. Use the replacement ID example on the page to redirect them toward genuine dilemmas.

ask: What makes a dilemma different from a task?
Why might some members avoid choosing their most serious problems?

396.title: Session 37 background: defining problems
396.gist: The background explains that each problem-solving step gets its own session. Step 1 requires describing the problem objectively, without emotion or opinion, and setting goals that consider others' thoughts and feelings, with three parallel examples running through the module.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Objective definition counters cognitive distortions. Beck's work showed how labels and assumptions can turn a manageable event into a catastrophe.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Goal setting that weighs others' feelings echoes ethics of care, in which moral reasoning begins with relationships rather than abstract rules.

ask: Can a problem ever be described without any emotion, and should it be?
How does weighing others' feelings change what counts as a good goal?

397.title: Session 37 materials and plan
397.gist: Supplies and an eight-part plan: review, introduce Step 1, model it with Isaiah's case, members complete the worksheet on their own problem, summarize, and assign the next two problems as practice.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The plan puts worksheet completion in group. Circulate while members write; the definitions they draft reveal thinking errors you can address in the moment.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Prepare one problem statement of your own written badly, full of opinion, to fix with the group.

ask: Why is in-group completion of the first worksheet important before practice work?
How would you support members who write little?

398.title: Starting Step 1: be objective
398.gist: After a review of now and later problems and the problem solving wheel, the three steps go on the board. The session focuses on defining the problem objectively, meaning dealing with facts without distortion by feelings, biases, or assumptions.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Objectivity here is a practical tool, not a philosophical claim. The aim is to separate what happened from the story told about it.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Philosophers debate whether pure objectivity is possible; Thomas Nagel called it the view from nowhere. In practice, aiming for it still reduces distortion.

ask: Is complete objectivity achievable about one's own problems?
How does the facts-versus-story distinction relate to cognitive restructuring?

399.title: Facts versus opinions sorting game
399.gist: Members learn clue words that signal opinion, such as best, awful, or I think, then sort sticky-note statements into fact and opinion columns and debate each placement.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Evaluative words carry emotion. Spotting them helps members notice when their problem description has slipped from fact into judgment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Add statements from members' world, such as my PO hates me or I got a violation, to make the game relevant.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some statements sit in a gray zone, such as claims about intentions. Use disagreements to show that interpretation is often hidden inside facts.

ask: Why do opinions often feel like facts when we are upset?
What statements in your members' lives are commonly mistaken for facts?

400.title: Getting cut off: objective or not
400.gist: A traffic scenario sorts statements as subjective, like calling the other driver an idiot or saying he wants trouble, or objective, like being cut off or reporting one's own discomfort. Misreading intentions fuels conflict, so slowing down to define problems objectively matters.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Mind reading, assuming you know another's intent, is a classic cognitive distortion. The examples show how quickly it escalates a neutral event.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Calling I feel uncomfortable objective is a subtle point: a report of one's own feeling is a fact about oneself. Make that explicit or members may find it confusing.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members retell a recent conflict using only objective statements, then compare it with how they first told it.

ask: Why is a statement about your own feeling objective, while a statement about someone's intent is not?
How does mind reading connect to the hostile attribution bias seen in aggression?

terms.d: Assuming you know what someone else is thinking or intending, without evidence.

401.title: Goals that hold room for others
401.gist: Session 37 moves from describing the problem to choosing a goal: start with your ideal outcome, weigh what others involved think and feel, then settle on a goal that fits both. Isiah's party invitation becomes the running case.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This mirrors D'Zurilla and Goldfried's social problem-solving model, where 'problem definition and formulation' includes setting realistic goals. Adding others' perspectives builds in perspective-taking, a skill many justice-involved adults never rehearsed because survival rewarded thinking only of self.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Kant's idea of treating people as ends, not just means, sits quietly here: Isiah's goal is not only to stay sober but to stay sober without using his friend as an obstacle to be dodged.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect someone to say considering others is how you get played. Agree that considering is not obeying: you can understand a friend's disappointment and still say no. That distinction lowers defensiveness.

ask: When does weighing others' feelings strengthen a client's recovery, and when does it become people-pleasing that sets up relapse?
How would you tell the difference between a goal that considers everyone and one that simply avoids conflict?

terms.d: The result you would pick if nothing and no one stood in the way; a starting point, not the final goal.

402.title: Writing Isiah's problem and goals
402.gist: The group agrees on Isiah's problem statement and two goals (stay safe, respect the friend), then members write their own objective problem and goals on the worksheet. Facilitators may model with a mild personal problem and must keep goals within members' control.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Bandura's coping model: a facilitator who shows working through a real, modest struggle is more persuasive than a flawless 'mastery' model, because members see the steps used by someone who also finds it hard.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Goals like 'get a new PO' or 'make my ex stop' fail the control test. Reframe them aloud: 'What part of that is yours to move?' The goal shrinks, but it becomes real.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The 'within your control' rule can feel like blaming people for structural barriers. Name that housing or employment limits are real, then locate the slice of action still available.

ask: What boundaries would you set for yourself before modeling a personal problem with this population?
How does Isiah's two-goal structure echo values-based work in ACT or motivational interviewing?

terms.d: A demonstrator who shows effort and small stumbles while using a skill, rather than effortless success.

403.title: Why objectivity comes first
403.gist: Closing Session 37, the facilitator asks what goes wrong without an objective problem and clear goal, then assigns the worksheet for problems 2 and 3. The point: feelings mixed into the definition steer every later choice.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Decision science calls this framing: how a problem is described shapes which options even appear. Tversky and Kahneman showed the same facts framed as losses or gains produce different choices.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to write one problem two ways: 'He disrespected me' versus 'He said X in front of Y.' Have them list options for each. The second version usually produces more and calmer options.

ask: Is a fully objective problem statement possible, or only a less loaded one?
Which earlier CBI-SUA skill (thinking reports, thinking traps) most directly supports this step, and why?

terms.d: The way a situation is worded or viewed, which changes how options and risks are judged.

404.title: Session 38: many roads out
404.gist: The background for Step 2 explains brainstorming: generate many options, good and bad, then weigh consequences to pick the best. It frames single-solution thinking as narrow vision that keeps people stuck.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Brainstorming was popularized by Alex Osborn, who separated generating ideas from judging them. In problem-solving therapy, 'generation of alternatives' is a core step because impulsive people tend to act on the first option that comes to mind.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on group brainstorming is mixed: people working alone and then pooling ideas often produce more ideas than freewheeling groups, partly because members wait their turn and self-censor. Quick silent listing before sharing helps.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Under stress, attention narrows; this is sometimes called tunnel vision. Practicing option generation while calm makes it more available when arousal is high.

ask: Why might people with long histories of trauma or incarceration default to one solution, and is that always irrational?
How would you measure whether brainstorming skill actually transfers outside the group?

terms.d: Seeing only the nearest or most obvious option, missing wider choices and longer-term consequences.

405.title: Check-in and recap of Step 1
405.gist: The standard check-in and review open Session 38: members revisit why goals and objectivity matter, review their practice work, and the three problem-solving steps go on the board as the frame for the day.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Eliciting the review with open questions, instead of lecturing it, follows MI's spirit: people believe what they hear themselves say. Pick a quieter member to state Step 1 first.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Spaced retrieval, recalling material across sessions, strengthens learning more than rereading. The repeated three-step recap is deliberate repetition, not filler.

ask: What would you do if most members skipped the practice work, without turning the review into shaming?
Why might egocentric interpretation be adaptive in some settings members came from?

406.title: Brainstorming Isiah's options
406.gist: The group lists options for Isiah's invitation on a chart with columns for consequences and goal fit, with no idea too crazy at this stage. Only options are listed now; judging comes next.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Welcome the absurd option ('leave town') with a laugh. Humor loosens the group, and silly options often contain a useful seed, such as getting physical distance for a night.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Deferring judgment separates divergent thinking (producing variety) from convergent thinking (choosing). Mixing them too early kills options before they are spoken.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: 'No crazy ideas' can backfire if a member offers something that glamorizes use. Write it down, but flag it gently for the consequences column instead of letting it become a war story.

ask: Which of Isiah's listed options would members privately find most tempting, and why might they not say so?
How does this chart resemble a decisional balance in MI, and where does it differ?

terms.d: Producing many different possible ideas or answers before narrowing down.

407.title: Weighing consequences, circling one
407.gist: After listing options, the group rates each for positive and negative consequences for Isiah and his friend and whether it meets each goal, then circles the best. Members then begin the Brainstorm Options worksheet on their own first problem.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This is a hand-built version of cost-benefit or multi-attribute decision analysis. Even a rough yes/no/maybe grid cuts the pull of the option that simply feels best right now.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for realistic consequences. Members may claim honesty will make the friend furious forever, or that going to the party is harmless. Ask 'What happened last time?' to anchor in their own history.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members rate each option twice: what happens in the next hour and what happens in the next month. The gap between the two is often the whole lesson.

ask: Why does the manual weigh consequences for the friend too, not only for Isiah?
How could present bias (preferring immediate rewards) distort a member's ratings even with the chart?

terms.d: A likely result of an option, which can be positive or negative, short-term or long-term, for you or others.

408.title: Small groups brainstorm each other's problems
408.gist: Members pair or triad up to brainstorm options for each other's real problems without rejecting any, then reconvene to weigh consequences and vote. The person who owns the problem must agree with the chosen option.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Others can see options we cannot because they are not inside our emotional state. Psychologists call the reverse effect Solomon's paradox: people often reason more wisely about others' problems than their own.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Watch for a dominant member pushing their solution. The ownership rule protects autonomy, a core need in self-determination theory, and choices people own are more likely to be acted on.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The manual links this to the Behavior Chain: both trace how a choice ripples into consequences, one looking back at what happened, the other forward at what could.

ask: What risks come with peers brainstorming solutions in a prison unit where social hierarchies are strong?
How would you handle a member whose 'best' option is legal but likely to provoke conflict?

terms.d: The finding that people tend to reason more wisely about others' dilemmas than about their own.

409.title: Large group check and homework
409.gist: The full group tests the small group's choice on one member's problem, voting on the option with best goal fit and least harm, while the owner makes the final call. Practice work extends Step 2 to problems 2 and 3.

deeper.label: In the room
