deeper.text: If the large group lands on a different option than the small group, treat it as a gift, not a correction: it shows that reasonable people weigh consequences differently, and the owner still decides.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Voting can drift into the group deciding for someone. Close by asking the owner to say, in their own words, why they chose it; that self-explanation is what carries outside the room.

ask: What does it teach members when the owner disagrees with the group's vote and keeps their choice?
How would you adapt this step for someone with low literacy who struggles with the chart?

410.title: Session 39: turning a choice into a plan
410.gist: The background for Step 3 explains that members will plan and rehearse their chosen solution, role playing it when others are involved and listing steps when not. Specific plans, scripts and anticipated barriers raise the odds of follow-through.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Gollwitzer's research on implementation intentions, if-then plans tied to a when and where, broadly shows they improve follow-through compared with simply intending a goal, though effects vary by person and task.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Role play is behavioral rehearsal: practicing a response under mild pressure so the words are already available when the real moment arrives with its stress.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Skill levels differ widely. For members who freeze, write the first sentence of the script with them; a ready opener is often all that stands between intention and action.

ask: Why might planning for barriers matter more for people in early recovery than for others?
Where is the line between a helpful script and one that sounds so rehearsed it backfires?

terms.d: An if-then plan specifying when, where and how you will act toward a goal.

411.title: Why a good choice still needs a plan
411.gist: Session 39 opens with check-in and a review of Step 2, then asks why planning matters after the best option has been chosen. It sets up the gap between deciding and doing.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Philosophers call the gap between knowing the better choice and doing it akrasia, weakness of will, a puzzle Aristotle wrestled with. Step 3 is a practical answer: shrink the gap with concrete steps.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name one decision they made in the past that they never acted on, and what got in the way. Those barriers become examples for today's planning.

ask: Is follow-through failure in your clients mostly a skills problem, a motivation problem, or an environment problem?
How does this step relate to stages of change, especially the move from preparation to action?

terms.d: Acting against your own better judgment; knowing the better choice but not doing it.

412.title: Mapping what, when, where, how
412.gist: Isiah's chosen option is to decline the party but offer another way to hang out; the group then plans it using what, when, where and how questions plus barriers and helpers. A sample script models the honest, warm decline.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Offering an alternative activity is a classic refusal-skills move from relapse prevention: it rejects the setting, not the person, protecting the relationship while removing the high-risk situation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask whether a movie or coffee with an actively using friend is truly safe. That question is worth a few minutes: it shows members that a plan can be good and still need its own risk check.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The what-when-where-how frame is the same structure journalists and investigators use; precision turns a vague intention into something you could check off.

ask: What does it mean that Isiah's goals are worded slightly differently here than in Session 37, and does it matter?
When is it right to keep a relationship with a still-using friend, and when is distance the healthier plan?

terms.d: A practiced way to say no to substances or risky invitations, often pairing a clear no with an alternative.

413.title: Barriers, then a modeled rehearsal
413.gist: Isiah's plan names a barrier (the friend may feel judged) and a response, then members draft their own plans on the worksheet, listing barriers and helpers. The facilitator prepares to model the full conversation.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Oettingen's work on mental contrasting suggests that pairing a desired outcome with a clear look at obstacles tends to strengthen commitment more than positive fantasy alone.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The fear of seeming 'better than' old friends is real in reentry. Help members phrase decisions as 'what I need' rather than 'what you're doing wrong'; it lowers the friend's defensiveness and the member's guilt.

ask: Which barriers do members usually miss: other people, their own emotions, or practical logistics?
Who counts as a safe helper for someone whose entire network used substances?

terms.d: Imagining a goal and then the obstacles in the way, which helps people commit and plan.

414.title: Modeling and role playing the plan
414.gist: The facilitator voices Isiah's thinking aloud (pointing to the head), performs the conversation, and asks for feedback. Members then role play their own plans when others are involved, or review steps when not, with observers tracking skill steps.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Pointing to the head while thinking aloud makes invisible cognition visible, a cognitive modeling technique associated with Meichenbaum's self-instruction work. Members see that the plan includes inner talk, not just words spoken.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Let the main actor pick a co-actor who will play the other person realistically, and stop as soon as the last step is done. Long role plays drift into improv and lose the skill.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have the co-actor apply pressure a second time ('Come on, just one hour'). Practicing the second no is where most real conversations are won or lost.

ask: Why might observers assigned to specific steps learn as much as the role player?
What would you do if a role play triggers strong emotion because it mirrors a real relationship?

terms.d: Saying your inner thoughts out loud while doing a task so others can learn the reasoning.

415.title: Closing Step 3 practice
415.gist: The session ends by asking why practicing the third step matters (trying out words, preparing to act) and assigns the planning worksheet for problems 2 and 3, setting up the full review next session.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Athletes and performers use mental and physical rehearsal for the same reason: practiced actions demand less effort under pressure, freeing attention for the unexpected.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before dismissing, ask each member to name the one plan they will actually try this week and when. Saying it in front of peers adds light accountability.

ask: How could you check next session whether anyone actually tried a plan, rather than only completed the worksheet?
What makes practice inside a facility different from the real situation after release?

416.title: Session 40: practice the whole loop
416.gist: The background explains that Session 40 has little new content: the group works real or drawn-from-a-hat problems through all three steps, sorting now problems from later ones. Sample scenarios span jobs, housing, relationships and program demands.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Varied practice, using many different problems, helps a skill generalize better than drilling one example. Mixing housing, work and relationship scenarios trains the method rather than one answer.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The box-of-scenarios option adds energy, but include one or two problems members actually face on the unit, such as commissary theft, so the exercise feels useful and not like a game.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Several sample scenarios (losing housing, rent due) are partly structural. Good facilitation names when a problem needs outside resources, like reentry services, not just better thinking.

ask: Which of the sample scenarios would your members find most and least realistic, and why?
How might the now/later distinction relate to emotion regulation skills taught earlier in the curriculum?

terms.d: A situation demanding an immediate response, where buying time with a quick skill can prevent a rash choice.

417.title: Session 40 materials and outline
417.gist: The materials list and outline for Session 40 add an overview worksheet, a full-steps worksheet, plan evaluation, goal progress tracking and skill cards. The outline moves from review to separating now and later problems to working several examples.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Skill cards are small but powerful: a pocket reminder acts as an external cue when stress wipes out memory. Encourage members to keep it where they will see it, such as with legal papers or a phone case after release.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Evaluating a plan after trying it closes a feedback loop, the same logic as the plan-do-check-act cycle used in quality improvement.

ask: Which of these worksheets would you keep if you could only use one, and why?
How could goal progress tracking link problem solving to the Success Plan members build?

418.title: Recap before the full practice
418.gist: After check-in, the group reviews why planning and practicing the solution matter, shares one plan from homework, rewrites the three steps, and receives the steps overview worksheet.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Letting members choose which homework plan to share respects privacy and increases participation. Thank the sharer specifically for one strong element, such as naming a barrier.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Three-step models stick because they fit easily in working memory; complex procedures under stress often collapse to whatever is simplest to recall.

ask: What would tell you a member truly understands the three steps rather than reciting them?
How might you adapt the review for someone who missed the earlier sessions?

419.title: Now or later, then all three steps
419.gist: Members sort each scenario as now or later. A now problem may be delayed or solved with a social or emotion regulation skill; otherwise the group works all three steps, aiming for at least three scenarios, and the module closes toward the Success Plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Delay is a protective factor: urges and anger typically rise and fall within a short window. Buying time lets the reflective system catch up with the reactive one, a theme across relapse prevention and DBT.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Kahneman's distinction between fast, intuitive thinking and slow, deliberate thinking maps neatly: now problems invite fast thinking, and the delay skill hands the problem to slow thinking.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When a group problem belongs to one member, the group contributes but the member decides each step. Say this rule out loud early to prevent pile-on advice.

ask: Can you think of a now problem where delaying is itself the dangerous choice?
How would you know whether problem solving or emotion regulation is the better first tool for a member?

terms.d: A situation that allows time to work through the steps before acting.

420.title: Why every step counts; evaluate the plan
420.gist: The module wraps up by asking why each step matters, then introduces evaluating a tried solution: note what went well, reward yourself safely, and revise what failed. Homework covers plan evaluation, goal progress and the skill card.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-reinforcement after success (positive self-talk, a safe treat) builds self-efficacy, Bandura's term for belief in one's ability to act. Mastery experiences are its strongest source.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Members with harsh inner critics may skip the 'what went well' part. Ask for at least one success before any revisions, or evaluation turns into self-punishment.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Use a quick three-line review: one thing that worked, one thing to change, one person to tell. It fits on a napkin and builds the habit.

ask: How would you distinguish a bad plan from a good plan that met bad luck?
What role should the counselor play in helping members evaluate plans tried after release?

terms.d: Confidence in your ability to carry out the actions needed to reach a goal.

421.title: Problem Solving Wheel: three risky situations
421.gist: Members see the three problem-solving steps as a wheel and list three substance-related risky situations where they could use them. These become problems 1, 2 and 3 carried through the whole module.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Drawing the steps as a cycle signals that problem solving loops: an evaluated plan that fails sends you back to Step 1 with better information. That echoes relapse prevention's view of setbacks as data.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: When debriefing, check that each situation is specific and real (a person, a place, a feeling) rather than generic ('drugs'). Vague entries make every later worksheet vague too.

ask: What do members' three chosen situations reveal about their personal risk profile?
Why might building the module around the members' own problems help more than using only scripted cases?

422.title: Step 1 worksheet: facts, then fair goals
422.gist: Members set aside their thoughts and feelings to write an objective problem, then list one or two goals that account for everyone's feelings and are good for self and others.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Asking members to notice and set aside feelings first is a form of cognitive defusion: emotions are acknowledged as present but not allowed to write the problem statement.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by reading a problem statement aloud and asking, 'Could a camera have recorded this?' If not, there is opinion in it. Then check each goal against the control test.

ask: What is lost when feelings are set aside, and how might that information be used later in the process?
How would you coach a member whose only goal is revenge to a goal that is good for self and others?

423.title: Step 2 worksheet: options and trade-offs
423.gist: Members carry over their problem and goals, list several options, note positive and negative consequences of each, mark which meet their goals without harm, and circle their choice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Putting pros and cons in writing reduces reliance on memory and mood. A visible grid makes it harder for one vivid consequence, such as immediate relief, to drown out the rest.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which option nearly won and why it lost. Hearing the runner-up teaches more about a member's values than the winner does.

ask: What does it suggest if a member's chosen option has more negatives than positives on the sheet?
How might you add a column for short-term versus long-term consequences without overloading the page?

424.title: Step 3 worksheet: plan, skill, date
424.gist: Members restate their problem, goals and chosen option, then write concrete steps, a social skill that could help, and the date they will carry out the plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Committing to a specific date turns an intention into an appointment with yourself, the same logic as implementation intentions. A plan without a when tends to stay a wish.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking what the very first physical action is, like picking up the phone. If a member can't name it, the plan needs one more step broken down.

ask: Which social skills from Module 5 would most often appear in these plans, and which would be missing?
How would you adjust the worksheet for a member still inside the facility whose options are limited?

425.title: The full problem-solving checklist
425.gist: A one-page overview of the three steps with checkpoints: delay a now problem, state facts, set specific and controllable goals; brainstorm freely and weigh consequences; then plan what, when, how, barriers, helpers and skills.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Checklists are used in aviation and surgery because experts under pressure skip steps. Atul Gawande's work popularized this idea; the same logic applies to someone facing a crisis on release day.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Invite members to mark which checkpoint they most often skip in real life. That self-diagnosis is more useful than reviewing the whole list again.

ask: Which checkpoint on this list do you think predicts success most strongly, and why?
Is the 'does it hurt you or others' test enough of an ethical guide for complex dilemmas?

terms.d: A short list of essential steps used to prevent skipping key actions, especially under stress.

426.title: All three steps on one page
426.gist: Members work a whole problem on a single sheet: problem and goals, up to five options with consequences and goal fit, a three-step plan, and the date they will act.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Moving from separate step worksheets to one integrated page is a fading scaffold: support is gradually reduced so the member can eventually do the whole process mentally.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by timing it: can a member complete this in ten minutes? Speed matters because real problems rarely wait, and fluency shows the skill is becoming automatic.

ask: At what point should members stop needing the paper version of this skill?
How might you test whether the skill has become automatic rather than worksheet-dependent?

terms.d: Temporary support that helps a learner do a task, gradually removed as their skill grows.

427.title: Evaluating my plan after trying it
427.gist: After attempting a plan, members rate how it went, note what worked, choose a safe reward, and identify what to improve and how.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Planned self-reward is a behavioral principle: reinforcing a new behavior soon after it happens makes it more likely to recur. Choosing the reward in advance keeps it safe and substance-free.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking members to explain a disappointing outcome without blaming only themselves or only others. Balanced attribution supports learning and protects against hopelessness.

ask: How would you respond if a member's chosen reward is risky or tied to old using habits?
What separates useful self-evaluation from rumination?

428.title: Goal readiness: importance and confidence
428.gist: Members rate how important their short-term goal feels right now and how confident they are, then list steps taken since the last session.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Importance and confidence ratings come from motivational interviewing (Miller and Rollnick). Low importance calls for exploring values; low confidence calls for building skills and small wins.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask why the rating is not lower, not why it is not higher. The answer pulls out the member's own reasons for change, which MI calls change talk.

ask: What would you do if a member rates importance high but confidence very low week after week?
Why might the rating scale wording (Need Improvement to Excellent) be awkward for importance, and how would you fix it?

terms.d: A person's own statements about desire, ability, reasons or need to change; in MI, it predicts actual change.

429.title: Pocket skill cards: three steps
429.gist: A sheet of cut-out cards repeating the three problem-solving steps, meant to be carried as a quick reminder in real situations.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cards work as environmental cues. When stress narrows thinking, a physical prompt can trigger the practiced routine that memory alone might fail to retrieve.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member where they will keep the card and to touch it once a day for a week. Linking it to a daily habit gives the cue a better chance to work.

ask: Where would a card realistically survive in a prison unit or a reentry setting?
What digital alternatives would serve the same purpose after release?

430.title: Module 7: Success Planning overview
430.gist: The title page lists the seven sessions of Success Planning, from developing a plan and finding sources to handling roadblocks, rehearsing and presenting the final plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is the maintenance phase of the program: earlier modules built skills, and this one organizes them into a personal relapse prevention plan, in line with Marlatt and Gordon's model.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Presenting a plan to peers resembles a rite of passage: a public commitment marks a transition in identity, which can strengthen follow-through.

ask: What would make a success plan feel like the member's own and not a program requirement?
How do the session titles map onto the stages of change, especially maintenance?

431.title: Module goals: from change to maintenance
431.gist: The module description lays out how members will build an individualized Success Plan: map life history and lifestyle factors, high risk situations, behavior chains, coping skills, healthy replacements, supports, warning signs and skill transfer.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is risk-need-responsivity in miniature (Andrews and Bonta): each plan targets the member's own criminogenic needs, like peers, substance use and leisure, rather than a generic list.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Relapse prevention approaches broadly show modest positive effects on substance use outcomes, with stronger effects in some studies on reducing the severity of relapses than on preventing any use at all.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A plan focused heavily on risks can feel like a list of dangers. Good Lives Model critics argue plans should equally build what a person is moving toward, not only what to avoid.

ask: Which of these objectives would be hardest for your members, and why?
How could you blend Good Lives Model ideas into a plan built mostly around risk?

terms.d: A changeable factor linked to offending, such as substance use, antisocial peers or attitudes.
A single slip back into an old behavior, distinct from a full return to the old pattern (relapse).

432.title: Module 7 worksheet map
432.gist: This page lists every worksheet used across Sessions 41 to 47, from the eight-step overview to behavior chains, coping strategies, support people, roadblock planning and feedback forms.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members check which earlier worksheets they still have. Many plans stall because past behavior chains were lost; planning a recovery of missing materials early saves frustration later.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The packet works like a portfolio in education: a collection of past work that shows growth and becomes evidence for a final presentation.

ask: How would you help a member who arrives at Module 7 with few completed past worksheets?
Which worksheet on this list do you expect members to find most meaningful?

433.title: Session 41: building a relapse prevention plan
433.gist: The background frames the Success Plan as a comprehensive relapse prevention plan drawn largely from members' past behavior chains and practice work. It notes the eight-step format came from a Correctional Service of Canada curriculum, adapted for substance use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Personalized plans work better than generic advice because high risk situations differ: for one person it is payday, for another a specific relative. The plan turns the program's lessons into a map of one person's terrain.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Canada's correctional service has long been influential in evidence-based corrections; the RNR model was largely developed by Canadian psychologists.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A plan adapted from a domestic violence curriculum may not fit every substance user perfectly. Watch for steps that feel forced and tailor them to the member's real pattern.

ask: What makes a relapse prevention plan actually used after release instead of filed away?
How would you check that a member's plan reflects their history and not just the worksheet prompts?

434.title: Session 41 materials and outline
434.gist: The materials and outline for Session 41 list the eight-step overview, the plan packet, earlier worksheets from Module 2, and new practice work for Steps 1 and 2: life history factors and high risk situations.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Revisiting Module 2 materials lets members see their own growth: how they described risks early on versus now. That contrast can itself boost motivation.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Before class, pull members' Module 2 worksheets if they are kept on file. Handing someone their own earlier words is a powerful start to this module.

ask: How much has a typical member's understanding of their risk factors changed since Module 2?
What would you do with a member whose earlier worksheet seems more honest than their current one?

435.title: Check-in: defining and managing success
435.gist: Session 41 opens with check-in, a review of success and the danger of getting too comfortable, and practice work sharing. The facilitator then introduces Success Planning as relapse prevention for the behaviors that cause trouble.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Getting too comfortable is a known relapse risk: once things improve, people drop routines that produced the improvement. Marlatt's model notes that seemingly unimportant decisions often precede relapse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the group to define success before offering a definition. Members' answers (freedom, family, respect, a job) show you what their plans should aim toward.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Greek idea of hubris, overconfidence before a fall, captures why managing success needs its own skill.

ask: Why might success itself be a high risk situation for some members?
How would you respond if a member says success means never needing a plan again?

terms.d: Small choices that look harmless but move a person closer to a high risk situation.

436.title: Patterns, not incidents; the eight steps
436.gist: The group lists what a success plan needs, and the facilitator stresses spotting repeating patterns of situations, thoughts, feelings and beliefs, plus support people. The eight-step worksheet is handed out and Step 1, life history and lifestyle factors, is introduced.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Functional analysis, a core behavioral method, looks for what reliably comes before and after a behavior. One bad night is an incident; the same trigger, thought and choice repeating is a pattern worth a plan.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Invite members to find a pattern in someone else's story first (a TV character, a song). It is easier to spot patterns at a distance, then turn the lens on themselves.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Nietzsche wrote of the eternal return: imagine living your life again exactly the same. Seeing one's patterns can be that jolt, a reason to change the script.

ask: How would you separate a true behavioral pattern from a story a member tells to make sense of the past?
Why does the manual put support people into the plan from the very first session?

terms.d: Examining what triggers a behavior and what it achieves, to understand why it keeps happening.

437.title: Past you can't change, life you can
437.gist: Members revisit the difference between life history factors, past experiences like childhood abuse or incarcerated family, and lifestyle factors, current habits like using peers or idle time. Step 2 then asks for the specific triggers behind those lifestyle factors.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This split mirrors static versus dynamic risk factors in corrections research. Static factors explain risk but cannot change; dynamic factors are the targets treatment can move.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Adverse childhood experiences research (Felitti, Anda and colleagues) links early abuse and household dysfunction to later substance problems, which supports naming life history honestly without treating it as destiny.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Listing childhood abuse on a board can open old wounds. Keep it general, offer a pass, and know your facility's process if someone becomes distressed.

ask: How do you hold a member accountable for lifestyle choices while honoring trauma in their life history?
Is 'lacking a meaningful relationship with your children' really history, or partly a lifestyle factor that can change?

terms.d: A fixed factor linked to risk, such as age at first offense, that treatment cannot change.
A changeable factor linked to risk, such as peers or substance use, that treatment can target.

438.title: High risk situations as prompting events
438.gist: The facilitator contrasts broad lifestyle factors with high risk situations, the specific moments just before a risky choice, also called triggers or antecedents. Homework updates Module 2 worksheets and lists as many specific situations as possible.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: 'Prompting event' is DBT language from Linehan's chain analysis. Marlatt and Gordon similarly found that negative emotions, interpersonal conflict and social pressure were among the most common precipitants of relapse.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to describe one trigger with five senses: where, who, time of day, what was heard, what was felt in the body. Specificity turns a vague risk into something recognizable early.

ask: How specific is too specific, so that the plan cannot generalize to new situations?
Which kinds of triggers do members tend to underreport, and why?

terms.d: Whatever comes right before a behavior and helps set it off.

439.title: Session 42: thoughts, feelings, skills
439.gist: The background and outline for Session 42 cover Step 3, mapping thoughts, feelings, actions and consequences in each high risk situation, and Step 4, choosing coping skills. A dice game called Roll a Role adds play to practice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Gamifying practice with dice adds novelty and unpredictability, which keeps attention high and forces members to apply skills flexibly rather than recite one rehearsed answer.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some facilities ban dice; the manual offers paper strips as an alternative. Check rules before the session so the activity is not derailed by security concerns.

ask: What risks come with using game elements in a group where gambling may be part of members' histories?
Why pair the thinking-mapping step with the skills step in the same session?

440.title: Check-in and linking skills to risks
440.gist: After check-in and review of what success planning is for, members share the high risk situations they tied to lifestyle factors. The facilitator frames today as linking learned coping skills to each situation from Step 2.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Recording points for homework is a token economy element. Use it lightly; praise for the content of the work tends to build more lasting motivation than points alone.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Contingency management, rewarding target behaviors with tangible incentives, has strong research support in substance use treatment, especially for stimulant use, though effects can fade after rewards stop.

ask: How does the packet checklist help or hinder members who feel overwhelmed by paperwork?
What would you watch for when a member's high risk situations seem copied from others in the group?

terms.d: A treatment approach that gives tangible rewards for meeting specific behavior goals, like clean drug tests.

441.title: A behavior chain for every risk
441.gist: Step 3 asks members to gather all past behavior chains and complete one for each risky situation from Step 2. A model chain shows conflict with a boss leading to thoughts of needing to unwind, anger, getting high, and a violation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The behavior chain applies Beck's cognitive model: situations do not cause actions directly; thoughts and feelings sit in between and can be changed. The model chain shows the classic coping-by-using belief.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The boss example shows the self-medication idea, linked to Khantzian: substances are used to manage painful emotional states, which is why emotion skills matter so much in relapse prevention.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note the honesty of listing 'temporary relief' as a positive consequence. Admitting the drug works short-term makes the analysis credible to members.

ask: Why might acknowledging the positives of using make relapse prevention more, not less, effective?
How many chains is enough before the exercise becomes repetitive for a member?

terms.d: A step-by-step map from situation to thoughts, feelings, action and consequences.

442.title: Coping by thinking: rewriting the chain
442.gist: Step 4 introduces coping by thinking, replacing risky thoughts with realistic prosocial ones, and coping by doing. The boss conflict chain is rewritten with thoughts about custody goals and riding out the urge, leading to calling a support person.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is cognitive restructuring in action. Notice the new thoughts link to personal values (custody of children), which makes them stronger than general rules like 'drugs are bad.'

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The manual mentions three types of skills but names two; you may notice this inconsistency. Clarify for the group that the session works with coping by thinking and coping by doing.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Replacement thoughts can feel fake if they're too positive. Encourage thoughts members could actually believe in a bad moment, even if modest, like 'I don't have to decide in the next ten minutes.'

ask: What makes a replacement thought believable enough to work under stress?
Why does the new chain still include a negative consequence, and why is that honest?

terms.d: Identifying unhelpful thoughts and replacing them with more accurate or useful ones.

443.title: Thinking skills and Roll a Role
443.gist: A list of coping-by-thinking tools (challenging thoughts, self-talk, urge surfing, calming words, thought stopping, cost-benefit analysis, counter beliefs) leads into Roll a Role, where dice match a skill to a situation. The model shows self-talk around taking an extra pain pill.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Urge surfing comes from Marlatt's mindfulness-based work: cravings tend to rise, peak and pass like a wave. Thought stopping has weaker support; research on thought suppression (Wegner's white bear studies) suggests pushing thoughts away can make them return.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The pain pill scenario is important for opioid-exposed members. Highlight the model's step of calling the doctor: legitimate pain needs real care, not only willpower.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Telling someone a craving 'will pass in 10 minutes' is a useful rough guide, but durations vary. Frame it as 'it will peak and fall' rather than promising an exact time.

ask: Given the suppression research, how would you teach thought stopping, if at all?
How could you handle a member with chronic pain who feels the program dismisses their real need for medication?

terms.d: Noticing a craving and riding it out, like a wave, without acting on it.

444.title: Coping by doing: name it, then use it
444.gist: Members roll dice to practice thinking skills, then shift to coping by doing: choosing motivation, emotion regulation, social or problem-solving skills for each situation. The facilitator should push beyond generic answers and require detail on how a skill will be used.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: 'Go to a meeting' or 'play basketball' are fine, but push: 'Which skill gets you from the urge to the gym?' Matching a specific program skill to a specific moment is the real learning target.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Explaining exactly how a skill will be used is a form of elaborative rehearsal. Deeper processing makes recall more likely than simply naming the skill.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask a member to describe the first ten seconds of using a skill, step by step. If they can't, they haven't learned it yet; they've learned its name.

ask: How would you judge whether a member can actually perform a skill versus only name it?
Which skills from earlier modules do members seem to forget most, and what might that say about how they were taught?

445.title: Matching skills to real situations
445.gist: Using a denied travel pass to see a child as an example, the group names multiple skills for one situation, then pairs list three skills for each of their own five situations. The debrief asks when to use thinking versus doing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Having several coping options for one trigger builds redundancy. If the first strategy fails, a ready second one prevents the 'nothing works, so I might as well use' spiral.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The travel pass example can stir frustration toward supervision. Let members vent briefly, then steer toward what is in their control; that move itself models problem solving.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The Stoics, especially Epictetus, separated what is up to us from what is not. Many members respond well to this ancient frame for supervision constraints.

ask: When is a member's frustration with supervision a valid concern to address instead of a thought to restructure?
How would you know whether a member has truly generalized skills across situations?

446.title: When there's no time to think
446.gist: The session concludes that coping by thinking suits moments with time to reflect, while coping by doing, especially emotion regulation, buys space when there isn't. Homework pairs every behavior chain with a coping strategies worksheet.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Under high arousal, the prefrontal cortex is less able to regulate impulses. Body-based skills like breathing work partly by lowering arousal so that reflective thinking can return.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: This is heavy homework. Ask members to aim for three or four chains well done rather than ten rushed ones; quality makes the final plan usable.

ask: How would you explain the thinking versus doing choice to a member who says they always act before they think?
What support might members need to finish many chains outside group time?

447.title: Session 43: reinventing my life
447.gist: The background for Session 43 targets Step 5: name current life factors too risky to keep and build healthy ones to replace them, with special focus on updating healthy leisure activities.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Removing a behavior without replacing it leaves a vacuum. Behavioral theory suggests new rewarding activities are needed to compete with the reinforcement substances provided.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The community reinforcement approach, developed by Azrin and later Meyers, has good support: building rewarding sober activities, work and relationships reduces substance use more than simply advising abstinence.

ask: Why might leisure be a bigger risk factor than work for many of your members?
What does 'reinventing' a life ask of someone's identity, not just their schedule?

terms.d: A treatment that makes sober life more rewarding through work, relationships and activities.

448.title: Check-in and sharing coping plans
448.gist: After check-in and review of the two coping types, members share full behavior chains with their coping strategies, receive affirmations, and are introduced to Step 5: replacing risky life factors with healthier ones.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Make affirmations specific, as MI recommends: 'You named the exact thought that starts your chain' lands better than 'good job.' Specific affirmations reinforce the skill, not just the effort.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sharing personal chains aloud is a form of public commitment; social psychology suggests public commitments are more likely to be kept than private ones.

ask: How do you keep sharing safe when members disclose risky situations involving people others may know?
What would you do if a member's coping plan relies entirely on avoidance?

449.title: Leisure time: what to keep, fix or drop
449.gist: The focus turns to leisure, time free of duties, with test questions about risk, values, cost and practicality. Members complete a Past Leisure Activities worksheet and sort activities into safe, risky but fixable, and best left alone.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Unstructured time is a recognized criminogenic need in RNR (leisure/recreation). The values question echoes ACT: activities chosen for values tend to be more sustaining than activities chosen only to avoid risk.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The 'risky but fixable' category is gold: fishing without drinking, watching a game at home rather than a bar. It shows members they need not lose everything they enjoyed.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to estimate their free hours in a typical week after release. The number often surprises them and makes leisure planning feel urgent.

ask: What leisure options are realistic for someone just released with little money or transport?
How might boredom itself be a high risk state worth naming in the plan?

terms.d: Time free from duties or obligations that a person can spend as they choose.

450.title: Neglected areas: body, spirit, mind
450.gist: Beyond leisure, the facilitator explores neglected areas like diet, exercise, spiritual development and mental health care, then members update their Healthy Lifestyle Activities worksheet, discuss roadblocks, and set goals with action steps.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Regular exercise has fairly consistent evidence for improving mood and reducing stress; its effect on substance use itself is promising but mixed across studies, so present it as a helpful support, not a cure.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Spirituality can be powerful, but members may have been harmed by religious settings or hold no faith. Keep it optional and broad, including secular meaning and mindfulness.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: This holistic list resembles the Good Lives Model's primary goods, such as health, relatedness, inner peace and spirituality, that everyone pursues in some way.

ask: Which of these areas do your members realistically have access to after release, and which need reentry service links?
How would you sequence lifestyle changes so they don't overwhelm someone in early reentry?

451.title: Why lifestyle shapes situations
451.gist: The session closes on why life factors matter: how you live decides which situations find you. Homework is the Reinventing My Life worksheet, listing risky factors to drop, healthy replacements, and one way to grow support.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Relapse prevention distinguishes immediate triggers from covert antecedents like lifestyle imbalance. Marlatt argued that a life heavy on 'shoulds' and light on 'wants' builds pressure toward indulgence.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Recovery capital, a concept from Granfield and Cloud, describes the personal, social and community resources that sustain recovery. This homework is a small inventory of it.

ask: How would you help a member who sees no healthy activities available in their neighborhood?
What does 'one thing to grow my support' look like for someone estranged from family?

terms.d: The resources, inner and outer, a person can draw on to start and sustain recovery.

452.title: Session 44: supports, warning signs, transfer
452.gist: The background for Session 44 covers the final three Success Plan steps: updating social supports, spotting warning signs and planning a way back, and transferring program skills into daily life. It pulls in worksheets from Modules 3 and 5.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Transfer of training is a known weak point in correctional programs: skills learned in a classroom often don't show up on the street. Planning transfer explicitly is the program's attempt to close that gap.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to bring their Module 3 support lists. Many will find names that no longer fit, which is itself evidence of change worth naming.

ask: What helps skills learned in custody survive the chaos of release week?
Which of these three steps would you expect to be weakest in most members' plans?

terms.d: Using skills learned in one setting, like a class, in real life situations.

453.title: Check-in and the support network
453.gist: After check-in, members review leisure planning and share Step 5 homework. The facilitator introduces Step 6, social supports, asking what matters when building a support network.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Social networks that support abstinence predict better recovery outcomes in many studies; network support approaches that help people add sober contacts have shown promise in trials.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Some members may have no one safe on the outside. Name formal supports too: sponsors, reentry case managers, faith groups, peer specialists. A network can start with one role.

ask: How do you assess whether a family member is a support or a risk when the member insists they're both?
What would you say to a member who says relying on others is weakness?

454.title: Lapse versus relapse; thinking lapses
454.gist: Members update their support list by asking whether each person helps or hinders. Step 7 then defines a lapse as any thought or action starting the path toward use, and relapse as repeated lapses, with examples of thinking lapses like blaming and justifying.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Expanding lapses beyond actual use to thoughts and feelings is a strength: it gives earlier warning signs. Gorski's work on relapse warning signs similarly argued relapse begins long before the first drink.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The thinking lapses resemble the criminal thinking errors Yochelson and Samenow described, such as blaming others and victim stance.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Defining a lapse so broadly risks making every bad thought feel like failure. Frame warning signs as information, not as a grade.

ask: Is 'I just smoke weed' always a thinking lapse, given changing laws and harm reduction views?
How do you help members notice thinking lapses without feeling constantly policed?

terms.d: A return to the old pattern of use or behavior, often after repeated lapses.

455.title: Feeling and behavior lapses; the spiral
455.gist: The facilitator lists feeling lapses (poor stress management, hopelessness, overconfidence) and behavior lapses (old places, using parties), then asks how members can spot their own warning signs and which thoughts after a lapse push toward relapse.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Marlatt called the post-lapse spiral the abstinence violation effect: after a slip, guilt and the belief 'I've blown it' make further use more likely. The page's negative self-talk examples are textbook cases.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on self-compassion, associated with Kristin Neff, suggests treating oneself kindly after failure supports getting back on track better than harsh self-criticism, which counters the common belief that guilt keeps people honest.

ask: Why might overconfidence appear on a list of feeling lapses, and how would members recognize it?
How would you challenge 'treatment didn't work' without dismissing the member's disappointment?

terms.d: The guilt and 'I already failed' thinking after a slip that makes further use more likely.

456.title: Learning from lapses; keeping skills alive
456.gist: Healthy self-talk treats a lapse as a lesson, and the plan is to stop the pattern fast, revisit behavior chains, practice with supports, and reset goals. Step 8 asks how members will keep skills fresh, including through aftercare and accepting corrective feedback.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The manual warns against implying relapse is inevitable. Walk the line: lapses are common and survivable, but not required. Saying 'many people slip, not everyone' keeps hope and realism together.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Engineers study failures through blameless post-mortems: what broke, why, what to change. Reviewing a behavior chain after a lapse is the personal version.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Asking support people for corrective feedback assumes stable, safe relationships. For members with controlling partners, 'feedback' can become surveillance; screen supports carefully.

ask: What would a blameless review of a lapse look like in practice with one of your members?
How do you balance accountability to supervision with honest reporting of lapses in group?

457.title: Equipping supporters to help
457.gist: Members learn to make it easier for supporters to speak up: respond well to criticism and share tools like values cards, a recovery letter, a photo collage, loss and gain lists, and a crisis code word. Then they recall past periods of success and what sustained them.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A letter to oneself, returned in a vulnerable moment, is a precommitment device: a calm self speaks to a future tempted self. Behavioral economists call this a Ulysses contract, after Ulysses binding himself to the mast.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The focus on past success is solution-focused therapy's exception question (de Shazer and Berg): when was the problem absent, and what were you doing then? It often uncovers strengths members forget.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members draft a three-sentence letter to their future self right now: why recovery matters, what a relapse would cost, one thing to do instead. Short beats perfect.

ask: What makes a code word effective in a crisis, and what could make it fail?
Why does the manual emphasize internal change processes over external ones when reviewing past success?

terms.d: A promise made in a calm state to bind your future self against a known temptation.

458.title: Remembering wins; Steps 7 and 8 homework
458.gist: Discussion questions probe what happens when successes are forgotten, which skills will help most, and whether behavior change without thinking change works. Homework completes the roadblocks and skill transfer worksheets and revises earlier steps.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Negativity bias means people recall failures more easily than successes. Deliberately revisiting wins counters this and supports self-efficacy, which predicts persistence.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The last question, changing behavior without changing thinking, touches an old debate between behaviorists and cognitive therapists. CBT's answer is that both influence each other in a loop.

ask: Can lasting behavior change happen without a change in thinking? What examples argue each way?
How might you help a member build a habit of noticing daily small wins after release?

terms.d: The tendency to notice and remember negative events more than positive ones.

459.title: Session 45: a skill for roadblocks
459.gist: The background for Session 45 presents Responding to a Roadblock as a skill with specific steps, taught in the same model-then-role-play format as the Module 5 social skills.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Structured skill training (model, role play, feedback, homework) follows Goldstein's structured learning approach, widely used in correctional programs such as Aggression Replacement Training.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Post the skill steps before members arrive. Visible steps act as a scaffold during role plays and save valuable group time.

ask: Why teach lapse response as a formal skill rather than just a discussion topic?
What limitations does the model-role-play format have for skills that mostly happen inside a person's head?

460.title: Check-in; planning for slips without expecting them
460.gist: After check-in and a review of lapse versus relapse, members share Steps 7 and 8 homework. The facilitator introduces the Responding to a Roadblock skill, stressing it is taught to plan for lapses, not because lapses are inevitable.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Fire drills don't predict fires; they make people safer if one happens. That analogy often helps members accept lapse planning without hearing it as a prophecy.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some abstinence-focused traditions worry that planning for lapses gives permission to use. Research on relapse prevention generally has not found that it increases use, but the framing still matters.

ask: How would you respond to a member who says, 'If you're teaching us what to do after using, you expect us to fail'?
What is the difference between a contingency plan and a self-fulfilling prophecy?

461.title: Three steps to recover from a roadblock
461.gist: The skill steps are: identify the roadblock and why it happened, plan steps to overcome it and add them to the Success Plan (both thinking), then practice the updated plan (action). The model scenario is joining old friends using after a hard day.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The model scenario captures memory fading for consequences: over time, the pain of past use blurs while its pleasures stay vivid. Recovery programs sometimes call this euphoric recall.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The manual advises restarting the model and apologizing if you make an error. That small act models how to handle a mistake without shame, which is exactly the lesson of the skill.

ask: Why might identifying reasons for a roadblock be harder than identifying the roadblock itself?
How does this three-step skill overlap with the problem-solving steps from Module 6?

terms.d: Remembering the good parts of past use while forgetting the harms.

462.title: Modeling the roadblock skill
462.gist: The facilitator models all three steps: naming boredom, stress and forgotten consequences as reasons; updating the plan with workouts, a clear message to old friends and a mirror note; then calling a sister to share it. Members prepare their own role play scenarios.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The model shows that a plan can fail because life changed (overtime) and not because the person failed. Updating the plan rather than blaming the self is the core move.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask the group what the model did not address: the friends showing up at home. Members often spot that housing or who has keys needs a plan too, a nice test of their analysis.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members where they'd post their own reasons for not using. A bathroom mirror works for some; for others it's a phone lock screen. The cue must sit where the eyes go daily.

ask: What does the model's boredom with sober life suggest about Step 5's importance?
How would you adapt the model scenario for a member returning to a shelter rather than a home?

463.title: Role play feedback protocol
463.gist: Members role play the skill with assigned observers watching specific steps, followed by a set feedback order: co-actor, observers, main actor, then facilitator praise. Members are told to finalize Success Plans for presentation and keep practicing the steps.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Ending with positive reinforcement after peer input follows basic learning principles: behavior followed by reward is more likely to repeat. Asking the main actor how likely they are to use it builds commitment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Asking the co-actor first how it felt to receive the skill models empathy and gives the actor realistic feedback about impact, not just technique.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Role plays inside a facility rarely capture the intensity of real cravings. Treat them as necessary but not sufficient practice, and encourage imagined rehearsal with strong emotional detail.

ask: Why might the feedback order matter, and what would change if the facilitator spoke first?
How could you make role plays feel more realistic without retraumatizing members?

464.title: Session 46: work time on the plan
464.gist: The background for Session 46 sets it up as a working session for finishing every Success Plan component before presentations, especially useful in outpatient settings or when members are stuck.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Structured work time levels the field: members with low literacy, unstable housing or chaotic schedules get the same chance to finish as those who can work alone at home.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Circulate with a checklist of the eight steps. Spotting a missing step now prevents a member from failing the final presentation over something fixable.

ask: What supports would help members with low literacy complete a plan this complex?
How would you decide whether a member's plan is complete enough to present?

465.title: Finalize the plan; finished members help
465.gist: After a brief check-in and review of managing roadblocks, members work individually to complete their plans, with those who finish helping others. Completion of the program depends on delivering a comprehensive plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Peers helping peers taps the helper therapy principle (Riessman): people often benefit from helping others, gaining confidence and deepening their own learning.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Tying graduation to the plan is a strong incentive but can push members to write what sounds good. Probe for authenticity, not just completeness.

ask: How can you tell when a plan is written to pass versus written to be used?
What risks come with stronger members helping weaker ones finish their plans?

terms.d: The idea that helping others in recovery also strengthens the helper's own recovery.

466.title: Session 47: presenting the plan
466.gist: The background explains that each member presents their Success Plan in about fifteen minutes, demonstrates at least one coping strategy, and receives rated feedback. Every member must present to complete the program, which may take several sessions.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Narrative identity research (Dan McAdams) and Maruna's work on desistance suggest people who tell a coherent redemption story about themselves are more likely to stay away from crime. A plan presentation can be a first draft of that story.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Public speaking is frightening for many. Offer a short structure (my risks, my skills, my supports, my plan if I slip) so members can focus on content instead of performance anxiety.

ask: How might presenting to peers change a member's commitment compared with turning in a written plan?
What would you do if a member refuses to present because of anxiety?

terms.d: The process of stopping and staying away from offending over time.

467.title: Presentations, feedback and graduated role play
467.gist: Members present respectfully while peers and the facilitator complete feedback forms, judged on detail and realism. Approved plans are shared with supervision officers and community supports, and each presenter role plays coping with at least one high risk situation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Graduated practice means making role plays progressively harder and more realistic, similar to exposure work, so confidence grows in step with challenge.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Sharing plans with supervision officers can build support, but members may then hide real risks to avoid scrutiny. Discuss openly what will be shared and why, to protect honesty.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Prompt peers to give one specific strength and one specific question each. It keeps feedback useful and stops it sliding into vague praise or criticism.

ask: How does knowing a supervision officer will read the plan change what a member is willing to write?
What makes a plan realistic in your judgment, and how would you explain that standard to members?

terms.d: Rehearsing a skill in steps that become more realistic and challenging over time.

468.title: Revise, finish, celebrate
468.gist: After presentations, members revise plans using peer suggestions and the facilitator's feedback form, and those still waiting prepare. In the final session the facilitator acknowledges progress and may hand out certificates.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Rituals of completion matter. Anthropologists describe rites of passage as marking a change in social identity; a certificate can be a tangible symbol of moving from 'offender' toward 'person in recovery.'

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Make encouragement personal: name one specific change you saw in each member across the program. For many members, it may be rare to hear an authority figure describe their growth.

ask: What would make a plan a living document after graduation rather than a finished assignment?
How might you follow up with members after the group ends, within your role's boundaries?

469.title: Eight steps mapped to earlier work
469.gist: A reference table pairs each of the eight Success Plan steps with the worksheets from earlier modules and Module 7 that feed it, from life history factors to transferring skills.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Linking every step to past work shows the program as cumulative: the final plan is not new homework but a synthesis. That framing reduces overwhelm and honors effort already made.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note a small typo: Step 4 lists a Module 8, which does not exist; it should read Module 7. Correct it for members so they aren't hunting for missing pages.

ask: Which steps rely most on earlier modules, and what happens if a member did those modules poorly?
How would you prioritize the steps for a member with only a few weeks left before release?

470.title: Success Plan packet checklist
470.gist: A checklist lets members tick off each required item of the Success Plan packet, from the cover sheet through all eight steps, to track progress toward a complete plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Visible progress tracking motivates through small completions. Each checkmark is a mini mastery experience and makes a large project feel finite.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note that Step 6 here lists only Disclosing Key Information, while the eight-steps sheet also names the support worksheets. Ask members to include their support lists too.

ask: How might this checklist be adapted for members who need extra structure, like those with ADHD or cognitive impairment?
What would you do if a member checks every box but the content is thin?

471.title: Step 1: history, traits, lifestyle
471.gist: Members fill in three areas: life events that shaped their substance use, personal traits like impulsivity, aggression or self-focus, and current lifestyle factors such as peers, free time, work and housing.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The traits section points to antisocial personality pattern, one of the central eight risk factors in Andrews and Bonta's work. Naming traits like impulsivity makes them targets for skills, not fixed labels.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking members to link one trait to one lifestyle factor, such as impulsivity leading to unplanned evenings with old friends. Seeing the connection makes the rest of the plan sharper.

ask: How do you discuss traits like aggression without members feeling permanently labeled?
Which column do members tend to fill most easily, and what does that suggest?

terms.d: Eight major risk factors for offending identified by Andrews and Bonta, including attitudes, peers and substance use.

472.title: Step 2: list every high risk situation
472.gist: A numbered page invites members to list as many high risk situations as they can, up to twenty-three, drawing on their Module 2 worksheet for help.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A long list helps reveal patterns: when twenty situations are written down, clusters such as conflicts, paydays or loneliness tend to emerge, which guides where skills are most needed.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by having members circle their top three and group the rest into themes. Few people need twenty-three separate plans; they need a plan for each theme.

ask: What does it mean if a member can list only three or four situations?
How might you use this list to prioritize which behavior chains to complete first?

473.title: Roll a Role: skill meets situation
473.gist: Members list their top six high risk situations; one die picks a coping-by-thinking skill (counter thoughts, self-talk, behavior chain, cost-benefit analysis, grounding, imagery) and the other picks the situation to practice it in.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Random pairing forces flexible application, a form of interleaved practice that tends to build better transfer than practicing one skill on one situation repeatedly.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note the worksheet lists slightly different skills than the session page (grounding and imagery here). Use the worksheet list during play to avoid confusion.

ask: Which skill-situation pairs are likely to be poor matches, and is that a useful lesson in itself?
How would you adapt this game for a member with limited reading ability?

terms.d: Techniques that bring attention back to the present moment, often using the senses, to reduce overwhelming emotion.

474.title: The full skills toolkit
474.gist: A reference list gathers every skill from the program in two columns: coping by thinking, such as behavior chains, self-talk and restructuring, and coping by doing, such as breathing, social skills and problem-solving steps.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The list resembles a pilot's quick reference handbook: no one memorizes everything, but a well-organized list lets you find the right tool fast.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members to star the five skills they've actually used, not just learned. A short personal list is more likely to be used than this full page.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Some items, like thought stopping, have weaker research support than others, like urge surfing or problem solving. Encourage members to test what works for them rather than treat every item as equal.

ask: Which skills on this list do you think have the strongest evidence, and which the weakest?
How would you help a member choose among so many options without feeling overwhelmed?

475.title: Step 4: coping plan per chain
475.gist: For each behavior chain's risky situation, members list up to five coping-by-thinking strategies and two coping-by-doing skills with their steps, using the Skills List as a reference.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Writing out skill steps, not just skill names, turns abstract knowledge into a procedure. Procedures are easier to execute under stress because they reduce decisions in the moment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking members which strategy they'd try first and which they'd try if that failed. Ordered backups prevent freezing when the first attempt doesn't work.

ask: How many coping strategies is too many for one situation?
Why might a member's past successful strategies be more valuable than skills from the list?

476.title: Blank behavior chain
476.gist: A simple five-box template (situation, thoughts, feelings, behavior, consequences) for members to chart each high risk situation for Step 3 of the Success Plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This simple template reflects the ABC model associated with Ellis: an activating event, beliefs about it, and the consequences that follow. The chain adds feelings and behavior as separate links.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking which link is easiest to change. Members often say behavior, but thoughts are frequently the most accessible lever in the moment.

ask: Why might separating feelings from thoughts be hard for many members?
How would you check whether a member's chain is accurate or a reconstruction that sounds right?

477.title: Past leisure: risky, fixable or drop
477.gist: Members list past fun activities, mark whether each was risky, decide whether a risky one could be made safe, and note changes that would lower its risk.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is harm reduction thinking applied to leisure: keeping the valued core of an activity while removing its risky parts. It reduces the sense of loss that can undermine recovery.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking what made a past activity fun: competition, belonging, excitement. The same need can often be met by a different, safer activity.

ask: What deeper needs (belonging, thrill, status) did members' risky leisure activities meet?
When is modifying an activity enough, and when must it be dropped entirely?

478.title: Healthy lifestyle activity ideas
478.gist: A handout describes five healthy lifestyle areas (diet, exercise, spiritual development, mental health care and meditation) and asks members which they'd like to explore further.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Meditation research shows some benefits for stress and mood, and mindfulness-based relapse prevention (Bowen, Chawla and Marlatt) has shown promise, though claims about brain changes and happiness are sometimes overstated in popular accounts.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Lead a two-minute breath-counting exercise in group before members choose. Trying meditation briefly makes the choice informed rather than abstract.

ask: Which of these areas do you think would most help your specific population, and why?
How would you address skepticism about meditation from members who see it as weak or foreign?

479.title: Step 5: drop, replace, act
479.gist: Members name lifestyle factors to avoid or better manage, then choose up to three healthy activities with concrete action steps to begin each.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavioral activation, used in depression treatment, shows that scheduling rewarding activities can improve mood. Action steps here apply the same idea to recovery.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by checking that each action step is small and dated, such as 'ask my cousin about the boxing gym on Sunday.' Vague steps like 'get healthy' rarely start.

ask: What makes an action step small enough to actually begin?
How would you help a member whose healthy activities all cost money they won't have?

terms.d: Deliberately scheduling rewarding or meaningful activities to improve mood and motivation.

480.title: Ways to equip your supporters
480.gist: A list of practical ways to help support people help you: share values cards, a letter to yourself, a photo collage, a list of losses from past behavior, and a crisis code word.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Note item 4 refers to aggressive or violent behaviors, likely carried over from a different version of the curriculum. Adapt it for members so it fits substance use, such as losses from using.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: These tools externalize motivation: in a crisis, a person may not remember their reasons, but a supporter holding the letter or collage can bring them back.

ask: Which of these tools would your members find most and least comfortable using?
What are the ethical risks of giving support people tools that could be used to pressure or control?

481.title: Step 7: warning signs and way back
481.gist: Members list their personal warning signs that a lapse is coming and write specifically what they'll do to get back on track if a lapse happens.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Personal warning signs work like an early warning system: catching risk during thinking or feeling lapses gives more options than waiting until behavior has already slipped.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking members which warning sign others would notice first. Supporters often see changes, like isolation or irritability, before the person does.

ask: How specific should a 'get back on track' plan be to actually work in a crisis?
Should members share this worksheet with their supporters, and what could go wrong if they do?

482.title: Step 8: keeping skills alive
482.gist: A single open question asks members how they will remember and keep using what they learned in the program after it ends.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Skills decay without use. Booster sessions and aftercare are common in addiction treatment because maintaining change usually requires ongoing practice and reinforcement.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for concrete answers: who, when, where. 'Keep my skill cards in my wallet and review them Sunday nights' is a plan; 'remember what I learned' is a hope.

ask: What does research on habit formation suggest about how long new skills need to be practiced to stick?
How might you build aftercare connections for members released to areas with few services?

483.title: Responding to a Roadblock steps
483.gist: The skill worksheet lists three steps: objectively identify the roadblock and its causes, find steps to overcome it by brainstorming and choosing the best approach and add them to the plan, then practice the updated plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The skill folds in problem solving: being objective, brainstorming and linking options to outcomes. Teaching a lapse response through a familiar method lowers the learning load.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking how this skill differs from simply starting over. The key is updating the plan with what the lapse revealed, not just resolving to try harder.

ask: Why does the first step ask members to leave out feelings and opinions?
How would you help a member who can't identify any reason for their lapse?

484.title: Facilitator feedback form
484.gist: The facilitator's form notes where a member's plan showed detail and realistic expectations, where it is unclear or thin, and which skills to keep practicing, ending with a signed congratulation.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Feedback that starts with strengths, then gives specific areas to improve, follows principles of effective feedback: specific, balanced and focused on behavior rather than character.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Write feedback as you'd want a member to reread it months later. A signed form may be one of the few documents praising them they keep after release.

ask: How specific should feedback be to help without overwhelming a member?
What would you write for a member whose plan still has serious gaps at the end of the program?

485.title: Peer rating of Success Plans
485.gist: Members rate each presented plan on a four-point scale from sketchy to practical and highly detailed, and note strengths and suggested additions; the facilitator decides the final rating.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Peer evaluation develops critical thinking: judging another's plan forces members to apply the standards to their own work as well.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Peer ratings can be skewed by friendship, rivalry or unit politics. That is likely why the facilitator holds the final rating, and why written strengths matter more than the number.

ask: How would you train members to give useful peer feedback rather than automatic high scores?
What does a rubric like this reveal about what the program values most in a plan?

486.title: Roadblock skill cards
486.gist: Cut-out cards repeat the three Responding to a Roadblock steps, labeled as thinking or action, for members to carry as a quick reminder.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Labeling steps as thinking or action reinforces that recovery after a slip starts in the head before it shows in behavior, a core CBT message.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to keep this card alongside their problem-solving card. Together they form a two-card emergency kit: one for solving problems, one for recovering after a slip.

ask: Why might carrying a card for lapses feel stigmatizing to some members, and how would you address that?
Which moment after a lapse is the card most likely to be useful?

487.title: Risky situation scoring sheet
487.gist: An appended scoring sheet totals a 50-item risky situation inventory into five categories: negative emotional or physical states, interpersonal conflict, social pressures, positive emotional states and cognition, each as a percentage of the maximum.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: These categories echo Marlatt and Gordon's taxonomy of relapse precipitants, which found negative emotions, conflict and social pressure common, along with positive emotions people often overlook.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Converting to percentages lets you compare categories with different numbers of items. Share the top category with the member as a starting point for which skills to prioritize in their plan.

ask: Why might positive emotional states be a high risk category, and do your members recognize it?
How reliable is self-reported risk data in a correctional setting where members may want to look good?

terms.d: A situation or state that commonly comes right before a return to use.

488.title: Risk category summary chart
488.gist: The summary chart for the scoring sheet shows the five high risk categories side by side, so a member's highest-risk area stands out at a glance.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Visual profiles help members who struggle with numbers. Point to the tallest bar and ask, 'Does this match what you know about yourself?' Disagreement is useful discussion.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: A chart can look more precise than the data behind it. Treat it as a conversation starter, not a diagnosis.

ask: How would you combine this chart with behavior chains to build a fuller risk picture?
What could cause a member's chart to misrepresent their real risks?

489.title: Naming what blocks engagement
