489.gist: Spanish version of the Pre-treatment, Session 1 obstacles sheet. Members list inner and outer barriers to treatment, then rank them, turning vague resistance into a ranked list the group can actually work on.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Start with each member's number-one obstacle and ask what would shrink it by a single notch. Resentment about being mandated often lands first; treat it as honest data rather than defiance, since arguing with it tends to harden it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Splitting barriers into internal and external reflects attribution: people tend to blame circumstances. Neither column is wrong, but only the internal one is fully within the member's reach.

ask: Which listed obstacles are really about the program or the institution, and would you act on them?
How would you tell a practical barrier from a face-saving one?

490.title: How use has paid and cost
490.gist: Spanish version of Pre-treatment Session 1, Worksheet 2. Members rate, from strongly negative to strongly positive, how substance use has touched relationships, basic needs, family, school, work and hobbies.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The positive half of the scale is the clever part. Motivational interviewing (Miller & Rollnick) holds that admitting what use gave someone makes the costs believable; a scale with only negatives invites cynical answers.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief a plus rating first. Asking what a substance did for someone opens the door to finding a safer way to get the same need met.

ask: What does a member gain by rating everything at zero, and how would you respond?
Could a positive rating ever be accurate, and what would that mean for the treatment goal?

491.title: The impact scale, second pass
491.gist: Spanish version of Pre-treatment Session 2, Worksheet 3a: the same impact scale as Session 1, now used as the opening of a longer life-areas inventory that feeds the reasons-for-change work. Re-rating the same items lets members and facilitator see whether views shift once the group settles.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Repeating identical items a session apart can show movement, but a shift may reflect growing trust in the facilitator rather than changed views. Read the change as information about the relationship as much as about the person.

ask: If a member's ratings turn more negative this week, is that progress, honesty, or pressure to please?

492.title: Freedom, money, safety, self-worth
492.gist: Spanish version of Worksheet 3b, items 8 to 16. The inventory widens to happiness, freedom, dependents, spiritual health, money, financial duties, safety, friendships and self-regard.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: These domains look a lot like the human goods in Tony Ward's Good Lives Model, which argues that offending is often a harmful route to ordinary goals such as autonomy, connection and competence. The sheet lets you see which goods use was serving.

ask: Which item here is most likely to be rated positive in prison, and why?
How might money and safety pull in opposite directions for someone in the drug trade?

terms.d: A strengths-based rehabilitation framework proposing people pursue universal human goods; treatment helps them reach those goods without harm.

493.title: Independence, principles, children, health
493.gist: Spanish version of Worksheet 3c, the last four items: self-reliance, living by one's principles, relationships with children, and physical health. It closes the inventory before members turn ratings into reasons for change.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask each member to circle their single most negative and single most positive item across all twenty, then say which one they would repair first. The pair often reveals the real motivational lever faster than the totals.

ask: Why might living by principles score worse than physical health for many members?

494.title: Turning reasons into personal goals
494.gist: Spanish version of Pre-treatment Session 2, Worksheet 4. Members list benefits of changing their current lifestyle and attach a personal goal to each, drawing on the substance-use impact ratings.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Reasons written in a member's own words count as change talk. Self-perception theory (Bem) suggests people partly learn their attitudes by hearing what they say, so voiced reasons weigh more than ones a counselor supplies.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Push for reasons that matter to the member, not to the parole board. A reason that would still hold with nobody watching is the one to build a goal on.

ask: How can you tell a genuine reason from one written for the file?
What happens to motivation when the goal belongs to the court rather than the person?

terms.d: Statements in which a person voices desire, ability, reasons, need or commitment to change; in MI, more of it predicts change.

495.title: Importance and confidence rulers
495.gist: Spanish version of Pre-treatment Session 2, Worksheet 5. Members rate on 1 to 10 how important finishing the program is and how confident they feel, then explain why they did not score lower.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is the classic motivational interviewing ruler. Asking why not lower draws out reasons for change; asking why not higher would draw out reasons to stay stuck, so the sheet deliberately asks only the first.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Importance and confidence are separable. Someone can care deeply and still doubt they can do it, and the two call for different work: building reasons versus building skills and small wins.

ask: What would you do differently with high importance plus low confidence versus the reverse?
Is a rating of 1 ever safe to probe with the why-not-lower question?

terms.d: A 0-10 or 1-10 scale used in MI to gauge importance or confidence and to elicit the person's own reasons for change.

498.title: Goal, steps, and the behavior's ledger
498.gist: Spanish version of Pre-treatment Session 3, Worksheet 7. Members name a personal goal and three steps, pick the specific behavior to change, and weigh its short- and long-term pros and cons.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The short-term versus long-term split targets delay discounting: rewards that arrive now feel far bigger than costs that arrive later. Research consistently links steep discounting with addiction, so making the future visible on paper is the point.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Expect the short-term pros box to fill fastest. Let it; the honest list of what the behavior gives is what the long-term column must beat.

ask: Which long-term costs feel abstract to members, and how could you make one vivid?

terms.d: The tendency to value a reward less the longer one must wait for it; steeper in many people with substance use problems.

499.title: The group agreement, signed
499.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 1, Worksheet 1. Members write why attending matters to them, review the group norms such as punctuality, respect, confidentiality and arriving sober, add their own, and sign.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Signing a written, semi-public commitment taps the pull toward consistency described in persuasion research (Cialdini). The personal reason at the top matters more than the signature: it ties the rules to the member's own goal.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Inside a facility, a signed form can feel like another disciplinary document. Let members add a rule of their own first so the sheet reads as a group pact, not a write-up.

ask: Which norm on this list is hardest to enforce fairly in a prison unit?
What does a member's added rule tell you about past group experiences?

500.title: Getting to know the member
500.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 1, Worksheet 2. Members describe a typical week, who they spend time with, who matters, what those people think of the program, past reasons for criminal behavior, and importance and confidence ratings.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Quietly, this is a criminogenic-needs scan. Andrews and Bonta's risk-need-responsivity model flags associates, family, leisure and attitudes as dynamic risk areas, and nearly every question here touches one of them.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Remind members they can skip identifying details. Answers about who they spend time with will be guarded early; revisit them once trust exists rather than pushing now.

ask: Which answers here would change your read of a member's risk level?
How do you balance getting useful information with not making the first session feel like an intake interrogation?

terms.d: Changeable factors linked to reoffending, such as antisocial attitudes and peers, substance use, and lack of prosocial leisure.

501.title: How sure am I about the rules
501.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 1, Worksheet 3a. Members rate, rule by rule, how confident they are they can arrive on time, show respect, participate, complete practice and stay open-minded.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Bandura's self-efficacy is task-specific: someone can be confident about punctuality and shaky about open-mindedness. Rating each rule separately locates the weak spot instead of producing one vague commitment.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A low score is a gift, not defiance. Ask what would move it up one point and you have the first problem-solving exercise of the program.

ask: Why might members inflate these ratings, and how would you lower the stakes of honesty?

502.title: Confidentiality, sobriety, extra rules
502.gist: Spanish version of Worksheet 3b. The confidence ratings continue for keeping peers' information private and attending sober, with space for any additional expectations the group agrees on.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Confidentiality in a correctional group has real limits: mandated reporting, staff access, and peers who share housing units. Promising more privacy than you can guarantee damages trust later, so name the limits plainly when members rate this item.

ask: What are the exact limits of confidentiality in your setting, and could members state them back to you?

503.title: Four truths about cravings
503.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 2, Worksheet 4. It normalizes cravings as common, expected, time-limited and a sign of change, then offers distraction options and a step-by-step progressive muscle relaxation script.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Cravings are partly conditioned responses to cues; they rise, peak and fade if not fed. Teaching that they pass undermines the belief that using is the only way to end one.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Progressive muscle relaxation, developed by Edmund Jacobson, reliably lowers felt tension for many people. Its effect on relapse itself is less clear, so frame it as a way to ride out a moment, not a cure.

ask: Is calling a craving a sign of progress always true, or could it ever mislead a member?
Which distraction options here are actually available on a housing unit?

terms.d: Tensing then releasing muscle groups in sequence to notice and reduce physical tension.

504.title: Daily urge log
504.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 2, Worksheet 5. Members log each urge between sessions, the coping technique they used, and the urge's intensity before and after, then note which strategies worked best.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Self-monitoring changes behavior on its own; simply recording an urge inserts a pause between impulse and action. The before-and-after ratings also give members their own evidence that coping works.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Debrief by asking for the urge that dropped the most and what was done. Members trust a peer's numbers more than a facilitator's claims.

ask: How would you handle a member whose after-ratings never drop?
What does a blank log tell you, beyond non-compliance?

505.title: Choosing ten values
505.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 3, Worksheet 6. Members circle ten personal values from a long list spanning relationships, environment, emotions and learning, adding their own where needed.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (Hayes) treats values as directions you travel rather than goals you finish. Being a good father is never done; it is chosen again each day, which makes it useful after a setback.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: After circling ten, have members cross out five, then two more. The forced cuts reveal what really ranks highest.

ask: Which values on this list might members circle because they sound right rather than because they guide them?

terms.d: Freely chosen life directions that give meaning to behavior; unlike goals, they cannot be completed.

506.title: When use collides with values
506.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 3, Worksheet 7. Members pick a problem behavior tied to substance use, list five top values, and write how use both helps and harms each one.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This builds discrepancy, a core MI move, and leans on cognitive dissonance (Festinger): seeing behavior clash with a cherished value creates discomfort people want to resolve.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Dissonance can be resolved by excuses as easily as by change. If shame floods in, members may defend the behavior harder, so keep the tone curious rather than prosecutorial.

ask: How do you tell productive discomfort from shame that shuts a member down?

terms.d: Tension felt when actions conflict with beliefs or values, prompting a change in one or the other.

509.title: One goal, three steps
509.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 4, Worksheet 9. Members set a personal goal grounded in their values sheet and break it into at least three concrete steps.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Implementation intentions, studied by Peter Gollwitzer, turn steps into when-where-how plans (if it is 7 pm in the dayroom, then I will...). Studies broadly find they raise follow-through compared with good intentions alone.

ask: Could you rewrite one member's step as an if-then plan, and does it get more doable?

terms.d: A plan linking a specific situation to a specific action: if X happens, I will do Y.

510.title: A goal you can reach by graduation
510.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 5, Worksheet 10. Members set a short-term substance-free goal achievable by program end, then answer questions about obstacles, stakes, benefits, strengths, helpers and a next step.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Gabriele Oettingen's research on mental contrasting suggests pairing a desired future with honest thought about obstacles works better than positive fantasy alone. The obstacles question at the top is doing that work.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Watch for goals the member cannot control, like getting early release. Steer toward goals about their own actions.

ask: Which of the six questions do members tend to skip, and what does that suggest?

terms.d: Imagining a wished-for outcome and then the obstacles in the way, which tends to strengthen commitment to feasible goals.

511.title: Feelings chart, first look
511.gist: Spanish version of the feelings chart used in Module 1, Session 6. It lists dozens of emotion words grouped under happy, sad, angry and other, giving members vocabulary beyond fine and mad.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on affect labeling (Lieberman and colleagues) suggests that putting a feeling into words can dampen its intensity, and work on emotional granularity (Feldman Barrett) links finer distinctions to better regulation. Findings are promising, not definitive.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Spanish emotion words vary by country; a word that is neutral for one member may be loaded for another. Let members offer their own regional terms.

ask: Why might angry be the most-used column in a prison group, even when it is not the most accurate?

terms.d: The ability to tell similar emotions apart precisely, such as frustrated versus humiliated.

512.title: The iceberg model
512.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 6, Worksheet 12a. A bilingual diagram places visible behavior above the waterline and feelings, body signs, thoughts, and attitudes and beliefs below it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The layers echo Beck's cognitive model, where surface automatic thoughts rest on deeper beliefs. Behavior is only the tip people see, which is why consequences alone rarely change it.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: The metaphor suggests influence flows only upward. In reality behavior also reshapes beliefs: acting differently is one of the strongest ways to change how you think.

ask: How would you explain to members that changing behavior can melt the iceberg from the top?

513.title: Filling in your own iceberg
513.gist: Spanish version of Module 1, Session 6, Worksheet 12b. Members pick a behavior with unwanted consequences and fill each layer: the behavior, feelings, body sensations, thoughts and beliefs underneath.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Start below the waterline with body signs; members find them easier and less exposing than feelings. A tight jaw or racing heart is a safe doorway into what was going on emotionally.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The beliefs layer is the hardest. Prompt with completions such as people like me always..., which surfaces core beliefs without jargon.

ask: Which layer do members most often leave blank, and what might that protect?

514.title: The behavior chain
514.gist: Spanish version of the behavior chain worksheet from Module 2, Session 7. Five linked boxes trace a situation through thoughts, feelings and behavior to consequences, the core analytic tool of the whole curriculum.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is CBT functional analysis in plain clothes, close kin to Ellis's ABC model. Its promise is practical: every link is a place to intervene, so members are never stuck with only the last step.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Have members fill the consequences box first. Working backward from a result they dislike feels less accusatory than starting with what they did.

ask: Which link of the chain do you think members can change most quickly, and which most durably?
Where does the chain oversimplify real decisions?

terms.d: Mapping the triggers and payoffs that surround a behavior to understand what keeps it going.

515.title: Life history versus lifestyle
515.gist: Spanish version of Module 2, Session 8, Worksheet 2. Members list life history factors, things that happened to them, and lifestyle factors, how they spend time and with whom, that shaped their substance use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The split mirrors static and dynamic risk factors in the RNR literature. History cannot be undone; lifestyle can. Naming both validates the past while putting attention where change is possible.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Trauma will surface in the history column. Acknowledge it without excavating it in group, and know your referral route for individual support.

ask: How do you keep history from becoming an excuse without dismissing it?

terms.d: Static factors are fixed history, such as age at first arrest; dynamic factors can change, such as peers or employment.

516.title: How risk hides in a party
516.gist: Spanish version of Module 2, Session 8, Worksheet 3a. A party vignette stacks several triggers at once, then explains that the questionnaire will measure both how risky each situation is and how often it occurs.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: High-risk situations are central to Marlatt and Gordon's 1985 relapse prevention model. The sheet adds frequency, a smart refinement: a hard situation once a year matters less than a moderate one every weekend.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which moment in the vignette would hit each member first. Some will name the offer, others the jealousy; that split previews the scoring categories.

ask: Why might emotional triggers in the vignette be more dangerous than the drugs themselves?

517.title: Facilitator notes on risk categories
517.gist: Spanish version of the facilitator page for Module 2, Session 8. It explains how to plot members' questionnaire results, define the five risk categories, point out individual differences, and link the findings to the later Success Plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The categories trace back to Marlatt's relapse taxonomy, which grouped relapse episodes into intrapersonal ones such as negative and positive emotional states and interpersonal ones such as conflict and social pressure.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Plotting differences publicly normalizes them. A member who scores low on social pressure but high on negative moods learns that relapse prevention cannot be one-size-fits-all.

ask: How would you present a member's high score without it sounding like a diagnosis?
What risk does a group chart pose to privacy?

518.title: High-risk questionnaire, items 1 to 18
518.gist: Spanish version of Worksheet 4a. Members rate situations such as feeling unhappy, angry or lonely, seeing alcohol ads, or having a great day, both for how risky each is and how often it happens.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The two-axis rating resembles risk assessment everywhere, from engineering to public health: likelihood times impact. Teaching members that framework gives them a portable way to judge any situation.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Situational inventories built on Marlatt's categories, such as those developed by Helen Annis, have long been used to tailor relapse prevention, with reasonable support for their usefulness.

ask: What would you infer from a member who rates almost everything zero?

519.title: Questionnaire continues, items 19 to 37
519.gist: Spanish version of Worksheet 4b, continuing the dual ratings of risk and frequency across further emotional, social and cognitive situations. Members keep separating how dangerous a situation is from how often they meet it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Long questionnaires breed autopilot answers. Pause midway and ask one member to read an item that surprised them; it re-engages the group and catches careless scoring.

ask: Which kind of situation do you expect members to underrate, and why?

520.title: Questionnaire ends, items 38 to 50
520.gist: Spanish version of Worksheet 4c, finishing the list. Scores then feed a sheet that converts each category into a percentage so members can see their dominant risk areas.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Several items capture permission-giving thoughts, the cognitive category. Beck's addiction work describes how thoughts like just this once can license use, often more than the craving itself.

ask: Are thoughts better treated as triggers or as part of the response to a trigger?

terms.d: A thought that licenses use, such as I deserve it or one won't hurt.

521.title: Four specific risky situations
521.gist: Spanish version of Module 2, Session 8, Worksheet 5. Members write four high-risk situations that led to trouble, sticking to facts and the moment right before the decision.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Specificity is the whole skill. Weekends is a category; payday Friday walking past the corner store with an old friend is a situation you can plan for. Model the difference live.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have a member describe a situation as if narrating security camera footage: no feelings, no excuses, only what a camera would record.

ask: Why does the instruction stop at the moment before the decision rather than including it?

522.title: Risky thoughts, replacement thoughts
522.gist: Spanish version of Module 2, Session 9, Worksheet 6. Members recall a situation with bad consequences, list five risky thoughts from it, and write a replacement thought for each.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This is cognitive restructuring. A good replacement is believable and specific, not a cheerful slogan; it should still sound true to the member at the worst moment.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Some studies suggest generic positive self-statements can backfire for people with low self-esteem, because they clash with what the person believes. Realistic, action-oriented replacements are a safer bet.

ask: What makes a replacement thought credible to someone who has heard every program slogan?

terms.d: Identifying unhelpful thoughts and testing or replacing them with more accurate, useful ones.

524.title: Behavior chain, Session 10
524.gist: Spanish version of the behavior chain as used in Module 2, Session 10, now applied after members have learned to catch and replace risky thoughts. Members map a fresh incident so the new thought skills have a specific link to target.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Run a chain on a success: a time a member was in a risky situation and did not use. Mapping what went right shows which links they already know how to break.

ask: What can a success chain teach that a failure chain cannot?

526.title: My history of quitting
526.gist: Spanish version of Module 3, Session 11, Worksheet 1. Members chart past periods of stopping: when, why they quit, what helped, how long it lasted, and what led to the return to use.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Past sobriety is evidence of capability, a strengths-based starting point. The last column brings in Marlatt's abstinence violation effect: viewing a slip as total failure often turns a lapse into a full relapse.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Many members will say they never stopped. Ask about forced breaks, including time inside, and what got them through.

ask: Does time sober while incarcerated count as a success story, and what does it leave untested?

terms.d: Guilt and loss of control after a slip that make continued use more likely, described by Marlatt.

527.title: Behavior chain, Session 11
527.gist: Spanish version of the behavior chain used in Module 3, Session 11, alongside the success story work. Here it helps dissect how a past period of sobriety came to an end.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Use the chain on the moment a sober period ended. Seeing the exact sequence that closed a good stretch makes relapse feel predictable rather than random.

ask: What patterns would you expect across members' end-of-sobriety chains?

530.title: Who is in my life
530.gist: Spanish version of Module 3, Session 13, Worksheet 4. Members privately list family, friends and acquaintances, using initials or nicknames if they prefer.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The privacy note matters. In prison culture, naming people can feel like snitching; initials protect both the member and the person named, which makes honest mapping possible.

ask: How would you keep a member's private list useful without asking them to share it?

531.title: Relationships measured against goals
531.gist: Spanish version of Module 3, Session 13, Worksheet 5. Members take their key people and rate what they like about each, how risky the person is, why, and whether they help with goals.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: In the risk-need-responsivity research of Andrews and Bonta, antisocial associates sit among the strongest predictors of reoffending. The sheet makes that abstract finding personal.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Asking someone to cut off everyone risky can leave them isolated, which is its own risk. Frame it as adjusting distance and contact, not ending every bond.

ask: How do you respond when the riskiest person is also the most loved, such as a parent?

532.title: What good support looks like
532.gist: Spanish version of Module 3, Session 14, Worksheet 6. It lists traits of helpful supporters, such as being available, honest and able to spot warning signs, and of unhelpful ones who encourage risky thinking or are unreliable.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Sociologists Granfield and Cloud call these resources recovery capital: the relationships and supports that make sustained recovery more likely. Supportive people are one of its main forms.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The list includes supervision officers. Expect pushback; invite members to judge the officer by the traits listed rather than by role.

ask: Which listed trait is hardest to find in someone leaving prison, and where might it come from?

terms.d: The personal, social and community resources a person can draw on to start and sustain recovery.

533.title: Rating possible supporters
533.gist: Spanish version of Module 3, Session 14, Worksheet 7. Members name six potential supporters and tick which helpful traits each has, such as honesty, reliability and recognizing trouble.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A grid makes gaps visible. Usually no single person ticks every box, which teaches that support works as a team: one person for honesty, another for availability.

ask: What would you suggest to a member whose grid is nearly empty?

534.title: Healthy lifestyle options
534.gist: Spanish version of Module 3, Session 15, Worksheet 8. It describes healthy activities such as balanced eating, exercise and spiritual development, linking each to mood and craving management.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Exercise reliably improves mood for many people; as an add-on in substance use treatment the evidence is encouraging but mixed. Present it as one helpful tool, not a guarantee.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: In custody, diet and schedules are largely set by the institution. Help members adapt the ideas to what is possible now and plan the rest for release.

ask: How would you discuss diet with people who cannot choose their meals?

535.title: Four activities to try
535.gist: Spanish version of Module 3, Session 15, Worksheet 9. Members choose four new activities for the coming month and record why, an action step, and a supporter to do it with.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The community reinforcement approach argues that substance-free life must become rewarding enough to compete with use. New activities with supportive people are how that competition is built.

ask: Why pair each activity with a person rather than doing it alone?

536.title: Goal check-in, Module 3
536.gist: Spanish version of Module 3, Session 15, Worksheet 10. Members re-rate the importance of and confidence in their short-term goal and list steps taken since last session.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The same check-in reappears later in the program. Keep each member's forms together; a trajectory of ratings says more than any single score, and members enjoy seeing their own line rise.

ask: If importance stays high but confidence drops, what does that tell you to work on next?

537.title: Three steps to regulate emotion
537.gist: Spanish version of Module 4, Session 16, Worksheet 1. It teaches emotion regulation as noticing body reactions and body language, naming the emotion with the feelings chart, and managing it with skills.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: In James Gross's process model, regulation can act early (choosing or changing situations) or late (changing the response). This sheet starts at the body because noticing physical cues is often the earliest warning a person gets.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members scan from head to feet and name where anger lands first for them. The answers differ, which personalizes the warning system.

ask: Why does naming come before managing, and what happens if a member skips it?

terms.d: Sensing internal body states such as heartbeat, breathing and muscle tension.

538.title: Feelings chart, second pass
538.gist: Spanish version of the feelings chart reused in Module 4, Session 16, now supporting the step of naming emotions precisely. Members use it to pick the most exact word for what they felt in a chain.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Use the chart to hunt for what sits under anger. Hurt, embarrassment and fear often hide behind it, especially where showing vulnerability feels dangerous.

ask: Which emotions does prison culture make unsafe to show, and how does that change regulation inside versus after release?

539.title: Behavior chain, Session 16
539.gist: Spanish version of the behavior chain used in Module 4, Session 16, where the focus shifts to the feelings link of the chain. Members trace an incident with special attention to the emotion that drove the action.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Feelings are the bridge between thought and action. Slowing down at that link, by noticing and naming, buys the seconds that skills need to work.

ask: Is it more practical to change the thought that produced a feeling or the response to the feeling?

540.title: My feelings and how they show
540.gist: Spanish version of Module 4, Session 16, Worksheet 4 practice. Members identify three feelings tied to substance use and describe the physical reactions and body language that accompany each.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The body-language column asks how others read you. Peers and officers react to signals members are not aware of sending, so feedback from the group here can be eye-opening.

ask: How could a member use others' reactions as an early warning about their own emotional state?

541.title: Skill practice: recognizing feelings
541.gist: Spanish version of Module 4, Session 17, Worksheet 5. A practice form: members write the skill's steps, plan when to use it, then later describe the situation, rate how well they followed the steps, and note what to change.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: This structure follows social learning theory (Bandura): learn steps, rehearse, try in real life, get feedback. The plan-when line matters most, since unplanned practice rarely happens.

ask: What counts as real-world practice on a housing unit, and how would you verify it without policing?

543.title: Calming skills menu
543.gist: Spanish version of Module 4, Session 19, Worksheet 7. It sets out step-by-step instructions for deep breathing, counting backward, pleasant imagery and taking a pause.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Slow breathing tends to shift the body toward a calmer state and is well supported for short-term arousal. Counting backward by threes works partly by occupying working memory, leaving less room for rumination.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Practice in the room, not just on paper. A skill rehearsed while calm is far more likely to show up when stressed.

ask: Which of these skills could a member use unnoticed in a tense dayroom?

544.title: Testing two calming skills
544.gist: Spanish version of Module 4, Session 19, Worksheet 8. Members practice at least two calming strategies and rate whether they followed the steps, how useful each was, and how likely they are to reuse it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The likelihood-of-reuse rating is the honest one. The best skill is the one a person will actually use, so these ratings should drive which skills enter the final Success Plan.

ask: What would you do if a member rates every skill as useless?

545.title: Urge surfing and grounding
545.gist: Spanish version of Module 4, Session 20, Worksheet 9. It teaches urge surfing, picturing a craving as a wave that rises and falls, plus mental, physical and soothing grounding techniques.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Urge surfing comes from Marlatt's work and later mindfulness-based relapse prevention: you observe the urge without obeying it. Grounding, popularized in Lisa Najavits's Seeking Safety, anchors attention in the present when emotion floods.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Treating an urge as a passing event echoes Stoic and Buddhist ideas: impressions arise, but assent is a choice.

ask: Why might observing an urge be harder than distracting from it, and when is each better?

terms.d: Mindfully watching a craving rise, peak and pass without acting on it.
Techniques that reconnect attention to the present through senses, body or soothing self-talk.

546.title: Practice: coping with urges
546.gist: Spanish version of Module 4, Session 20, Worksheet 10. Members picture a high-risk situation, choose urge surfing or a grounding skill, practice it, and rate its usefulness and their likelihood of using it again.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: A brief imagined cue in session lets members try the skill with a mild urge present. Keep it gentle and end with grounding so nobody leaves activated.

ask: What are the risks of rehearsing with craving cues in a group, and how would you manage them?

547.title: Skill practice: self-control
547.gist: Spanish version of Module 4, Session 21, Worksheet 11. The standard practice form, applied to self-control: steps, a plan for when to practice, then a self-rating and reflection afterward.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: The popular idea that willpower is a fuel tank that runs out (ego depletion) failed major replication attempts. Treating self-control as a skill built by practice and planning, as this form does, stands on firmer ground.

ask: How might telling members willpower is limited become a self-fulfilling excuse?

549.title: Daily stress checklist
549.gist: Spanish version of Module 4, Session 23, Worksheet 13. Members tick daily stressors from the past month, including arguments, unsafe neighborhoods, money problems, unstable housing and health issues, and add their own.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Many items, such as housing and money, are structural. Coping skills help a person endure them but do not fix them, so pair this sheet with practical reentry planning and referrals.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Stress is a well-documented relapse trigger. Small daily hassles can wear people down as much as big events because they pile up.

ask: Which of these stressors can a counselor influence directly, and which need case management?

558.title: High-risk situations, revisited
558.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 25, Worksheet 1. Members write five specific high-risk situations, using their Module 2 results and the five risk categories, to set up the social skills module.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask which of the five involve another person. Most will, which is the bridge into the social skills work: if people are in the situation, people skills are part of the exit.

ask: How have members' situations changed since Module 2, and what does the change say?

559.title: Behavior chain, Session 25
559.gist: Spanish version of the behavior chain used in Module 5, Session 25, now looking at situations shaped by other people. Members map an incident where another person's actions formed part of the trigger.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: In interpersonal chains, the other person's actions are part of the situation, not a link the member controls. Focusing on one's own thoughts and responses keeps the analysis useful rather than blaming.

ask: How do you keep a chain about conflict from turning into a list of what the other person did wrong?

566.title: Practice form: assertive talk
566.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 31, Worksheet 9. The standard skill practice form for assertive communication: list the steps, plan when to use it, then rate and reflect after a real attempt.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Across CBT studies, completing between-session practice is broadly associated with better outcomes, though cause and effect are hard to untangle. The when-and-how line raises the odds practice happens at all.

ask: What makes a member actually attempt a new skill with a real person rather than only in role-play?

567.title: Practice form: taking criticism
567.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 32, Worksheet 10. The practice form applied to responding to criticism, with planning beforehand and a self-rating afterward.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Self-ratings are often off in both directions. Ask the member what a witness would have rated them; the gap between the two is a good conversation.

ask: How could you calibrate members' self-ratings without undermining their confidence?

568.title: Practice form: avoiding trouble
568.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 33, Worksheet 11. The practice form for staying out of trouble with others: steps, a plan, then a description of the real attempt and a self-rating.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The final question, what would I do differently, mirrors the after-action review used by the military and emergency teams: what was planned, what happened, why, and what to change next time.

ask: Why might the what-would-I-change question be more valuable than the rating itself?

570.title: Practice form: celebrating safely
570.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 35, Worksheet 13. The practice form applied to celebrating a positive event, with planning beforehand and a self-rating afterward.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Ask members how they used to celebrate. Good news was often the trigger, so planning a celebration is as protective as planning for a bad day.

ask: What healthy rewards are realistic in custody, and how would that list change after release?

571.title: Goal check-in, Module 5
571.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 35, Worksheet 14. Members again rate the importance of and confidence in their short-term goal and list recent steps.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Revising a goal is not failing it. If ratings have stalled, the goal may be too big or no longer relevant, and rewriting it is a legitimate problem-solving step.

ask: How do you tell a member who needs a revised goal from one avoiding a hard one?

572.title: Skill cards: active listening
572.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 26, Worksheet 15a. Pocket cards repeat the listening steps: watch the speaker, focus on their words, and check you understood, each tagged as a thinking or action step.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Tagging each step as thinking or action is a CBI signature: it shows that skills are partly invisible mental moves. Listening echoes Carl Rogers, who saw accurate understanding as central to helping.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Watching the speaker can read as a challenge in some settings. Discuss what attentive looks like without a hard stare.

ask: Why make a pocket card for a skill as basic as listening?

573.title: Skill cards: others' feelings
573.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 27, Worksheet 15b. Cards list steps for understanding someone else's feelings: read words and body language, guess the emotion, stay calm and open, check the guess, and ask an open question.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Psychologists distinguish cognitive empathy, knowing what someone feels, from affective empathy, feeling with them. These steps train the first, which can be taught and is useful even when warmth is not yet there.

ask: Could cognitive empathy alone be misused, for example in manipulation, and how would you address that?

terms.d: Accurately understanding another person's thoughts and feelings, as distinct from sharing them.

574.title: Skill cards: saying no
574.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 28, Worksheet 15c. Cards break refusal into steps: decide if the situation is risky, think of ways to decline, pick and deliver the best one, and suggest a safe alternative.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Role-play with the real pressure lines members hear, in their own slang, not polite textbook offers. A refusal practiced against weak pressure collapses against strong pressure.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Offering an alternative saves face for both sides, which matters where reputation is on the line.

ask: Why might suggesting another activity work better than a flat no with old friends?

575.title: Skill cards: stating my needs
575.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 29, Worksheet 15d. Cards outline asking for what you need: pick a calm time and place, ask permission to talk, describe facts and feelings, make a request the other can decline, and say thanks.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: The structure resembles DEAR MAN from Marsha Linehan's DBT: describe, express, assert, reinforce. Allowing the other person to say no separates a request from a demand.

ask: Why is accepting a possible no the hardest step for many members?

576.title: Skill cards: seeking help
576.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 30, Worksheet 15e. Cards set out help-seeking: name what bothers you, choose who can best help, share thoughts and feelings, listen openly to their view, and ask for help solving it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: For many men, asking for help clashes with ideas of toughness. Reframe it as strategy: experts consult others, and choosing the right advisor is a skill.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Research on help-seeking consistently finds that stigma and masculinity norms lower willingness to seek support.

ask: Who in a correctional setting is safe to ask for help, and who is not?

577.title: Skill cards: assertive communication
577.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 31, Worksheet 15f. Cards guide assertive speech: spot why a situation could turn into conflict, decide your end goal, think of what would serve it, then choose and say it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Assertiveness sits between passive and aggressive. Putting the goal before the words is the key move: once a person knows what they want from the exchange, winning the argument stops being the point.

ask: How does deciding the end goal first change what someone says in a confrontation?

578.title: Skill cards: handling criticism
578.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 32, Worksheet 15g. Cards break down responding to criticism: hear the message over the tone, stay calm and sort what is useful, repeat it back, thank the person, and make helpful changes.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Kenneth Dodge's research on hostile attribution bias shows some people read ambiguous actions as hostile, which fuels aggression. Listening for content over tone directly counters that tendency.

ask: How would you teach members to thank someone whose criticism felt unfair?

terms.d: Tendency to interpret others' ambiguous behavior as having hostile intent.

579.title: Skill cards: avoiding trouble
579.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 33, Worksheet 15h. Cards outline steering clear of trouble: notice the risky situation, recall your goals, think of ways to decline, and tell the person you will not take part.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Recalling goals in the moment is a form of precommitment, like Ulysses having himself tied to the mast to pass the Sirens. The decision is made early, when thinking is clear.

ask: What is the modern equivalent of tying yourself to the mast for someone leaving prison?

580.title: Skill cards: positive activities
580.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 34, Worksheet 15i. Cards guide joining positive activities: pick one, think of ways to take part, decide the best time and way, then do it.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Behavioral activation treats action as a route to mood rather than waiting to feel motivated. Three of the four steps are planning, because removing friction ahead of time is what makes the fourth step happen.

ask: Why might motivation follow action rather than precede it?

581.title: Skill cards: celebrating wins
581.gist: Spanish version of Module 5, Session 35, Worksheet 15j. Cards outline marking a positive event: decide if it deserves celebrating, choose a healthy reward that supports your goal, and reward yourself.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Positive emotional states are one of Marlatt's relapse categories. Good news without a plan can slide into the old way of celebrating, so a chosen reward protects as well as encourages.

ask: What is the difference between a reward that supports a goal and one that only feels good?

582.title: Problems worth solving
582.gist: Spanish version of Module 6, Session 36, Worksheet 1 (the footer misprints the module). Members list three substance-related risky situations where the problem-solving steps could help.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Problem-solving training traces to D'Zurilla and Goldfried's 1971 work and later Nezu's problem-solving therapy, which treat solving problems as a learnable sequence rather than a talent.

ask: What makes a problem good for practice: small and winnable, or big and meaningful?

terms.d: A structured approach teaching people to define problems, generate options, choose, act and evaluate.

584.title: Brainstorm and weigh options
584.gist: Spanish version of Module 6, Session 38, Worksheet 3. Members carry over their problem and goal, brainstorm options, list positive and negative consequences of each, check which reach the goal without harm, and circle a choice.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Brainstorming works best when judging is postponed; criticism during idea generation shrinks the list. The harm check then brings in ethics: a solution that hurts others fails even if it works.

ask: Why should members list options they know they will reject?

585.title: Planning and trying the solution
585.gist: Spanish version of Module 6, Session 39, Worksheet 4. Members restate the problem and chosen option, write steps to carry it out, name a social skill they could use, and set a date to try it.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The social skill line ties Module 5 into Module 6. Ask which card from the skill deck the plan needs; most real solutions involve talking to someone.

ask: Why does setting a specific date change follow-through so much?

586.title: Problem-solving at a glance
586.gist: Spanish version of Module 6, Session 40, Worksheet 5. A summary of the three steps: define the problem and goal, brainstorm and choose, plan and try, with tips such as turning a now problem into a later one.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Turning a now problem into a later one means cooling down before deciding. Metcalfe and Mischel described a hot, emotional system and a cool, reflective one; solving problems happens best in the cool one.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The goal tests, such as whether it hurts anyone and whether it is in your control, are worth memorizing as a quick filter.

ask: How would you help a member create a pause when a problem arrives in the middle of a confrontation?

587.title: Full problem-solving worksheet
587.gist: Spanish version of Module 6, Session 40, Worksheet 6. All three steps on one page: define problem and goals, brainstorm with consequences and goal checks, then plan steps and set a date.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Have members trade sheets and add one option to a peer's brainstorm. Using all resources includes other minds, and outsiders often see options the stuck person cannot.

ask: When does input from peers improve a plan, and when might it pull a member back toward old solutions?

588.title: Evaluating my plan
588.gist: Spanish version of Module 6, Session 40, Worksheet 7. After trying their solution, members rate themselves, note what went well, how to reward themselves, what needs work, and how to improve the plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Evaluation closes the loop. Members learn to judge the process, not just the outcome: a good plan can fail by bad luck, and a poor plan can succeed by chance.

ask: How would you respond to a member whose plan worked but who broke a rule to carry it out?

589.title: Goal check-in, Module 6
589.gist: Spanish version of Module 6, Session 40, Worksheet 8. Members again rate the importance of and confidence in their short-term goal and record steps taken.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Lay out a member's earlier check-ins beside this one and sketch the confidence line together. A visible trend makes progress, or a stall, concrete.

ask: What would explain confidence rising while importance falls?

590.title: Skill cards: problem solving
590.gist: Spanish version of Module 6, Session 40, Worksheet 9. Pocket cards repeat the three problem-solving steps for use outside the group.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Under stress, complex procedures collapse. Three short steps that have been rehearsed many times are more likely to be recalled when it counts, which is why the cards strip the method to its bones.

ask: Where would a member realistically keep and use these cards?

591.title: The eight-step Success Plan map
591.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 41, Worksheet 1. It lists the eight steps of the Success Plan, from life factors and high-risk situations through coping, lifestyle change, support, roadblocks and skill transfer, with the earlier worksheets each step draws on.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The Success Plan is a personalized relapse prevention plan in the Marlatt tradition, assembled from the whole curriculum. Linking each step to earlier worksheets shows members they already did most of the work.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Present it as an assembly job, not new homework; that framing reduces overwhelm.

ask: Which step do you predict members will find hardest, and why?

592.title: Success Plan checklist
592.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 41, Worksheet 2. A checklist of every Success Plan component, from cover page to skill transfer, to tick off in order.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Checklists cut errors in complex work, a lesson popularized by Atul Gawande's writing on surgery and aviation. Here the checklist also gives visible progress, a small motivating win with each tick.

ask: How could you use this checklist to spot a member who is quietly falling behind?

593.title: Step 1: my life factors
593.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 41, Worksheet 3. Members record life history events and lifestyle factors behind their use, plus traits such as impulsivity, aggression or putting themselves first.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: The trait boxes echo what the RNR literature calls an antisocial personality pattern. Framing these as habits of response rather than fixed identity keeps them open to change.

ask: How do you help a member own a trait like impulsivity without it becoming who they think they are?

594.title: Step 2: every risky situation
594.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 41, Worksheet 4. Members list as many high-risk situations as they can, up to twenty-three, drawing on their Module 2 work.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Quantity first, then prioritize. A long list surfaces the less obvious situations; afterward, ask members to star the three most likely to happen in their first month out.

ask: Why might the first month after release deserve its own risk list?

595.title: Roll the dice and act
595.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 42, Worksheet 5. A game: one die picks a thinking-based coping skill, the other picks a situation, and the member applies that skill on the spot.

deeper.label: Evidence
deeper.text: Learning research by Robert Bjork and others shows that varied, mixed practice feels harder but transfers better than drilling one skill in one context. Random pairings force members to adapt skills to new situations.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: The game format lowers the stakes of trying, which helps quieter members participate.

ask: Which random pairings are most likely to expose a skill a member has only memorized?

terms.d: Practicing a skill across changing conditions, which tends to improve flexible use later.

596.title: Master list of skills
596.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 42, Worksheet 6. It lists every skill from the program, sorted into coping by thinking, such as behavior chains and cost-benefit analysis, and coping by doing, such as breathing, exercise and social skills.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to circle the three skills they would bet on in a crisis. A plan built on a few mastered tools beats one listing twenty half-learned ones.

ask: Is the thinking versus doing split always clean, or do some skills belong to both?

597.title: Step 4: coping for each chain
597.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 42, Worksheet 7. For each behavior chain in the Success Plan, members choose thinking-based and action-based coping strategies, using the skills list.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Matching skill to link is the design logic: a risky thought calls for a thinking skill, a surge of feeling may call for breathing or a break, and a risky place calls for leaving.

ask: How would you check that a member's chosen strategies actually fit the links in their chain?

598.title: Behavior chain, final round
598.gist: Spanish version of the behavior chain as used in Module 7, Session 42, feeding the Success Plan. Members map the chains whose exit points become coping strategies in Step 4.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Put a member's first chain from Module 2 beside this one. Comparing the detail, honesty and number of exit points shows growth that members rarely notice on their own.

ask: What signs of growth would you look for between a first and final chain?

599.title: Old fun, made safer
599.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 43, Worksheet 9. Members list activities they used to enjoy, judge whether each is risky, and write changes that could make a risky one safe.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Activities come bundled with people, places and times. Changing one element, such as the crew, the venue or the hour, can keep the enjoyment while dropping the risk.

ask: When is modifying an old activity realistic, and when is it a setup?

600.title: Healthy lifestyle options, revisited
600.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 43, Worksheet 10. It repeats healthy lifestyle examples such as diet, exercise and spiritual development as members plan Step 5.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: This version mentions a school cafeteria, a sign the text was adapted from a youth edition. Small mismatches like that can quietly tell adult members the material was not written for them, so adjust the examples aloud.

ask: What other wording in shared curricula might signal to members that it was not made for them?

601.title: Step 5: reinventing my life
601.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 43, Worksheet 11. Members name current life factors too risky to keep and three healthy activities they will try, each with action steps.

deeper.label: Connection
deeper.text: Shadd Maruna's desistance research in Making Good found that people who leave crime often build a new life story, a redemption narrative, rather than simply stopping behaviors. Reinvention is identity work, not just a schedule change.

ask: How could you help a member tell the story of who they are becoming, not just what they will avoid?

terms.d: The process by which people stop offending and sustain that change over time.

602.title: Step 6: sharing what matters
602.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 44, Worksheet 12. Ideas for letting supporters help: give them your values cards, write a letter to yourself, make a collage, list what was lost, and choose a crisis keyword.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: A letter written while clear-headed and handed to a supporter is a precommitment device: your calm self speaking to your future stressed self. One item mentions aggressive behavior, suggesting the list was borrowed from an anger-focused edition.

ask: What would make a crisis keyword actually work in the moment?

603.title: Step 7: warning signs and lapse plan
603.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 44, Worksheet 13. Members list warning signs that relapse is near and write exactly what they will do to get back on track if it happens.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Planning for a lapse is not giving permission; it counters the abstinence violation effect. A slip with a plan is a stumble, while a slip without one can feel like proof that change was never possible.

ask: How do you discuss a relapse plan without members hearing that relapse is expected?

604.title: Step 8: taking skills outside
604.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 44, Worksheet 14. Members plan how they will remember and keep using program skills in real life.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Transfer is the weak point of many correctional programs: skills learned inside fade without practice and support after release. Aftercare, booster sessions and a named person to practice with strengthen this step.

deeper.label: Try this
deeper.text: Ask members to name the first day, place and person where they expect to use one skill after release.

ask: What would aftercare need to include for this plan to survive the first month out?

605.title: Responding to a roadblock
605.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 45, Worksheet 15. It gives three steps for setbacks: identify the roadblock and its causes objectively, find steps to overcome it and add them to the Success Plan, then practice the updated plan.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: Setting feelings aside to describe the roadblock objectively applies the problem-solving module to the plan itself. The plan becomes a living document, revised rather than abandoned when reality pushes back.

ask: What roadblocks do you expect most often in the first weeks after release?

606.title: Facilitator feedback on the plan
606.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 47, Worksheet 16. The facilitator notes where the plan was detailed and realistic, where it was vague, and what to keep working on, then signs off.

deeper.label: In the room
deeper.text: Make feedback specific: name the exact section and what makes it strong or thin. Specific praise teaches; general praise only pleases.

ask: How would you give honest feedback on a weak plan in a way that still motivates?

607.title: Peers rate each Success Plan
607.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 47, Worksheet 17. Members score each presented plan on a four-point scale from incomplete to practical and detailed; facilitators set the final rating.

deeper.label: Critique
deeper.text: Peer ratings build ownership and attention, but can drift into popularity votes. Anchoring each score to the written descriptions, and keeping the facilitator's final say, limits that drift.

ask: What do members learn from rating others that they might not learn from presenting their own plan?

608.title: Skill cards: roadblocks
608.gist: Spanish version of Module 7, Session 45, Worksheet 18. Pocket cards repeat the three roadblock steps, two thinking and one action, for use after the program.

deeper.label: The idea underneath
deeper.text: These are the last cards in the deck and the only ones about the plan itself. Ending on how to repair a plan, rather than on a perfect plan, signals that setbacks are part of the design.

ask: Which earlier skill card pairs best with this one in a real setback?

609.title: Appendix: worksheet index (A to C)
609.gist: Spanish appendix listing the program's worksheets alphabetically with module, session and worksheet numbers. Useful for finding where a form first appears.

610.title: Appendix: worksheet index (continued)
610.gist: Continuation of the Spanish worksheet index, including the practice forms with their module and session references.

611.title: Appendix: worksheet index (end)
611.gist: Final page of the Spanish worksheet index, covering the Success Plan step worksheets and remaining forms.
